en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chángqìng Zōngbǎo, Compiled by His Dharma Heir, Huánshì.
The carving of the *Huashou Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Huashou) has been completed.
The Venerable Master specially dispatched a messenger to command Huánshì to compose this preface. Huánshì respectfully [accepts this command].
He prostrated himself twice with his head to the ground and said: "How could I possibly be worthy to praise the Master?
Nevertheless, I have heard it said that no one knows a disciple better than his teacher. For six or seven years, I have personally received your instruction and guidance;

the extent to which I have been refined and nurtured by you, Master, whether through your raising of an eyebrow or a blink of an eye, or even when you did not raise an eyebrow or blink an eye—how could I express it?"
Since it is so grand, one must assume that its reception was necessarily profound;
thus, he intended for me to personally encounter and witness this, so as to demonstrate it to the world and posterity—this is something I, Shì, dare not decline.
I recall that in the year Jiǎxū, when I first learned of this matter, I traveled throughout the land; at that time, my mind was occupied solely with the two monasteries of Huángyán and Tiāntóng.
I have merely grown old. Upon arriving at Huangyan, I resolved to cease my travels; this was not because there were no people in the world.

An old man in a mountain hollow, day after day looking weary, possesses neither great skill nor extraordinary insight, yet he exhausts his years without ever reaching his ultimate goal—how, then, could one go to him? Among your disciples today, I am the only one who lacks wisdom.

The rest were all extraordinary, eminent, and magnificent; those who emerged could serve as teachers for humans and devas, while those who remained hidden were equally capable of establishing the standards for mountain forests.
Yet they pursued their worldly affairs with such haste and agitation, as if clinging to something and unable to depart. Who, indeed, would consider this right?
From this, one can generally discern the state of the world and future generations. As for that which upholds the ultimate truth, it was the hundred [schools] of antiquity.
Master Huangbo was more than a match for him; his recorded sayings (yulu) remain extant, and those with true discernment can distinguish them.
If you read his writings and long to see the man himself, he is right now at the base of Mount Huashou, sitting there as solidly as ever.

He possessed neither exceptional skill nor extraordinary insight; yet, when one drew near him, it was as if nothing were being imparted, while when one distanced oneself, it was as if something were being lost.
In such a state, it is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known only by oneself. I hope you will not, during my lifetime, sit idly by and lose this.
This is why I have thus addressed the world and future generations. Nevertheless, in the end, it is insufficient to praise the Master (Heshang) for this alone.
Preface:
To examine this in detail, the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs was originally titled "Directly Pointing to the Human Mind to See One's Nature and Attain Buddhahood.

It takes awakening as its standard. Now, since the human mind is [itself] that very [Buddha-nature], there is no need for any manual labor or artifice. It simply depends on whether one awakens or does not awaken.

It is merely a matter of distinction. If one awakens, then the ordinary person and the Buddha are in accord; by means of the ordinary mind, one perceives the Buddha-nature. Truly, there is no turning or shifting.
If one does not awaken, then karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no fundamental basis to rely upon;

this is precisely the sea of birth and death suffering. In truth, it does not come from elsewhere. The Original Dharma has never been moved in the slightest degree. Therefore, from the empty kalpa to the present moment—
It is forged into a single whole. How could there be two—sentient beings and Buddhas? When one traces back to the root and exhausts the source, it is simply this One Mind alone.
In this One Mind, there is not even a hair’s breadth of anything else to be obtained. Deshan said: "There is no Buddha, and there is no Dharma. He also said:
"If, throughout the entirety of the ten directions of the world, there were even a single dharma or a speck of dust that you were to grasp..."
Those who grasp at this and give rise to conceptual understanding fall entirely into the realm of celestial Māras, external paths, and the spirits of water and land;

they themselves are not true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), nor is there any Chan or Way to be learned. To proclaim it in such a manner may be said to leave no room for even a hair’s breadth [of deviation].
When the First Patriarch came from the West, he secretly transmitted the seal of mind; heart-mind was certified by heart-mind, and mind was transmitted through mind. He opened no gates or portals.
I grant that you understand this; however, it is essential that you awaken directly and immediately.

As for extending one’s hand to receive others—whether by shouting or striking upon entering the gate, or by seizing someone by the chest, or through skillful speech that strikes the vital point like a needle—it even reaches the point of saying, "Three pounds of flax" or "A dried piece of dung.
In these instances, the Way of Direct Pointing is fully exhausted. I alone do not know what good fortune it is that I have been so permeated [by this].
Having attained this mind, upon hearing for the first time that "the mind itself is Buddha," one immediately gains sufficient faith. Abandoning this, there is certainly nowhere else to turn.
By chance encountering the *Platform Sūtra*, a single word brings awakening, like nectar poured over the crown of the head or clarified butter moistening the heart.

Thereafter, one may still harbor doubts that there is something else, engaging in contemplation or investigation, questioning or study, exhausting both spirit and mind and wasting both physical strength and mental effort. Thus it continues...

Exhausting my physical frame, I have compared and studied the Five Houses and the "back-of-the-head" hammer-strokes of the various patriarchs, reaching the ultimate point where nine times nine returns to eighty-one.
Although I have previously expended great effort, in the final analysis, there is nothing else to it.
From this point on, I intended to live in deep seclusion, keeping company with the deer; how could I ever dare to stand before others?

Proclamation: Is this speaking of right or speaking of wrong? There is no help for it; as for the Dharma-character "Wan" (卍), my karmic conditions from past lives have ripened, and upon seeing it once, I believed it instantly—like glue and lacquer.
Unaware of it, the needle in the bag has finally been revealed. Furthermore, I have led several others here to taste a bit of this bitter flavor, bringing trouble upon this mountain monk.
Unable to keep my mouth shut in silence, I have happened to answer as questions arose, and these disciples have followed suit.
I compiled these excerpts into a single volume and earnestly requested that it be circulated. The mountain monk repeatedly declined this, saying:
"The recorded sayings of many ancient masters have been bound away on high shelves; have modern people now surpassed the ancients?

Furthermore, I truly rely on my own mind for conviction and do not seek the faith of others; what need is there for carving and printing? Although the disciples continued their entreaties without ceasing, he finally—
Having obtained it, I follow it accordingly.

Volume One of the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chongqing Zongbao Du.
Dharma Grandson of Danxia, the present-day monk Zhongbian,
ascending the hall, held up the incense and said: "This one portion of incense, though fundamentally natural and not obtained from another, nevertheless ultimately exists."

This is the occasion for offering incense. Burning it within the brazier, I respectfully offer this for the sake of my late Master Wuyi Dashi of Bosan, Jiangxi Guangxin Prefecture, to repay the debt of gratitude for the milk of the Dharma.
Adjusting his robes and taking his seat, a monk asked: "The Flower Hall is opened once more, and we behold again the picking up of the flower and the smile.
As the Dharma assembly begins, we observe clearly that the Great Dharma is fully upheld—before the empty kalpa..."
[The Master] did not answer. [The student] said, "Today the world is at peace; the various officials perform their duties. Why is it that Your Lordship’s mind is not yet at ease?
The Master said, "What you say, benevolent one, is too intimate. The student continued, "In ages of antiquity when the Way prevailed, the inner chambers and curtains were deep and secluded."
"The common people do not know. After all, what kind of person would you have to enjoy such abundance and prosperity? The Master said, "The faceless fellow.
The monk stepped forward and asked, "If that is so, then the stringless lute has no sound or melody and does not offend the hands or mouth.

Today, before this assembly of humans and devas, I request the Master to play it high once. The Master said, "You, Dharma brother, thoroughly understand the wind that comes from afar. The monk covered his ears and returned to the assembly.
A monk asked, "In the past, when the Tripitaka Master Jñānabhadra was here, five hundred bodhisattvas requested the precepts but remained hidden and did not appear.
I do not ask about that; where is Jñānabhadra now? The Master struck the desk and said, "He comes! He comes!"
The monk turned his body and pointed to the assembly, saying, "The Dharma assembly of Jñānabhadra is still intact, as if it had not yet dispersed. The Master said, "I accept the Layman’s praise;
now, retreat three steps. The monk bowed. The Master then gave a shout. He looked back at the assembly and asked, "Is there anyone who wishes to ask a question?
A monk came forward and, upon bowing, the Master gave a shout. The monk bowed again. The Master shouted once more. The monk bowed yet again. The Master—
[The Master] said, "Great assembly, look! This monk does not even know shame. [The student] stepped forward and asked, "When Bodhidharma came from the West, what was the sutra?

The Master said, "This is the howling of a jackal. He then held up his whisk and said, "In the past, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, among the hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, only Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said, 'I have the True Dharma...'"
The Eye-treasury and the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* were entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. Today, at Huashou, the hall is opened and the whisk is raised;
the great assembly stands solemnly. Tell me, is this the same as that, or is it different? All you venerable elders, if you possess a single eye here, [you will see].
It will not hinder you; do not hesitate further. Do not enter into the realm of the mental faculty to calculate or speculate.
Even if you were to succeed in such speculation or achieve completion through calculation, it would only cause you to drift even further from your fundamental matter.
Venerable elders, this is one matter, clear and manifest—why is it so exceptionally difficult to carry forth? If you turn the light back for a single moment, let go...
I have employed many skillful means, yet there is not a single thing [to be attained].

It is only because you, throughout immeasurable kalpas, have turned your back on your own nature and pursued sounds and forms, that I have used expedient teachings to instruct you in turning the light inward to reach the source. Yet you do not understand;
instead, you sit within a ghost cave, identifying with a state of "no-seeing and no-hearing" that is merely empty and hollow. For this reason, the Great Master Huineng said:
It is said: "People of the world are externally deluded by attachment to forms and internally deluded by attachment to emptiness.
If one can be free from form within form and free from emptiness within emptiness, then one is undeluded both internally and externally, and the original true nature will manifest.

O Venerable Elders, if you simply do not externally cling to sounds, colors, names, phrases, or meanings, and do not internally maintain a subject that knows or perceives, then [the nature] will naturally be revealed in its nakedness."
Naked! Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single speck of dust or a single dharma that does not manifest by virtue of this majestic radiance.
Does it take much effort to realize this? Do you understand? Whether you understand it or do not understand it, it is you. Even going to the east, it is you.
To go westward is also you. Since it is you, it matters not whether one is capable or not. Have you not seen Xuan Sha say:
"All of you are like being submerged head-first in the great ocean; yet you still stretch out your hands and ask others for water to drink.
This mountain monk raises this matter because there is no other way; it is simply to cause you venerable seniors to turn the light back within and attain realization.
Fundamentally, from the perspective of one who has attained thorough understanding, there is no such thing as "speaking. Do you all understand? [He strikes the meditation platform with his staff.
"Returning home is entirely the business of descendants; the patriarch has never left the door. Take care.

The Vice Abbot Huánjì requested the Master to ascend the hall for the funeral of his father. A monk asked, "Linji said: 'If one realizes the first phrase, you can become a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
if one realizes the second phrase, you can become a teacher to humans and devas; if one realizes the third phrase, you cannot even save yourself.
We humbly beg the Reverend to compassionately grant us his instruction. The Master said, "Ask from the beginning. The monk stepped forward and said, "As for..."
"What is the first phrase? The Master said, "No Buddha, no Patriarch. The student asked, "In that case, you have extended your hand from within the light.
The Master said, "From where did you get this news? The student said, "Presented face-to-face, not separated by even a thread.
The Master said, "That is still just idle talk. The student said, "Yellow Dragon opens his mouth and laughs; the Jade Cock crows atop the cloud-peak."
The Master said, "Yesterday someone already passed this way. The monk bowed, rose, and let out a shout. The Master said, "A fine shout!
The monk stepped forward and said, "Poverty breeds filial sons; wealth and status produce pampered children. The Master said, "Set it aside for now.
A brand-new set of rules—bring forth a single phrase. The monk stepped forward and said, "Last night, the Golden Ox was smeared with mud and mire; he has mistakenly killed the plowman."
[The assembly] lost their way. The Master said, "Withdraw for now. He then held up his whisk and said, "In my school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others.
How am I, this mountain monk, to open my mouth? Good monks, since in my school there are no words or phrases..."
Huashou enters the hall today. What does he say? Since there is not a single dharma to give to others, what do you, the assembly of elders, seek from Huashou?
Elders, this is a thoroughgoing act of compassion on his part; do not fail to look beneath your own feet.
Do not simply keep taking steps forward, seeking it from him. As the ancients said: "Even if you seek it, it is not found."
It is attained. Yet even this attainment is not real. What the mountain monk speaks right now is precisely what you, the venerable elders, hear;
what you, the venerable elders, hear is precisely what the mountain monk speaks. Apart from what the mountain monk speaks, there is nothing for you all to hear.
"Listen, all you people: apart from what you hear, there is nothing here for this mountain monk to say. Do you understand? [The Master] cites the case of Yaoshan asking Shitou:

'I have a rough knowledge of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. I have heard that in the South they point directly to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha, yet I have truly not yet mastered it.
Shitou said: 'It cannot be attained by being thus, nor can it be attained by not being thus. Being thus...'"
"It is not that you cannot do so at all. How will you proceed? Yaoshan was at a loss.
The Master said, "Your karmic conditions do not lie here. Go see Mazu Daoshi. Yaoshan went to see Mazu and recounted the previous circumstances.
Mazu said, "Sometimes I instruct him to raise his eyebrows and blink; sometimes I do not instruct him to raise his eyebrows and blink; sometimes I raise..."
"One who raises his eyebrows and blinks his eyes is [right]. Sometimes one who raises his eyebrows and blinks his eyes is not [right].
What do you say to this? Dongshan bowed. The Patriarch said, "What principle did you perceive that you bow? Dongshan said, "When I was with Shitou, it was like a mosquito on an iron ox.
The Master said, "This is the direct pointing to the human mind, seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha."
A model. Herein there is killing and there is giving life; there is letting go and there is seizing.
In our school, one must possess such skillful means before one can truly be a person of realization. Today, I shall explain this for all of you: even to do so is not permitted.
It is not that one must not do so; it is not that one must both do so and not do so. How could the turtle ever have escaped from the jar?
Sometimes I let them raise their eyebrows and blink; sometimes I do not let them raise their eyebrows and blink.
Sometimes those who raise their eyebrows and blink are right; sometimes those who raise their eyebrows and blink are not. The vast ocean follows the fish.

Leap! The sky allows birds to fly as they please. Does the assembly understand? Again, it is cited that when the Seven Virtuous Sisters were wandering in the Śītavana charnel ground, one sister said, "The corpses are here;
where is the person? Another sister said, "How? How? At that moment, the seven sisters simultaneously realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Master said, "Record-keeper, take this memorial tablet for the late Elder Jingzong Liang, his father."

The bones were brought to Mount Luofu to erect a stupa. The mountain monk was invited to ascend the hall to form a bond with the assembly for the sake of *prajñā*, thereby providing merit for the deceased's peace in the afterlife.
Suddenly, someone asked: "If the Venerable Liang’s bones are here, where is the person?
And how would you, Mountain Monk, respond? After a long silence, he said: "Tomorrow is the Qingming Festival; may the assembly take care."
On his birthday, he was invited to ascend the hall. A monk asked, "I do not ask about the time before the kalpa of dust-points; what is the present Amitāyus?

The Master said, "Two eyes facing two eyes. The monk pressed further, "The World-Honored One had already descended to the royal palace before leaving Tuṣita Heaven, and even before emerging from his mother’s womb, his work of saving beings was complete.
Does the news of him still saving beings persist now that he resides at Huashou?"

The Master raised his whisk. The monk stepped forward and said, "The cock crows on the mountain peak; the moon shines in the sea where the fish leap. The Master said, "You have troubled me with such elaborate usage.
A monk asked, "Today is a fine day for the Master. I only wish that you would take one coin as the capital for your livelihood and ten thousand coins as the profit.

The Master remained silent for a long while and asked, "Do you understand? The monk stepped forward and said, "When the capital is small, few people see it; when the profit is great, it fills the world."
"Thousand. The Master said, "Let this one instance pass for now," and then he said, "Venerable elders, what is the matter before the void kalpa?
What is the matter right now? Nanquan said, "Before the void kalpa, there was no name for Buddha and no name for sentient beings.
At such a time, it is precisely the Way; it is simply that no one is aware of it. The Old Teacher Wang may truly be said to embody the Way.
This is so. If it were as the Flower Peak [Sutra] suggests, it would not be thus. Right now, the world is established;

the distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas exists; mind and objects are in turmoil; sounds and forms intermingle—this is no different from before the empty kalpa. Venerable Elders, do you believe this?
If you can believe it, then directly below there is not even a single hair’s breadth of a thing. Each person is their own original patriarch.
In the field of reality, there is not even a single thread of anything to be gained. It simply requires knowing one’s home right here and now. To conceive of it with the mind is already a deviation;
without conceiving of it, everything is authentically true and each thing is luminously wondrous. As the Venerable Prajñātāra said: "In the womb, it is the body; in the world, it is the person;
in the eye, it is called seeing; in the ear, it is called hearing; in the nose, it discerns fragrance; in the mouth..."
In discourse, it is grasped in the hand; in movement, it runs on the feet. It manifests everywhere, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm, yet is gathered within a single atom.
Those who recognize it call it Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*jinghun*). At Huashou, however, it was not so:

those who recognized it called it the vital spirit, while those who did not recognize it instead called it Buddha-nature. Tell me, is there any distinction of superiority or inferiority here? Those with the eye [of wisdom] will know.
Examine this discernment. If you are still unable to do so, look further into the karmic conditions of the wind and the banner.
At that time, when the Sixth Patriarch arrived at Faxing Temple, he heard two monks debating; one said it was the wind moving, and the other said it was the banner moving.

The Patriarch could not restrain his impatience and spoke directly to them: "It is not the wind moving, nor is it the banner moving; it is your own minds, O worthy ones, that move. All you venerable ones—
Sitting. If you can realize this, you will immediately see where the Sixth Patriarch rests his body; you will immediately see where Śākyamuni rests his body;
you will immediately see where your own self rests its body. It penetrates from top to bottom; there is no further dharma beyond this.
An ancient had four lines that are already perfected: "Beautiful as Xi Zi leaving the Golden Palace, lovely as Yang Fei."
Descending from the Jade Tower, day after day you shall be intoxicated beneath the flowers; what more could be lacking in elegance?
The mountain monk takes this up to provide a commentary for all of you: "It is not the wind moving, nor is it the banner moving.
As beautiful as Xi Shi departing the Golden Palace, as graceful as Yang Guifei descending from the Jade Tower—O virtuous ones, your minds are stirred, day after day beneath the flowers.
"Intoxicated! What more could one find lacking in elegance? [The Master] struck the desk with his whisk and descended from the seat.
On the day of the Buddha-bath ceremony, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Regarding the eighth day of the fourth month before the empty kalpa and the eighth day of the fourth month now present:

are they the same or different? The Master said, "Mount Luofu. The monk stepped forward and said, "When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward..."
The Sixth Patriarch said, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. This is inherently possessed by every person; it is lacking in none.
Why, then, did the World-Honored One speak of being "alone honored"? The Master said, "A hair-whisk from a tortoise is three feet long.
A monk asked, "Before the Master has ascended the Dharma seat, and before this student has left the meditation hall, I pray that the Master will point out this one phrase for me. The Master said:
[The Master] said, "This is already too much of a fuss for you, *ācārya*. The student asked, "How about you, Preceptor?
The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, have found a place to withdraw. The student asked, "Today, an ugly daughter-in-law cannot avoid meeting her mother-in-law. The Master said:
[The Master] led them out himself. The monks prostrated. The Master then said: "Today is the eighth day of the fourth month, the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth.

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: 'The Tathāgata appears in the world for one great cause and condition, solely to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, to be shown the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The Sixth Patriarch said: 'You should know that...'"
The Tathāgata has already fully realized this knowledge and vision; what need is there to open it further? That which is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is none other than your own mind.
Venerable Elders, this Dharma of the single mind is such by its very nature, whether a Buddha appears in the world or not. It is simply unbearable that no one recognizes it.
Now that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, he has merely revealed this news for the sake of sentient beings. Although he has revealed this news...
This is still merely a matter for descendants. This Dharma of the One Mind has never been moved at all. Have you not heard?
"Before leaving Tuṣita, he had already descended into the royal palace; before emerging from the womb, his work of saving sentient beings was already complete. I say:

"O Venerable Elders, you have already attained Buddhahood, finished saving sentient beings, and completed your entry into Nirvāṇa. Do you still believe this? O Venerable Elders, do not say otherwise."
The Buddha was accomplished through cultivation over many kalpas; I am but an ordinary person of the mundane level. How could I possibly grasp this?
If you hold such a view, you are merely opening up the cognitive perspectives of a sentient being.

Furthermore, do not say that the Buddha appeared in the world emitting light and shaking the earth, surrounded by dragons and devas, and revered by spirits and ghosts, while I lack such supernatural powers and wondrous functions. If...
To have such a view is simply because your mind, O benevolent one, harbors high and low, and does not rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom.

An ancient said: "The Tathāgata manifests his physical form merely to accord with worldly sentiments; fearing that people might give rise to the view of annihilation, he provisionally establishes empty names.

These thirty-two marks are but false appellations, and the eighty secondary characteristics are likewise hollow sounds. To possess a body is not the essence of awakening; to be without form is the true manifestation. This...

The Buddha of No-Form is, right now, fully present before each and every person, eternally perfect and luminous. A "Buddha" is nothing more than the realization that one possesses the capacity for freedom;
though situated within the cycle of birth and death amidst the five aggregates, such a one has no birth or death.
Though amidst the intermingling of the sense organs, their objects, and the myriad realms, such a one remains solitary and detached. Linji said: "This is your four great elements."
The physical body does not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma; empty space does not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma.
What, then, understands how to preach and listen to the Dharma? It is this very thing, vividly present before your eyes, which has no form or substance.
This is what understands how to preach and listen to the Dharma. Venerable elders, are you not right here listening to the Dharma? You are needlessly seeking it elsewhere.
The eye cannot be apprehended at all. Although it cannot be apprehended, its function in every instance is nonetheless distinct and clear. What is this?
It is like water, which has no sinews or bones, yet can support a ten-thousand-bushel ship. Be careful!
Ascending the hall at the beginning of the summer retreat, a monk asked: "It is not permissible to act thus; it is not permissible not to act thus.
When acting thus and not acting thus are both impermissible, what then? The Master said: "I, this mountain monk, cannot say. The monk pressed further:
"If that is so, then the rain darkens Luofu Mountain, deeper and deeper; the tide returns to the great ocean, entirely without sound. The Master said: "The void beneath the courtyard."
"I shall tell you. Jìn said, "Last night the old man danced upon the southern tower; the jade maidens sang and played the flute before the emerald screens.
The Master struck his staff once. Jìn said, "Now today, as we enter the summer retreat and ascend the hall, you raise the mallet and brandish the whisk.
I wonder, by what dharma do you instruct what kind of person? The Master struck it twice more. The monk bowed. The monk...
Question: "The preceding awakening does not arise; the subsequent awakening does not cease. The present is suchness (*tathatā*). Stepping back one pace, I beg the Master to speak quickly.
The Master said: "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. The monk stepped forward and then stepped back.
The Master said: "Why do you step forward and then step back? The monk prostrated and said: "Let it go. The Master said: "You will make the entire assembly laugh to death. A monk asked: "Huashou..."

The furnace is opened; there is neither firewood nor charcoal. A fragrant breeze strikes the face, tearing the skin. The assembly of monks in the hall forgets all news. Before our eyes, we together realize the Ancient Vairocana. "What is Vairocana? The Master raises one fist. The monk steps forward and says, "When the sentiments of sage and ordinary are exhausted, is it still permissible to refine and test them further? The Master again raises one fist. The monk asks, "What is 'face-to-face'? The Master says, "No. The monk asks, "What is 'no'? The Master says, "Face-to-face. The monk asks, "What is 'face-to-face'? The Master raised one fist and said, "Reverend, do you still know pain and itch? A monk offered this verse: "When the stone tiger roars, the wind fills the valley;
where the clay dragon cries, the mist veils the heavens. The Master said, "Today the mountain monk has suffered a loss.
He then called to the assembly, struck his staff once, and said, "As Red-Eye Guizong says: 'If you understand it, then you are on the path...'"
This is the internal enjoyment. If you do not understand, then it is merely the proliferation of worldly conventions. This mountain monk does not follow in the footsteps of the ancients.

Sitting and cutting off the sentiments of the holy and the ordinary—if you can penetrate this point, you will become a liberated patch-robed monk, able to drive the plowman’s ox and snatch the food from the hungry man. If, however, this is not yet so, [you remain bound].
"Always a fellow who fiddles with mud-clods. He then struck the ground once and said, "If you understand this, you will have provisions for the journey;
it will at least save you half the way. Thereupon he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth Festival, a monk asked, "I do not ask about that which illuminates the past and soars through the present.

[The Master] let out a shout and said, "The one shout before you—please respond to this prompt. The Master said, "I do not respond to the prompt. The monk stepped forward and raised a fist. The Master said, "Laughter kills the whole assembly. The monk let out another shout.
The Master said, "Setting aside one shout and two shouts for a moment, what of three shouts and four shouts? The monk... [remained silent].
"Muòluó. The Master then struck him. A monk asked, "To eliminate the mad rebels and cast aside armor and weapons is still a matter of military merit.
For ruler and minister to be in accord, bringing peace to the seas and clarity to the rivers, is still a matter of the realm of Dharma. What is the fundamental matter of a patch-robed monk?
The Master said, "The mouth is horizontal and the nose is straight. He then added, "No sooner has the eighth day of the fourth month passed than it is again the Dragon Boat Festival."

Section. A report to all you virtuous Chan practitioners: Time passes like a flash of lightning; worldly affairs are as if they exist and yet do not exist; human sentiments are sometimes joyful and sometimes weary.
King Prasenajit said: "Change and transformation shift secretly; I truly do not perceive them. Cold and heat flow on and replace one another."
Gradually arriving at this point, venerable elders, do you still know of anything that does not undergo flux? [The Master] suddenly picks up his staff and says:
"Only this staff is solitary and detached; cold and heat cannot shorten its lifespan, and ghosts and spirits cannot begrudge it its fortune.
Although it is thus, from the perspective of a patch-robed monk, even a speck of dust in the eye is too much. [He] strikes once with the staff.

[The Master] said: “Below. He cited the case of Ruiyan asking Yantou, “What is the fundamental, eternal principle? Yantou replied, “Movement. The Master said, “The Vajra-jewel sword cuts it off at once.
Ruiyan asked again, “What is it like when there is movement? Yantou replied, “One does not see the fundamental, eternal principle.

After a long silence from Ruiyan, Yantou said, “If you consent, you have not yet shed the root and dust; if you do not consent, you will sink forever into birth and death. Ruiyan then attained great [enlightenment].
[The Master] said, "This is far too much pressing down on the ox's head. "Be careful, everyone!

When the Official of the Monastery (Ke Dusi) requested that the Master ascend the hall on behalf of his father, State Councilor Han Mun-gak, a monk asked, "There is a person who walks and dwells with me;
why do you not ferry him across? The Master took up his whisk and made a gesture.
[The Master] drew a circle, then swept it away three times to indicate [the meaning]. A monk asked, "One may have mastered a thousand scriptures and ten thousand treatises;

why is it that when facing the front line of battle, not even a single word can be brought forth? The Master said, "One does not consent to stay at the upper rapids; one has no concern with the lower rapids.
The monk pressed further, "Everyone has a great highway beneath their heels. When a man is questioned, he simply stares with wide eyes and remains speechless."
The Master said, "Your question, *śrāmaṇera*, is excellent. Do you know it for yourself? The monk stepped forward and said, "The Master’s compassionate heart is too earnest.
Before this assembly of devas and humans, one ought to prostrate. As for the sitting mat (*kaṣāya*), I have hidden nothing from you. The Master said, "Even this ordinary formula is unnecessary.
The monk rose from his bow and shouted, "If you wish to listen to this tune with a focused mind, your faculty of hearing is blind!"
He blinked his eyes and went deaf. The Master said, "You have brought this defeat upon yourself. He then said, "The Great Master Jiashan said:
'Before one's eyes there is no dharma; the meaning lies before one's eyes. It is not a dharma of the present moment; it is beyond the reach of ears and eyes. Raising his whisk, he said:
Today, Jiashan manifests a vast and expansive body that fills and obstructs all of space. Do you practitioners of Chan see it?
Jiashan emits a great, perfect sound and addresses the practitioners of Chan: "You must not see me through form; you must not seek me through sound.
If you see me through form or seek me through sound, such a person walks a deviant path and shall not see me."
The Mountain Monk said, "Not seeing by means of form; not seeking by means of sound. How can one see the Great Master?
Jiashan said, "Have you not heard? To deliberate between before and after, or to establish center and periphery—to fail to grasp even a single dharma is to drown in a deep spring.
The Mountain Monk said, "When it is not like this at all, what then? Jiashan said, "I dare not speak. The Mountain Monk said, [and continued].
[The Master] said, "I truly dare not speak. Jia Shan said, "The Abbot may do so, but I fear that the various Zen practitioners might give rise to intellectual interpretations based on words.
This mountain monk says: 'In official matters, even a needle cannot pass; in private affairs, a carriage and horse may go through. I pray that the Great Master will not withhold his compassion.
Jia Shan asked, "Do you understand? [The Master replied,] "None of it is 'I' or 'mine. All you present Zen practitioners, please open your eyes! Here, blink!"
Above the eyebrows—already missed! Hurry, hurry! Quickly, quickly! Standing on water wearing boots; riding a horse to Chang'an before the boots are even wet.

Today, the Head Abbot Zu Chan, together with the three lay practitioners Shengxin, Yuanxin, and Miaoxin, have prepared a vegetarian feast and invited this mountain monk to ascend the hall to dedicate merit for the posthumous benefit of his father, Duke Wenke. We humbly pray:
Within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one does not maintain a self-nature; thus, one finds peace and happiness everywhere, whether in the heavens or among humans.
To illustrate this, [the text] cites Mañjuśrī’s question to the lady Akṣayamati: "What is the meaning of birth? The lady replied, "The meaning of birth is non-birth. Mañjuśrī said:

"What is the meaning of 'birth' being defined by 'non-birth through birth'? The woman replied, 'If one can clearly know that the four conditions—earth, water, fire, and wind—have never themselves attained any state of combination, yet are able to function according to their respective suitability, this is the meaning of birth.
Again, Śuddhipanthaka asked, 'What is the meaning of death? The woman replied, 'Death has "non-death through death" as its meaning. Śuddhipanthaka asked, 'How so?'"

"Death has as its meaning dying by means of non-death. The woman said: "If one can clearly understand that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never themselves attained any state of separation or dispersion, yet can act according to what is appropriate—this is the meaning of death. All you virtuous practitioners of dhyāna!"
If you understand it in this way, then birth has never occurred, and death has never occurred; all is the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
I grant that you have grasped the Tathāgata-dhyāna, but you have not even dreamed of the Patriarchal-dhyāna. Tell me, what excellence does the Patriarchal-dhyāna possess?
After a long silence, he again raised the case of Master Jin asking Master Xiu: "Though one clearly knows birth..."
"This is the principle of non-arising. Why, then, does one transmigrate through birth and death? Xiu said, "A bamboo shoot will inevitably become a bamboo.
Can you make bamboo strips out of it right now? Jìn said, "You will realize this for yourself in the future. Xiu said:
"I am just like this," said the monk. "What about you, Senior? The Master replied, "This is the Director's quarters;
that is the Steward's quarters. Xiu then prostrated. The Master said, "This is the Director's quarters;
that is the Steward's quarters. What Chan, what Way, what Buddha-dharma is there? Even the merchants and cowherds in the villages today, and those on the streets—"
"Shiwei, you also understand how to speak like this; what is so extraordinary about it? Do you all, venerable practitioners of Zen, understand? Striking the desk with his whisk, he said:
"The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip; the sweet melon is sweet from stem to fruit. He then descended from his seat.

At the conclusion of the summer retreat, the Master ascended the hall. A monk came forward and prostrated. The Master immediately shouted. The monk stepped forward and said, "Please give another shout. The Master shouted again.
The monk said, "The setting clouds and solitary wild goose fly together; the autumn waters and the vast sky are one color. The Master asked, "Why do you bring up this ready-made phrase?
The monk said, "I ask the Master to speak something new. The Master said, "Today I have lost ground. The monk said, [and the Master did not respond].
"Such-and-such has also made a great mistake," the Master said, without looking back at him.
He then continued, "All you senior monks, during this summer retreat, have you finally grasped it? If you have not grasped it, then this summer has been spent in vain.
The monk Fangshang asked Fayan, "Master, you studied under Changqing for a long time; why did you instead succeed to Dizang? Fayan replied, "Because I could not understand him."
"Among the myriad phenomena, you alone manifest your true body. Master Fang held up his whisk. Yuanyan said, "Do you negate the myriad phenomena, or do you not negate them?

Fang said, "I do not negate the myriad phenomena. Yuanyan said, "Then you alone manifest your true body, do you not? Fang said, "I negate the myriad phenomena. Yuanyan said, "Among the myriad phenomena, do you not?
Fang said, "Had it not been for this point, I would have nearly spent my entire life in vain. The Master [said: "..."
He said: "If you wish to penetrate and transcend birth and death, take this one koan and reflect upon it repeatedly;
naturally, there will be a point of entry. Have you not seen how Mañjuśrī said: 'I am truly Mañjuśrī, yet there is no such Mañjuśrī. If there were such a thing,'..."
These are the two Mañjuśrīs. Yet, it is not that I am currently without Mañjuśrī; within this, there is truly no duality of "is" and "is-not.
These very elders here—directly beneath them, there is no second person. If you do not give rise to thoughts of difficulty or ease here, you may then walk alone and stride forth.
Do you understand? Furthermore, Master the Sixth Patriarch said: "I have a thing; it has no head and no..."
The tail has no back and no face; it has no name and no character. Do you all still recognize it? Heze said, "It is the original source of all Buddhas, the Buddha-nature of Shenhui.
The Patriarch said, "I told you it has no name and no character, yet you call it the 'original source' and 'Buddha-nature.
In the future, even if you cover your head with thatched grass [to live in seclusion], you will only become a follower of the school of intellectual understanding."
Fellow monks, today I shall open up the eight characters for you and provide a commentary for your sake.
If you are a man who does not blink when killing people, as soon as you hear the Patriarch say, "I have," you should immediately let out a thunderous shout of defiance.
"Even if you possess the skillful means that pierce the heavens, you must still suffer a total humiliation. Why is this so? All you venerable seniors stand like walls ten thousand fathoms high;
every one of you has nostrils reaching toward the sky. With these words, he struck the desk with his whisk and descended from the seat.
The Provincial Governor Lin Jie’an recommended Lady Zhang and requested that the Master ascend the hall. The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally already perfected. Throughout the entire ten directions of the world, it is all, without exception, this very adamantine true body. Sentient beings and Buddhas—"
Sentient and insentient beings—the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the sun, moon, and stars—all receive this radiance and are manifested through it.
It is like the nature of space, which is not itself the various phenomena, yet does not obstruct their manifestation. At the very moment they are manifested, they are no longer those phenomena.
Therefore it is said: "In the place where the Way-man acts, there is truly not a single dharma that can be grasped by the mind, nor is there truly a single thing."
"To serve as a condition and as an object. Daowei An said: "A high-minded traveler must sleep amidst sounds and forms, and sit or lie down amidst sounds and forms.
But what do you call 'sounds and forms'? And how can one sit, lie down, sleep, or wake within sounds and forms?
Have you not seen the ancient saying: 'Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are without obstruction; sounds, scents, tastes, and touches are always [present]...'"
Samādhi is like a bird flying through the air: there is neither grasping nor rejecting, neither aversion nor attachment.
If you can realize that, in its proper place, the mind is fundamentally non-existent, only then can you be called Avalokiteśvara. Venerable elders, it was just so even before the empty kalpa.
It is just so at this very moment; it will be just so throughout the bounds of the future. If you can believe this, Śākyamuni Buddha and you are fellow practitioners.
If you cannot believe it, you will wander aimlessly, clinging to external objects. Once you are attached to external objects, [you are lost].

Within, thoughts arise; mind and objects confront one another; delusive imaginings ceaselessly continue, thereby forming the karmic bonds of birth and death—these are called the "companions of worldly toil.
You should try to reflect back upon this: from where does this delusive imagination arise?
Does it arise from the mind, or does it arise from the object? If it arises from the mind, the mind is fundamentally without birth. If it arises from the object, the object is fundamentally...
Sentient beings and insentient things: that which is empty before one's eyes is not called "empty," and that which is present before one's eyes is not called "existent.
This deluded thought arises entirely from one’s own single moment of inverted grasping at appearances. Know that mind and objects fundamentally do not reach one another;
every phenomenon is liberated in its own place, and in its own place, it is entirely true. Long ago, the Second Patriarch cut off his arm seeking peace of mind from the First Patriarch.
The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind and I will settle it for you. The Second Patriarch replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is ultimately unattainable.
The Patriarch said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. "Venerable seniors, do you feel refreshed yet? After a long pause, he said:
"When searching for the mind, nothing is found; thus the mind comes to rest. To put on clothes and eat food remains as it was before. A large month has thirty days; a small month has twenty."
Nine. As previously proclaimed regarding Prajñā, this is respectfully offered for the sake of Lady Zhang and all deceased kin.

We pray that boundless karmic obstructions may melt like frost in a single thought-moment, and that the dust-laden labors of kalpas may be instantly stilled. Now tell me: how do you express the single phrase for repentance and the guidance of the deceased?
"Turning the light back is the path to the heavens; mother and child ascend together to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing."
[The Master] descended from his seat and addressed the assembly.
Huangyan addressed the assembly: "This matter is truly not easy. At that time, Fengyang went last to Shoushan and raised [the case]."
Rolling up the mat, he spoke. Then he attained great enlightenment. Look! “When the dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, the whole body is revealed;

where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of the fox. This is truly casting off the body and relinquishing life. One who understands this will surely be able to penetrate that case of the wind and the banner.
Today, the mountain monk brings this forward: if someone asks, “It is not the wind moving, nor is it the banner moving,” [what would you say?]
What is the meaning? He said to him: "The dragon’s sleeve sweeps aside, and the whole body is revealed.
When [the student] moved his mind, what was the meaning? He replied: "Where the Elephant King walks, there are no traces of foxes. Does the assembly understand?
Furthermore, when Dahui at that time studied the "phrase with words" and "phrase without words," he repeatedly requested Yuanwu to cite the circumstances of the dialogue he had with Wuzu.
Wuwei was already awakened; only then did Mahamati attain great penetration. Today, I, this mountain monk, have once again brought it forth.
If someone were to ask, "It is not the wind moving, nor is it the banner moving—what is the meaning of this? I would say to them: "It cannot be depicted, nor can it be painted.
If they ask, "What is the meaning of 'it is your own mind that moves'? I would say to them: "It follows along with you."
Do you understand? Do you understand?
At Shuangbo Forest, I address the assembly: "You tell me, where does the sickness of people nowadays lie?
Each and every one of you exhausts your mind and strength, yet you learn nothing but the *caitta-dharmas* (mental factors). What connection is there [to the Way]? It is just like my own age..."
Come and contemplate the phrase "this very mind is Buddha. Its wondrousness is beyond words; alas, those who truly understand it are few.
At that time, there was only Daimai who directly took it up; how much more so for later generations? Look:
a monk asked Daimai, "For what reason do you dwell on this mountain? Daimai said, "When I first met Master Ma, he told me: 'This very mind is Buddha.'"
"The mind is itself Buddha. He then remained dwelling in this. The monk said, "Nowadays, the Great Master also says 'neither mind nor Buddha.
Mei said, "This old fellow continues to delude people without end. Let him say 'neither mind nor Buddha' as he pleases; I am simply 'mind is itself Buddha.
O assembly, who among you does not know this causal connection? Why [do you still ask]?"
In each person’s own portion, there is no need for anything else. But tell me, where does the sickness lie?
*Ei!* This matter is extremely difficult to take up. Even if one were able to take it up in a single phrase, it would already be eight *ke* too late.
To further exhaust one's heart and mind would be laborious and fruitless. Do not, by all means, miss the road at the very beginning. Take care!
Guizong addressed the assembly: "In our school, there is something truly extraordinary. At that time, Huanglong Nan [recited] the verse on Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman:
'Standing out from the forest is Zhaozhou; the old woman was thoroughly seen through, for which there is a reason.
Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror; travelers need not treat the road as an enemy. It was precisely because this verse was so profoundly significant that later..."
Many people emerged from this lineage: Huanglong Xin, Zantang Zhun, and Zhenjing Wen—all belonged to this very branch.
Zantang’s verse on begging for alms says: "The 'zhi-hu-ye-ra'—the nostrils of the patch-robed monk point their great heads downward; if you do not understand this..."
It is asked: "Take Dongcun Wang Dajie; Zhenjing resided at Guizong. There was a monk who carried his *fayu* (Dharma discourse) to Huangmei.
Wuzu Yan hurriedly called for the Head Seat, Yuanwu, saying: "Zhen is a truly great *shanzhishi* (spiritual benefactor). This *fayu* is truly rare. Within it, he says:
'Nowadays, there are two kinds of people among those who study the Way. One kind merely recognizes a state of evenness...'"
"Constantly. It is like saying that a vajra is made of clay or that a pillar is made of wood; one leans upon it and relies upon it.
Yet there is another kind who sits in a place of non-reliance, not realizing that they have already relied [upon something]. These are two kinds of people.
When one’s own eyes are suddenly opened, both walking staffs are cast aside; walking alone and stepping forth, the ten directions are vast and open, with nothing that is not permissible.
The Fifth Patriarch was deeply impressed by these words and praised them with palms joined. Therefore, Master Yunju Deng said:
"Even if you study until you reach the very side of the Buddha, it is still a mixed state of mind. Why is this? It is simply because...
Because one seeks the Way by means of the mind. If one seeks the Way by means of the mind, this is simply the functioning of consciousness;
it is the very root of birth and death. Xuansha also said: "Do not rely upon conditioned mental phenomena (*saṃskṛta-citta-dharma*). Over the long course of years, they provide no benefit at all.
This matter is extremely difficult. People today merely study some intellectual principles; [the Way] is far too remote. [The assembly prostrated.]

[The student] bowed. The Master spoke again: "The reason I everywhere emphasize 'this very mind is Buddha' is that I take 'this very mind is Buddha' as my fundamental tenet. You all must understand this."

Guizong addressed the assembly: "When a person of heterodoxy practices the True Dharma, the True Dharma becomes entirely heterodox. When a person of orthodoxy practices heterodox teachings, the heterodox teachings become entirely orthodox.
Nowadays, there are certain heterodox people who take up the words and phrases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
these too fall into heterodoxy. This is because they have, within the True Dharma, created many complications and elaborations. Truly, such people enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow."

How deeply pitiable! From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity down to the present, they have only sought to point directly to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and attain Buddhahood;
there are no further stages or levels. A person of great capacity realizes this immediately, which is what is called "awakening.
Prior to awakening, there is truly no path and truly no method. It is simply a matter of causing them to harbor doubt; therefore it is said: "Believe thoroughly."
He then fell into doubt. When his doubt reached its peak, he attained awakening. Zhaozhou said:

"If you wish to guide people according to their capacities, there are plenty of expedient means within the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. Here in my place, I only guide people by means of the fundamental share.

Assembly, if you can believe these words, simply continue to harbor doubt; there is no need to try to understand them. After a long time, you will naturally have a sudden flash of realization. Only then...
Know that this mountain monk is not deceiving you; take care.
To the assembly at Xiaxiechang: Since Master Shibeng departed, my heart has become suddenly and utterly cold. For his entire life, he was diligent and tireless in this matter;
as soon as he had a glimpse of realization, it would have been the perfect time for him to practice, yet already he had already departed.

If one cannot even manage one's own hands and feet, what need is there to speak of other matters? Even when observed with the eye of the Way (*dōgen*), there is no distinction between those who live long and those who perish young.
Yet, I already lament that the days for practicing the Way are so short; if judged by the worldly eye, it is even more unbearable to bring up. Alas!

For people of the world, faith is difficult to give rise to and roots of goodness are difficult to grow. Unable to have deep conviction in cause and effect, they cannot avoid being subject to immediate retribution.
This is what causes delusion. Whenever I see people give rise to a single good thought, they immediately fall ill with vexation and lose their sense of purpose in whatever they do.

I have known him for a long time. It is simply that he has recognized the mind and reached the source; there is no one who surpasses him.

Formerly, there was a monk who visited a Zen master; every time he saw him, the master would shake his hand and say, "Not so, not so. Just like this...
For these twenty years, one day from afar he saw [Hui]k'an and immediately said, "It is! It is!
Huik'an had been at Daohui’s gate for twenty years, yet he simply did not realize it. Daohui further ordered him to send a letter to Xiangyang;
Huik'an became even more resentful and intended not to go. His friend Zongyuan scolded him, saying, "You must not [desist] midway on the road."

Cán could not attain Chan realization. He subsequently traveled together with Yuán, who spoke to him again, saying, "I can take over all matters for you, except for five things that I cannot take over for you.

At that moment, Quán understood the meaning. Upon his return to Jìngshān, he greatly...
Hui saw him from atop the pavilion and said, "This fellow has even changed his very bones! Look! The ancients had no fixed methods;
they simply raised up this one pivotal point so that students might recognize it for themselves.
There was nothing else to say. For one who has seen their nature, it is like reaching out one's hand and seeing one's own palm—what more could there be? Great assembly!"
"Is there anyone else who can believe this? At that time, a monk stepped forward and said, "I once read the *Recorded Sayings* of Dahui.

Is this not following after delusion? Today, having received the Master’s instruction, I have finally gained further benefit."
"Faith and Inclination. The Master said: "At present, you simply must have faith. If you cannot directly take it up, you must investigate from time to time:
'How is it that mind itself is Buddha? Look into this constantly and with clarity. Once you have realized it, only then will you have the capacity for discourse.

This book is indeed clean. It is easy enough to praise him for that. However, as for those who have long engaged in study, if they did not encounter a true master at the outset, they have accumulated a great deal of intellectual views. When they arrive before a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one must first wash them clean;
only then can they be rescued. How could people of today understand this? This matter requires great effort.
Only those with merit encounter a true master; such a beginning can only be attained through fortune.

As for those of meager merit, when they see a false teacher discoursing on Chan or the Way with various elaborate branches and details, they immediately find it to have flavor. Yet, upon seeing a true *kalyāṇamitra*, they find nothing at all and conclude that a true spiritual friend is merely like this.
Furthermore, there are those who willingly settle for inferiority, claiming that the ancients spent twenty or thirty years [in practice].
Only now has it been truly settled. All day long they have been rushing outward in search; yet after twenty or thirty years of such pursuit, they have found no trace at all.
When they reach this point, one must ultimately cause them to turn back toward that single, direct path, for only then will they find peace and security.
It would be better to let go early on, thus saving effort. *Ei!* A great elephant does not roam where a hare runs.
The direct path: great enlightenment does not depend on minor details. This rare Dharma is truly difficult to believe. As the Sūtra says:
"If there is someone who, throughout a thousand lifetimes, has practiced with diligence and cultivated various roots of goodness—for such a person one may preach this.

If there is someone who, throughout a thousand lifetimes, has only read and recited the Mahāyāna, and has not looked upon other vehicles or the scriptures of non-Buddhists—for such a person [one may preach it]."
Only then may it be explained. The World-Honored One offered this exhortation: "In whatever region you travel, do not propagate this recklessly. The Sixth Patriarch also said:
"I fear that foolish people will not understand and will slander this Dharma-gate; for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, they would sever the Buddha-nature.

Therefore, know that the secrets of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are rare and difficult to believe. The assembly must trust them thoroughly from the very bottom, without leaving behind even a single hair’s breadth of doubt.
Only through deliberation can it be attained. Take care.
[The Master] hung the bell and struck the wooden board to address the assembly. Raising the mallet, he said: "Does the great assembly understand? A thousand strikes, ten thousand strikes."
All the attendants rise at one stroke; he then strikes the wooden board once. He speaks again, saying, "Why? The regulations of the monastic community take this as their standard.
As he strikes the bell once, he returns to the abbot’s quarters.
At the commencement of the retreat, he addressed the assembly, citing the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta* of the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*:
"With great perfect enlightenment as my monastery, body and mind dwell in peace within the wisdom of equality. Today, at Huashou, I take Mount Luofu as my pasture for tending the ox.
Whether east or west of the stream, let everyone roam freely and at ease; there is only one vital word that must not be transgressed.

King Guo said, "The Way of Fenyang: if even a single hair’s worth of thoughts regarding sagehood or ordinariness is not exhausted, one cannot avoid entering the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse.
Baizhang Yuan also said, "If even a single hair’s worth of thoughts regarding sagehood or ordinariness is completely purified, [one enters the Way]."
"You will still not avoid falling into the womb of a donkey or a horse. As for you, venerable elders, what will you do?
You must establish your own livelihood from within this very place. Have you not seen Master Wáng say: 'Since my youth, I have raised a water buffalo.
If I intend to graze it on the east bank of the stream, I cannot avoid trespassing upon the King’s water and grass; if I intend to go to the west bank...'"

"Herding cattle does not exempt one from trespassing upon the water and grass belonging to other kings. It would be better to 'contribute a little according to one's means,' yet even this is not seen at all.
What is this 'contributing a little according to one's means' that is not seen at all? Venerable elders, if you can understand this..."
This is precisely one’s livelihood. Within this single period, you must exert yourselves with great effort. To the assembly:
An ancient said, “Of thousands and tens of thousands of people, all are men seeking the Buddha; among them, can you find a single true practitioner?
If you wish to become a disciple of the Empty King, do not let the sickness of the mind be that which is most difficult to cure. All you venerable seniors, for now—
The Way: Consider how far apart the man who seeks the Buddha and the man of the Way truly are; you must distinguish between black and white with great care, for you must not be superficial.

I have traveled on foot to this place solely to study the Buddha and the Dharma. Why, then, do you speak of it as if encountering an enemy?
Have you not seen Dongshan say: "To attempt to learn the profound mystery with the mind is much like heading west while facing east"?
If you seek to learn the Buddha or the Way with the mind, you will exhaust your kalpas and your entire life without ever attaining it. It is better to cease discursive thought and forget [the self].
Consider this: the Buddha manifests before you in person. At this time, having no other choice, we teach people to strike down that side’s news from the side they follow;

this is merely to provide a point for discussion. Beyond this, what connection is there? O venerable elders, it is spontaneously present as it is. Any conceptualization of the mind is already a deviation.
To speak in terms of ultimate reality, one must not fall into the traps of seeing and hearing; only then can one return home in stability.
Seated. Take care. Addressing the assembly:

These matters regarding the traces of the teachings are merely peripheral; they are not yet that very message. If one were to discuss that message, it cannot be known by wisdom (*prajñā*), nor can it be recognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*).

For this reason, the Gate of Chan brings the mind to an end, entering suddenly into the power of non-arising insight. Venerable Elders, how does one bring the mind to an end?
How does one suddenly enter the power of non-arising insight? One must simply be without mind. This state of no-mind is not something to be produced through deliberate effort.
Come, you clever monk! As soon as you hear such words spoken, you should be able to overturn them. Now, if you all attempt to deliberate upon this "no-mind," how can you succeed?
Yongming said: "If you personally realize it, then even the profound words and wondrous meanings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs will all be demonic teachings.
How can you deliberate upon them? It is most difficult, most difficult!"
Addressing the assembly: To investigate this matter is truly no small undertaking; one must cultivate profound reverence before it can be mastered.
Today, those who preach the Dharma throughout the world are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet those who have realized the Way are like hemp seeds or millet grains.
They all recognize only that which is bright and lucid before their eyes—what the ancients called "the man behind the donkey and the horse. You venerable monks, you must know this well.
Only then can you truly experience the sensation of pain and itch. Changsha said: "Before one's eyes there is not a single dharma; in this very place there is no person.
Vast and expansive is the diamond-like essence—neither false nor real. If you can directly perceive this, you will immediately cut off hearing and seeing;
all dharmas will sink into stillness. Pure and naked, there is nothing to take up; bright and clear, there is no room for evasion. If you can step upon this...
In such a state, one naturally understands how to make a living. How does one understand how to make a living?
Listen. Why is it necessary to make a living? Listen. The ancients had great examples. When Caoshan took his leave of Dongshan, Dongshan asked, "Where are you going?
Caoshan replied, "I am going to the place of non-transformation. Dongshan said, "In the place of non-transformation, how can there be going?"
Yaoshan said, "Even when departing, it does not undergo change. This is the first model for understanding how to establish one's livelihood.
While Yaoshan was sitting on a rock, Shitou asked, "What are you doing here? Yaoshan replied, "I am not doing anything at all.
Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are sitting idly. Yaoshan said, "If it were idle sitting, then I would be doing something. This is the second...
These two cases serve as models for those who understand how to make a living. Have you all, venerable elders, ever made a living in such a manner?
Today, I shall once again circulate this message for your sake. Let us not speak of the distant past; consider even this very body born of your parents right now.
At the age of one or two, your faculties of seeing and hearing were complete, and your six sense organs were at ease. Your mind—
The objective realm is one and the same. There are eyes as if not seeing; there are ears as if not hearing. The six faculties are at ease.
At such a time, everything is perfectly complete. As one gradually grows up, one gives rise to feelings of attachment and aversion.
From birth until old age, one remains deluded and does not return [to the source]. Now tell me, where does the fault lie? Is it that those things did not exist back then? O monks!
[The Master] ascends the seat. "All day long, one follows sounds and pursues forms; yet at every step, one is treading upon them.

If you do not overturn them once and for all, there will be no place for you to make a living. Great assembly, what do you say? After a long silence, he raises his whisk and says: "If one understands this point, there is nothing at all;
how could essence and function be hindered by being divided or undivided? He then strikes the desk with the whisk and descends from the seat.

When one does not dwell upon any phenomena from moment to moment, there is no bondage. Therefore, to be detached...
The Dharma-gate of mindfulness is the most honored, the most noble, and the foremost. Only the Buddha alone is called "free from thought.
One who does not perceive the path yet awakens to the Dharma of non-thought will fully penetrate all dharmas; one who awakens to the Dharma of non-thought will see the realm of all Buddhas.
One who awakens to the dharma of non-thought reaches the stage of Buddhahood.
If you were not truly in such a state, then at some future time, you would certainly lack self-confidence. Why is this so? It is simply because this monkey of yours has never died;
your heels will never touch the ground. All the patriarchs of the past have fully emphasized this point. It is, for example, like a great...
It is a mass of fire; there is no place for you to draw near, and no place for you to rely upon. If it were not so, what could be done?

Nevertheless, this is spoken for those who have attained it. If one has not overturned the face of one's parents before their birth—the true place of departure—then one still remains in a state of shame (*mala*). How, then, will you proceed? What means do you have at hand?
"A thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are but a single doubt; a thousand barriers and ten thousand barriers are but a single barrier.

When this one doubt is shattered, then a thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are all shattered; when this one barrier is penetrated, then a thousand barriers and ten thousand barriers are all penetrated.

Venerable elders, what is this one barrier? Listen. After a long silence, he said: "To call it a bamboo stick is to strike against it (*chu*); not to call it a bamboo stick is likewise to strike against it."
To call it a "bamboo pointer" is to turn one's back on it. One must not speak; one must not remain silent. All of you, look well! To the assembly:
this school is difficult to master in its subtlety. You must apply yourselves with meticulous care. There has never yet been a Maitreya born by natural means.
Śākyamuni is naturally so; he is one who has returned once more. Yet, one must still apply the mind for a while before it can be fully realized. Therefore it is said:
"Only when a person is willing themselves will they be intimate. This is simply because the essence of the verbal teachings must be applied to one's own hidden subtleties.
In the end, it is difficult to pass through. One must reach that state with absolute sincerity and clarity;

only then will one be willing to let go of the mind, only then will one find rest, and only then is one’s insight truly certain. Even if one understands the words and phrases perfectly, that accounts for only half;

it is only when one truly reaches the point of realization that it is difficult. Baizhang said: "If your insight is equal to your teacher's, you have already diminished your teacher’s virtue by half. Insight—
"Only when you have surpassed your teacher can you truly receive the transmission. As for the various elders, how do they fare? People today cannot comprehend this; where does their sickness lie?
Their sickness lies in identifying with the vivid, numinous awareness present before them, failing to realize that this vivid, numinous awareness exists only in dependence upon conditions.
Xuansha said: "If this vivid, numinous awareness were your true self..."
Indeed. Why is it that when one is drowsy, one does not attain this brilliant and numinous clarity?
If you abandon this, you are yet another black lacquer bucket, cast into a cave of neither seeing nor hearing.

Even if you do not involve yourself in either of these two paths and achieve a state of inconceivable harmony, it remains a matter belonging to the shore of birth and death. O venerable seniors, the ancients' realization of their nature was like ten suns.

"Both are illuminations; neither is this principle. [The Master] cites Chan Master Wuzhuo: When he went to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, he encountered an old man who asked, "Where have you come from recently?

ordinary people and sages dwell together. Zhaozhou asked, "How many followers are there? The old man replied, "Three before, three after, three before, three after. Zhaozhou did not understand.
The old man picked up a glass cup and asked, "Is there such a thing as this in the South? Zhaozhou said, "Yes."
Wuzhu said, "What do you usually use to drink tea? Zhe was unable to respond and took his leave. The old man ordered a youth to see him out.
As they were leaving, Zhe asked the youth, "Three by three in front, three by three behind—how many is that? The youth called out, "Virtuous One! Zhe responded. The youth asked, "How many is that?
At that moment, Zhe finally realized that the old man was none other than Mañjuśrī, whereupon he prostrated himself.
The youth requested a verse before taking his leave. The Master said, "Three by three in front, three by three behind.

Since the youth could not grasp this, he missed the talk about the glass cup right before his eyes. At the moment the Master called him once, the youth continued as before to gaze at the moon in the sky and lost the pearl in his hand.
Later, when he visited Yangshan, he finally attained realization. He often served as the head cook (diànzuò). [End of] Text.

"Vital energy (qi). It is simply like this: from morning until evening, when hunger comes one eats, and when thirst comes one drinks; how free and easy it is!
