Yet, if one were to set it down and seek another with which to respond, one would immediately be far removed from the truth. Thus, those who have attained it do not engage in any further deliberation;
they cut off the throat [of doubt] all at once, such that directly beneath them there is no second person. As the *Four Prohibitions Verse* of Caoshan says: "Do not..."
When the mind travels along the path, it does not hang upon its original garment. Why must one insist on "just this way"? One must strictly avoid the time before birth.
This is roughly similar in meaning to the five questions the mountain monk posed yesterday. At such a stage, how could you possibly reach it with words and phrases?
Even if you were to reach it with words and phrases, the meaning would still not have arrived; how much more so when the words and phrases themselves have not yet arrived?
“Where do you intend to place it? Great difficulty, great difficulty!
[The Master] addressed the assembly: “In a mere instant, another half-month has passed. I ask you, venerable elders: what is this fundamental matter?
The passing of time is like a flash of lightning; it does not pause for even a moment. You must earnestly and deeply contemplate birth and death; do not spend your time chasing after pleasures.”
Everyone should try to examine themselves: how will you deal with birth and death? Xueyan asked Gaofeng, "During the day, when you are in the midst of a great bustle, can you maintain your mastery?
Gaofeng replied, "I can maintain my mastery. Xueyan asked, "At night, while you are asleep and dreaming, can you maintain your mastery?"
Feng said: "When one is the master, while sleeping soundly—without dreams, without thoughts, without seeing, and without hearing—where is the master?
Feng was left with nothing to say. "Venerable elders, when there are no dreams, no thoughts, no seeing, and no hearing, where ultimately is the master?
I, this mountain monk, always say there are three critical points. Many people [rely] on the absence of dreams..."
It is difficult to act as the master when there is no thought, no seeing, and no hearing; it is easy to act as the master during the day when everything is bustling and active.
Yet one does not realize that acting as the master during this daytime bustle is actually extremely difficult. Alas!

People nowadays do nothing more than identify with that which is able to see and hear within the field of the five aggregates (skandhas), and then claim, "This is it. This is called playing with a monkey. One.
The morning drum has broken; the monkey has fled, and its whereabouts are unknown.
Generally speaking, when those who consider themselves clever look at the sayings of the ancients, they find them quite easy.

They claim that whatever is brought forth in daily life is everywhere present—such as Dongshan’s "three pounds of flax," Yunmen’s "dry dung-spoon," and Zhaozhou’s "pine tree in front of the courtyard."
Shuzi, you have brought them all together and claim that there is nothing that is not so; yet you must still distinguish between the true and the false before you can succeed.
Dongshan said, "I habitually observe with the eye of my mind, observing again and again, only then distinguishing the true from the false.
O assembly, do not take this lightly, yet it is not difficult either. Where can you seek that which is found? Set it aside.
"At present, it is not that there is something else here either. In this matter, how is it ultimately? Yunmen said:
"Even when heaven and earth are free from even a hair’s breadth of affliction, this is still a 'turning phrase. Only when you do not see a single form is it half-raised.
You must further know that there is a time for the full raising of the upward path: the three pounds of flax, the dried piece of dung, and the cypress tree in the courtyard."
The saying, "The dog has no Buddha-nature," is precisely this very message. Do not treat it with superficiality.
As the Dharma-ending age approaches, many people do not seek the actual reality; they merely dwell in various monasteries, acquiring a bit of intellectual insight.
One can easily comprehend the entirety of the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, yet one truly cannot resolve the fundamental matter. How could you possibly [resolve] it yourself?
Do you not understand? It is merely a mind of victory and defeat. To accept and pass through such things in blind ignorance is to delude oneself and others.
Therefore, a true practitioner disregards fame, profit, and gain in every way; they desire only to realize the truth for themselves in earnest.
They do not restrict themselves by time or season, nor do they shrink from toil and hardship. Look at the ancients—could it be that their faculties were all inferior?
Inferior! He does not resemble people of the present day at all. Yangshan Fen had studied under seventy-one spiritual teachers;
it was only after meeting Shoushan that he attained great enlightenment. One might ask: did he not know Chan before then?
Was there any Buddha-dharma he did not understand? Why was it only upon seeing Shoushan that he spoke of "the eternal blue pool, empty and still"?

"Jièyuè (Realm-Moon), you must understand this only after repeated searching and grappling. Such a person as Yuánwù remained at the Fifth Patriarch’s place for ten years before his mind finally ceased to follow external conditions.
How could people today expect it to be easy? Everyone, you must exert yourselves with true earnestness;
only then will it be well. He spoke again: "This mountain monk has meager merit; from the beginning, I have only delighted in retreating. Today, since I am already here..."
This matter of upholding [the Dharma] cannot be fully explained here. However, for all other matters, you must rely on the collective effort of the assembly.
Originally, there is no "you" or "I" within this monastic community; everyone is of one kind. There is no distinction between the interior and exterior of the hall.
Nevertheless, the interior of the hall serves as the standard for the entire community, and thus its regulations must be strictly observed. I, this mountain monk—
I am most displeased by people engaging in idle chatter. Gathering in groups of three or five to speak a few words takes up the time of an entire incense stick;
how long are days? Even outside the hall, you must strictly admonish yourselves:
each person has their own assigned duties and must perform them with single-minded sincerity and diligent effort. How could it be otherwise for each individual?
"Living in seclusion—can one achieve this without diligent effort? Does rice cook itself? Do vegetables grow themselves? Since my youth, I too have lived in seclusion;
during the day, I have done nothing more than burn a stick of incense, carry firewood, fetch water, cook over the stove, and dig the earth.
Which of these tasks was not performed by myself? In the monasteries today, a single person [takes charge]..."
Regarding a single matter of monastic duty: it is most excellent to bury one's head in practice. This mountain monk cannot help but long to mingle among the assembly and bury his head in practice;
it is truly full of interest and truly peaceful. Zhenjing said: "In this floating life, only monks have nothing to do;
having realized the True Vehicle, one grows more leisurely with age. In this world, there are only those who understand how to practice; the older they grow, the more leisurely they become.
It is not like the worldly person who spends a lifetime in restless toil, only to find at the end that they can rely on nothing at all.

You, the assembly, have cultivated yourselves over many lifetimes; having now become monastics within this school and come to know of this great matter, you must exert yourselves with diligence while there is still time, seeking liberation early on. Do not wait for another day, lest you regret it when it is too late.
Furthermore, Zhongfeng said: "Once the one Master is lost, hundreds of thousands of skin-bags are difficult to heal. Take care! He addressed the assembly:
"A single thought tied to a hair is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting emotion arises and one is shackled for ten thousand kalpas.
All you venerable elders, while your physical strength and vigor are still good, each of you must seek a way of entry. Once you have found a way of entry, you must also have a way of exit."
That which is first attained by the body is not something easily obtained; only after repeated searching and grappling does one finally reach a definitive conclusion.

When Zhaozhou was eighteen years old, he already knew how to dismantle his household and scatter his home, yet he still said, "Except for the two times of rice gruel and meals, all else is a place where the mind is distracted.
How could people of today easily grasp this? Nevertheless, this matter is also quite profound.
This is clear. It is not that one does not see the monk’s question to Ciming: "What is the ancestral style of the ancient Buddhas? Ciming replied: "The silver moon first emerges from the sea;
where is it not clearly manifest? Gaofeng’s verse says: "The silver moon emerges from the sea, shining without partiality;
everywhere it is clearly manifest—who is this? There is no need for further questioning face-to-face; let it be exposed by the sun and blown by the wind as it pleases. Directly...
If you understand this, there is no need for further explanation. If you have not yet realized it, do not deceive yourself.
In the past, Zhantang said to Dahui: "Upādhyāya Gao, you understand the Chan of my school; if I tell you to speak, you can speak;
if I tell you to answer a question, you can answer; if I tell you to provide a verse on an ancient case, you can provide one. However..."
"One point remains unresolved. If you do not attain this one understanding, then while you are within my quarters there is Chan;
as soon as you go out, it vanishes. While you are alert there is Chan; once you fall asleep, it vanishes.
How can you withstand birth and death? Mahamati said, "This is precisely where I am in doubt. Look at how much substance and reality there was in the ancients! He...
At that time, I had not yet met Yuanwu. Everyone in the various quarters was unwilling to accept him; it was simply that I myself was unwilling to submit with a willing heart.
You monks, each of you must seek for yourselves that point where you can submit with a willing heart. Only when birth and death arrive will you have a handle.
Why is it so? Because for one who has attained, not a single moment among the twelve hours of the day and night ever passes in vain.
At that time, Xianglin stayed with Yunmen for eighteen years; Yunmen called him out every day until one day he attained realization.
Yunmen then said, "From now on, I will no longer call you. Later, however, he remarked, "I [have been here] for forty years."
Only then did they become one. Yongquan also said, "You all must not open your mouths too wide.
Even after forty-nine years, this old monk still has room for error. Look! The ancients were all people who practiced with genuine earnestness;
they did not seek merely to understand and then consider it finished. As for me, I have known this since childhood, and only now, after twenty or thirty years, have I finally—"
One must come to a state of complete rest. Thus the ancients said: "Those who understand the Way are many; those who practice the Way are few.
Even today, though so-called "knowledgeable ones" fill the world, those who have truly understood it are still rare. Even if you possess a point of entry, [you must still rest].

This is precisely when one should practice; this is precisely when one should draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra). Yongquan further said: "A student of the Way must thoroughly understand 'dryness.
If your understanding is not dry, I fear you will continue in saṃsāra; I fear there will come a day of weeping.
Yet nowadays, people, upon catching even a slight whiff [of the teaching], immediately turn their heads away and pay it no mind, not realizing what will become of them in birth and death.
"It has arisen! It has arisen! All you senior monks, exert yourselves forward; do not let it pass in vain. Zhaozhou said, "I do not like to hear the word 'Buddha.
If I do not even like to hear the word 'Buddha,' what else is there left for the mind to become entangled with?
Do not see that because some youths of the world possess sharp faculties and act with quick ease, you then say: 'The Buddha-dharma is merely...'"
It is thus. One does not know whether he has undergone hardships in past lives. If one is of middling or inferior capacity, one must ultimately examine the *huatou*.
Practice it while walking and investigate it while sitting. Even if you do not attain enlightenment in this life, you will emerge in a future life without difficulty.
In all cases, each person must have a sense of urgency regarding birth and death; only then will it be possible. Take heed.
Addressing the assembly: "If one is a true practitioner of the Way, they do not see the faults of the world. If you see the wrongs of others, your own wrongs are indeed perverse.
If others are at fault but I am not, then my own faults are self-evident. Simply put aside the mind that seeks out faults, strike away afflictions until they are destroyed.
Let neither hatred nor love concern you; stretch out both legs and lie down. Such were the words of the Great Master, the Sixth Patriarch.
Although this may appear plain and simple, it is in fact the very practice of those who have transcended the ordinary.

It is not like the people of today who merely drape themselves in empty principles, clustering flowers and brocades; what difficulty is there in that? Yet the ordinary mind of attachment and aversion, of likes and dislikes, is not easily dispelled.
As the First Patriarch Bodhidharma said: "Externally, cease all conditions; internally, let the mind be free from panting. Let the mind be as..."
Only after [the wall] has been broken through can one enter the Way. After the Second Patriarch had attained peace of mind, as soon as he faced Bodhidharma, he said:
"How could there be anything else? It is simply to seek a point of reality. Nowadays, let us not discuss whether the inner mind is free from labored breathing;

but as for the phrase "ceasing external conditions," how is it so? Before one's eyes are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; light and darkness, form and emptiness—since external objects already exist, then...
Within, there must be a mind; when mind and objects confront one another, every movement risks injury at the edge of the blade.

Only those who truly know that "there is" can remain here in a state of perfect composure, not committing even a hair’s breadth of error in their actions. If you have not yet reached this stage, [you cannot].
It cannot be forced. Wait for you to bring it forth through awakening and insight; by then, it will already have been missed. *Ei!* Once one attains the state of no-mind, this is called the Way.
When the six gates are at rest, there is no need for laboring the body. Those with the karmic affinity are not my friends; those who find no use for their eyebrows are brothers.
After a long silence, he said: "That which has already passed cannot be recovered; always reflect upon it, and let every thought thereafter be so."

One who is perfectly enlightened is someone who has attained [realization] for the sake of others; only such a person can understand a discourse like this. Otherwise, as soon as there is something held as precious, it becomes a fixed trap.
One must be able to turn [the mind] with effortless spontaneity before one succeeds.
Addressing the assembly, a monk asked: "The precept of self-nature is the absence of transgression in the mind-ground. What is this precept of self-nature? The Master said:
"Today there was a layperson who came from Botou. The monk pressed further: "The light of the precepts issues from the mouth. What is the light of the precepts?"
The Master said, "What a heavy rain! The monk stepped forward and asked, "Why does one who breaks the precepts not fall into hell? The Master said, "A holeless iron hammer.
The monk said, "In that case, the mud ox roars through the moon at the edge of heaven, and the wooden horse leaps into the void across the northern pass.
The Master then gave a shout. The monk said, "What a fine shout! The Master said, "Withdraw for now. The monk bowed and, rising, said, "Mute!"
After the man finished singing the song of non-arising (*anutpāda*), he clapped his hands and strolled before the Hall of the Black Moon. The Master said, "Your failures are not few.
Another monk had just stepped out when the Master gave a shout. As the monk prepared to advance, the Master said, "There is someone behind you laughing at you.
The Master raised this case: A monk asked Longya, "When the two mice gnaw on the creeping vine, what then? Longya said, "A *śrāmaṇera* must have a place to hide."

Only then did he attain it. The Master summoned the assembly and said: "Tell me, what is the place where one hides the body? In the past, there were four brothers who together attained the Way of the Immortals.
Foreknowing that their lives were coming to an end, one hid himself within the water, and another hid himself within the air."
One is hidden within a rock; one is hidden among people. Yet when impermanence arrives, he who hides in water will ultimately drown in the water;
he who hides in space will fall from space; he who hides in a rock will be shattered by the rock;
and he who hides among people will die among people. You must know that none of these are places for hiding the body. Furthermore—

"How is it that this is precisely the place for concealing one's body? Furthermore, Impermanence once seized a monk. The monk earnestly requested a seven-day extension, and Impermanence granted his request.
After seven days, Impermanence returned, but though he searched for the monk, he could not find him at all. "O Great Assembly! [he cried.]
Do you know where the monk has gone? If you can know where the monk has gone, then when birth and death arrive, you will finally possess the method for concealing yourself.
Otherwise, you cannot avoid being flustered and at a loss. This matter must be settled while there is still time;
it cannot be sought through mere effort, nor can it be substituted by another. Since I was young, this mountain monk has studied the Way, doing nothing but personally feeling a deep sense of urgency.
Regarding birth and death, there was no means by which they could be resolved. Later, I read the *Platform Sutra*, which says: "To see one's nature is to become a Buddha.
Like driving a nail into wood, I sought only to see my nature through every possible means. For twenty or thirty years prior, not a single person in Lingnan spoke of this matter;
even those who spoke of it were few in observing the precepts or reciting the Buddha’s name. At that time, I, the mountain monk, [found myself]...
Suppose there were someone who could adjudicate for me; I would have been willing to offer my body as a bed and seat, or my body as a servant.

I have encountered many people, yet met with none at all, until this very *Platform Sūtra*. Day and night, I have not parted from it. Now, at last, I have found a point of resolution and a guiding thread.
I realize that it has always come from this source. I remember back then, I only wished for this matter to be settled, and then—deeply...

In mountain fastnesses and deep valleys, he lived with herds of wild deer; even had he been at the crossroads of the city, wearing tattered rags and eating coarse rice while begging all day long, he would have been content.

Later, together with his younger brother Lingbi, he went to visit Boshan. He had already severed all thoughts of Lingnan, for it was solely because of the "Dharma" character and the *swastika* (卍) mark that he felt a karmic affinity with this mountain monk from a former life and came specifically to seek him out. However, he could not find him. He then proceeded to...
Upon seeing him at the Jinlun Pass, tears fell from his eyes in profusion, and he was immediately moved to inspiration.

Now, the current Head Seat, the Abbot, the Chief Administrator, the Librarian, the Scribe, and all the other disciples have likewise gained faith and devotion under Lady Han’s family. Thus, the conditions have converged.

This composition was made only occasionally; it was truly not my original aspiration as a mountain monk. Last year, when the Chief Administrator arrived at Mount Kuang, I remained hesitant and undecided.
I reflected that the assembly had already expended much effort and heart, yet I was repeatedly pressed with earnest and sincere entreaties.
Having no choice in the matter, I have complied. Although I have always preferred profound seclusion, I have been suspected of adhering to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). However, I recall...
When the Great Master of Tiantai was about to pass away, his disciples asked him about the stage of realization he had attained.

The Master said, "Had I not been leading a community of followers, I would certainly have purified my six sense faculties. Now, because I have sacrificed myself for others, I have only managed to reach the fifth stage.

Indeed, the practices of a Bodhisattva are truly difficult to perform; while it is relatively easy to prevent one's own afflictions from arising, causing others' afflictions not to arise is far more difficult.

The afflictions are extremely difficult to overcome; one can only do so according to one's own strength and by exhausting one's own spirit. If you can believe and trust me, I shall certainly not let you down.
When I first arrived here, I heard Chief Seat Li say, "Now, it is only by crushing the mind until it is a pulp that one succeeds.
I have engraved these words into the very marrow of my bones, having received such instruction from the Chief Seat.
Without sparing even diligent toil, this mountain monk ought to exert his full mental and physical strength so that everyone may be inspired and encouraged.

However, as for all external affairs, one who is frequently ill finds it difficult to attend to them; we must rely entirely on the support of the assembly. This is the tradition of the monastic communities of the ten directions:

originally, there is no distinction between "inside" and "outside. Those who sit in meditation sit in meditation; those who perform circumambulations perform their circumambulations—all are likewise so.
Generally speaking, nowadays everyone says that those who practice seated meditation (*zazen*) are superior, while those who engage in daily activities are inferior.
One person knows this convenience and no one is willing to do the latter; this is truly laughable. How could it be that those who engage in daily activities are truly inferior?
The Head Cook of Xuefeng and the Steward of Mt. Huangbo are revered throughout the ages. Furthermore, both the Yunmen and Fayan schools of the two traditions originated from Xuefeng.
"Come. Guishan then brought forth Yangshan and asked, "Who is this person? Yangshan replied that he was willing to serve as the head cook and the steward.
Great Bodhisattvas are hidden among the multitude; there are many who practice in this way.
If one cannot completely forget even these slight traces of self and other, how can one speak of the Great Matter? From this day forward, the assembly must let loose a great public spirit.
Minds, do not distinguish between self and other; do not distinguish between high and low. Strive forward together to repay the kindness of the Old Śākyamuni; this is no small matter.
We, the mountain monk and the assembly, have resided here for nearly half a year. The fourth month has arrived, and the retreat (*kṣetra-bandha*) is drawing near.
It is essential that every matter be properly settled before we may proceed. Monks, these are the regulations of the monastic grove (*saṃghārāma*).
The standard must be maintained; one must resolutely put it into practice, for it cannot merely exist as a name.

This evening, I, this mountain monk, shall not begrudge cutting open my liver or draining my gall to speak to the great assembly. You all must collectively embody this mind; this is one matter of the precepts and must never be neglected.
In these present days of the Final Dharma, things cannot be compared to those of antiquity. If you seek only the reputation of striving upward, then...

If one’s actual practice does not even reach the level of the middle or lower grades, what is there to be ashamed of? Yet, seeing such a decadent wind with one's own eyes, one should all the more exercise caution and vigilance.
This was also the instruction that the Great Master Fu (Fu Dashi) gave to his sons, the two Dharma Masters Pu Jian and Pu Cheng, as he approached his passing:

"Be careful to guard the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. Do not say, 'Even a three-year-old child can speak like this,' and thus vainly open a wide mouth. In a field of disaster, there is no [harvest]."
The merit of a single basketful of earth. The Iron Ring Mountains endure the agony of a hundred punishments. Long-standing, I offer my respects. Addressing the assembly:
Among the immeasurable and wondrous gates of Dharma, Zen is the primary meaning. If one is a true lion cub, they do not enter the herds of others.
Venerable elders, if one speaks of the swift path for transcending birth and death, there is only this school; all others are merely...
This is a skillful means. You should try to reflect upon it repeatedly: what, in the final analysis, is this? I have often seen certain people who do not understand the ground of mind;
they merely arrange things from east to west based on intellectual principles. Thus, their study does not reach fruition, and that which they seek to learn never comes to completion.
In the end, it all comes to nothing. You need only seek a way of entry within the ground of your own mind;
after a long time, you will naturally be liberated. Why not exert yourself early on?
To wait until your eyes fall to the ground—when you are but a crab scalded in hot water—it will be too late. The Buddha said that human life lasts but a single breath; you all...
At this moment, one must be willing to die at every instant; once one has attained the ability to die, that is enough.
If one cannot yet attain the ability to die, one must urgently seek a skillful means. Gao Feng said: "Simply take up a 'tasteless' *huatou* and harbor it within your breast.
Investigate it while walking and study it while sitting. Naturally, there will be a path of entry. This is not a matter of seeking some other principle; it simply values..."
To know where one returns upon hearing these words—everyone must truly rouse their spirit and look! Where is there any doubt? Simply continue to doubt;
with great doubt comes great awakening, with small doubt comes small awakening, and without doubt there is no awakening.
These words of the ancients are certainly not mistaken. You should simply examine and measure this for yourself: how, in the end, will it be resolved? Do not let it go.
To "pass over" is precisely doubt. There is no need for further calculation. I often hear various Chan practitioners ask, "How can the state of doubt be aroused?
How can it not be aroused? They do nothing but seek principles within the *huatou* (critical phrase) and deliberate upon the Great Enlightenment—how laughable!
The single character "doubt" (*yi*) is merely another name for "cutting through" (*qie*). It is, in essence, birth-and-death itself.
The matter is urgent. You must give rise to doubt yourself; through this process of doubting again and again, a natural turning point will surely arise.

If you pass your days indifferently and do not apply yourself with genuine resolve, waiting for others to awaken you on their own, there is absolutely no such principle. All you venerable seniors, exert yourselves while there is still time!
In the past, there was a merchant who entered the sea together with a bhikṣu. They encountered a malevolent dragon that stirred up a great storm and wind.
The dragon spoke to the merchant, saying, "Simply bring this bhikṣu to me and it will be finished. "This man was my teacher in a previous life," [the dragon continued].
"He refused to teach me how to practice, which caused me to receive this karmic retribution. My suffering is immeasurable, and my heart harbors deep resentment toward him. The mountain monk now...
I tell you this with utmost sincerity. Whether you believe it or not is up to you. At a later time or on a future day, do not turn around and resent me, this mountain monk.
If you say, "I am truly a lion cub," yet do not enter this very assembly, you must nonetheless have actually reached such a state.
This Black-faced Old Man is fierce and biting; he will not accept mere words from your mouth—even if you were the Yellow-faced One himself.
Laozi was compassionate, yet he never authorized what you have just spoken. Take care. [The Master] addressed the assembly:
"Venerable elders, the dust and toil of the three realms are as vast as the sea; from time immemorial until now, they have been a constant clamor.
All arise from the thoughts within one’s own mind. When not a single thought arises, there is total liberation. Since it depends entirely upon oneself, why should it be difficult?"
To achieve Buddhahood requires no more than a single snap of the fingers. Viewed in this light, it seems quite easy.
Nevertheless, even so, one must be a person of true caliber to attain it. An ancient also said: "The moment a single thought arises, that is the realm of objects; simply have no thought at all."
This is what is meant by "the object perishing and the mind extinguishing of its own accord; there is nothing further to be sought.

If one possessed roots of goodness from previous lives, upon hearing such an explanation, they would understand it immediately. However, those of dull faculties must examine it repeatedly, wondering, "Ultimately, what is this principle?
This matter requires nothing but doubt. Therefore, Gaofeng said: "It simply requires you to remain alert and intentionally harbor doubt; doubt!"
When you reach the point where emotions are forgotten and the mind is severed, the golden crow flies through the sky at midnight. Venerable elders, this is simply your own original nature;
even if you do not awaken to it, you have never been more than an inch away from it. Take care.
Addressing the assembly: Where does the Buddha-dharma reside? It resides in the places of dressing and eating; in the places of carrying firewood and drawing water;
in the places of welcoming guests and seeing them off. The moment you raise a thought or stir a念 (nian), it is already no longer so.

You venerable seniors, do not seek it outwardly. You must see your own mind through to its depths and put it into practice; only then will there be a place of rest. This is why you have shaved off your hair and beard.
Regarding this gate: what is it ultimately for? Worldly people, for the sake of some trifling fame and achievement, will even neglect sleep and forget to eat;
how much more so regarding the great matter of birth and death! How many laypeople, hearing of this matter, employ a thousand schemes and a hundred stratagems seeking liberation.
Yet how is it that those who have left the home-life spend their entire days by the side of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)?
To lift it up a thousand times or ten thousand times, yet fail to take it as a matter of concern—among ordinary people, there are none who are born with this knowledge.
It requires nothing more than a heart that is earnest, clear, and lucid. Yet you alone are unable to construct it; where does the fault lie? The fault lies in your own negligence and indulgence.
There were times when they would touch upon it, yet in the blink of an eye it would vanish; as before, their karmic consciousness remained vast and desolate. Such cases were very numerous.
They were not like those of antiquity, who were pure, simple, and sincere—those who would believe immediately upon hearing [the teaching], and having believed, would act accordingly.

Every one of them left the household life and made this their primary urgency, traveling across thousands of mountains and ten thousand waters to seek out those who possessed the Way, seeking only to reach a definitive resolution regarding this matter.
Matters of fact: one must certainly not travel through prefectures or hunt in counties, nor spend one’s time in vain with but a single robe for clothing and mouthfuls of food for sustenance.
Venerable Elders, this matter is no small feat. If you harbor arrogance or pride, it will only serve as an obstacle to yourself.
Since my youth, I have been clear about this matter; I have always gone to pay respects to others, and even when there were those who spoke irrelevant things, I likewise—
Prostrations. Why is this? I seek a definitive resolution regarding my own matter; what does it matter whether others approve or not?
Nowadays, those who call themselves students merely put on the appearance of a virtuous teacher (kalyāṇamitra), as if they were terrified that their reputation might diminish.
How unbearable it is that your own minds are shrouded in darkness! The First Patriarch said:
"How can you, with meager virtue and meager wisdom, and with a frivolous or arrogant mind, hope to attain the True Vehicle? You will only toil in vain.
If you wish to become true sons of the Dharma, do not follow the worldly trends. Cast away these evil views and understandings entirely; let them go until your mind is empty and vast. As soon as...
Apply your minds with diligence. Only then can you properly undergo the forging of a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). If it is not like this, you are still far from the mark. Take care.
This was shown to the assembly on the anniversary of the passing of the Old Monk of Boshan. When there is a cause, there is a reason for the matter. As for me, the mountain monk, from my youth...

However, the very "nose-ring" of the Chan school remained unresolved. Then, he encountered the case of "the bamboo shoots growing crookedly under a stone," which he investigated.

I only regret that at that time there were no good spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in Lingnan with whom I could verify my realization. In the year Jisi, I crossed the mountain range to visit Master Boshan.
Even he never spoke a single word of the fundamental principle to me. One day, taking up the phrase "riding a cow backward into the Buddha hall," I asked Master Shan:

To think it is so is still a reversal. An ant drags a great millstone; A stone man claps his hands and laughs. This is a distinct, living mechanism;
It does not fall within the scales of the musical modes. The former master said, "Too coarse, you fellow! I, this mountain monk, replied, "Even if one were to be truly great and capable..."
"Person, how would you open your mouth toward the Monk? My late teacher looked at me for a long time and said, 'What need is there to say?
At this point, I clearly saw where my late teacher was acting as a person. In the fourth month of the Gengwu year, I took my leave of my late teacher;
he tried to detain me with great earnestness, but I could not stay. He instructed me that I must certainly return in the eighth month, making this agreement two or three times. I did not expect..."
The Master entered nirvana in the ninth month. Thus he said: "When there is a cause, there is a reason for the matter.
Today, as I offer this incense, I dare not fail my late teacher. After a long silence, he called to the assembly, saying: "The true likeness of the late teacher is right here.
But where, ultimately, is the late teacher? He drew a circle with his whisk and said: "Majestic and dignified—his fame covers all!"
The color of the horse: it pervades the entire world and has never been hidden. *Ei!* It is clearly and manifestly just this—how magnificent!
Addressing the assembly: This matter has nothing else to it. It does not increase in sages; it does not decrease among ordinary people.
It is only because of defilement and purity that there is a distinction. Nanyue said: "All dharmas arise from the mind and its perceptions. If the mind does not arise, dharmas have no power."
Abide. If you reach the ground of the mind, your actions will be unimpeded; yet unless you encounter those of superior faculties, you must be cautious with your words.
You all should simply trust your own mind: outside the mind there are no phenomena. All dharmas are established in dependence upon the mind; apart from the mind, nothing at all can be found.
O Venerable Elders, simply turn the light back toward your own mind for a single thought-moment, and the numinous wisdom of *prajñā* will manifest spontaneously.

To illuminate oneself is not at all laborious. People of the present day merely rush outward in search of some conceptual understanding to rely upon, or they perform some kind of practice that can be grasped, taking this to be the essential core. As for the matter of their own fundamental nature, they pay it no heed.
It becomes pitch black. Truly pitiable! This matter is like space, and also like the body and its shadow;
there is simply no place for you to evade it. Why do you not grasp it right where you stand? After a long silence, he said:
"Extremely clear. He spoke again: "Too extremely clear! Ehi! Precisely because it is too extremely clear, it causes what is attained to be delayed. Be careful!"
Addressing the assembly: "All you senior monks, one month passes after another, one day follows upon another.

How do you apply your mind? You must seek thorough penetration from beginning to end. Look at the ancients: they sat here until seven meditation cushions were worn through. What kind of application of mind was that?
Nowadays, as soon as people set out to travel for study, they already think of holding the whisk and opening the hall. Zhaozhou said: 'You..."
Simply investigate the principle while sitting and observing for twenty or thirty years. If you do not attain realization, then cut off this old monk’s head!
There is not much to the Buddha-dharma; it is difficult to find those who will persevere for the long term.

Thirty years ago, when I was at Boshan, I saw many people who applied themselves with great hardship to investigation; nowadays, I see none at all who truly exert their minds. This kind of exertion of mind is simply...
To wait for awakening with the mind is for this illness to have entered the vital organs; it will remain untreated for the rest of one’s life.

Great assembly, you must practice with absolute sincerity. Whether it takes twenty or thirty years, or even if you do not achieve penetration in a single lifetime, continue to practice in this manner.
Provided you maintain a pure heart, what is there that cannot be accomplished?

Addressing the assembly: "Venerable seniors, do not engage in idle conceptualization. Spending your whole day studying words, displaying your cleverness, composing verses and gāthās, and seeking out clues from books—what benefit is there in this? If the matter of the Zen school were found in books,"
The Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the teachings—how could these be without words? Why, then, did Bodhidharma come from the West and sweep everything away?
Why do you not simply rest right where you are? Lately, the maladies of the Chan path are beyond counting.

There is one kind of person whose consciousness is vast and turbulent, who ceaselessly fabricates strange phenomena and provokes countless others to play with their karmic ignorance. There is another kind...
To sit fixedly upon the meditation cushion, suppressing the arising and ceasing of thoughts, is to make one’s living in a ghost cave.
Foyan said, "In all quarters, they either kill you by sitting you down, or they kill you by making you run. Students must be extremely careful.

All you venerable seniors, examine this carefully! Yet, it is precisely at the moment when one is serene and free of intention that there is a fine message—provided, however, that you do not [seek it] on purpose.
The ground does not change. Whether opening or closing the eyes, whether on the upper bunk or the lower bunk—who, ultimately, is it? Do you understand? Take care. To the assembly:
When the ancients reached greatness and maturity, they still remained deeply hidden in hills and valleys. Only when pressed by the dragons and devas did they emerge to act for others.
You, venerable seniors, must tread with reality at every step. Only when there is something remaining within yourself can you reach out to others. Not otherwise.
He met Grand Master Lu Xun, who asked Nanquan, "Among the seven hundred people at Huangmei, why did no one receive the robe and bowl, while only the Layman Lu received them?
Nanquan replied, "The seven hundred people all understood the Buddha-dharma; only the Layman Lu did not understand the Buddha-dharma.
Nowadays, there is no patch-robed monk who does not say, 'I understand the Buddha-dharma. Try asking him a single question."

Immediately, his eyes flickered with realization as he investigated the source of his illness. It was simply because he had forcibly displayed his "head and horns" rather than applying effort at the "heels.
Thus, the ancients said: "The more one retreats, the clearer one becomes; the less one understands, the more power one possesses.
But tell me, what is it that one does not understand? If you have not yet reached this state, then even if you exhaustively master all principles, it will be of no avail.
It is merely the work of a madman or an ignorant person; how could such a one know how to pull out nails and extract wedges for others?
In the past, Master Bobshan once said, "Twenty years after my passing, the ancestral wind will have been swept from the ground, and even in a local shrine, people will be giving formal sermons.
On that day, he spoke with a sense of urgency, never imagining that today we would personally witness this very event. How lamentable! How tragic!

[The Master] sighed and addressed the assembly: "The karmic conditions regarding the bamboo stick are extremely direct and incisive. When I was in seclusion at Golden Wheel Temple, I saw a monk sitting upright upon a rock.
I asked him what kind of practice he was engaged in, and he replied, 'I am contemplating the bamboo stick. I asked him—"
"How do you look at it? he asked. He replied, "In the place of non-illumination, I press forward and pursue it all the more.
The mountain monk said to him, "You must rather look back from behind; first, see what principle this 'non-illumination' is.
At this, he felt a sense of acute awareness. The mountain monk merely gave him a brief point with a single phrase, and he immediately acted according to what was taught.
He departed. At midnight, he suddenly attained realization. The mountain monk tested him with the story of the *bājiāo* staff, asking:
"What is your staff? I give you my staff. He replied: "Sweeping bird tracks in the air. "What is it when you have no staff?
I take your staff away from you. He replied: "A single spark in a red-hot furnace."
Snow! How joyful this is! Therefore, regarding this matter, it is essential that you attain it within your own mind;
then it will naturally roll on and on. Be careful.
Addressing the assembly: This mountain monk has no choice but to serve as the abbot of this mountain.

While I certainly accept the earnest invitation of the officials and lay devotees, it is also because I have personally observed that the site of the nineteenth patriarch’s practice hall has remained neglected for so long that I could not set my mind at ease.

However, as we are now merely establishing the foundations, the four necessities are not yet complete. Therefore, if you members of the assembly truly wish to associate with me through the Way, you must not be indifferent to these matters.
To have few worldly thoughts and to be able to endure a life of simplicity is precisely the vessel for entering the Way.
It has been my constant prayer to the Bodhisattva Weituo that I might remain without karmic ties to this world; this is not a pretense of emotion.

Even if one were fully endowed with blessings and favorable conditions, how could such a spectacular emergence—startling heaven and shaking the earth—have any connection to the fundamental matter? It is just as when the World-Honored One [spent] forty-nine...

Over the course of his life, he preached the Dharma in more than three hundred assemblies, and immeasurable numbers of humans and devas attained liberation. A single episode from his life is like a dream or a phantom;
how much more so the worldly abundance of body, clothing, speech, and food—such luxuriant enjoyments ultimately end in transformation and extinction.

You who have left the home-life for the sake of transcending birth and death must recognize that which does not change or perish. Before the six patriarchs departed from the assembly, the assembly all...
[The assembly] wept bitterly. The Patriarch said, "I know my own destination myself, which is why I have told you.
Right now, is there anyone who knows where the Sixth Patriarch has gone? Look, look!"

The practice of emptiness and stillness. Penetrating the characteristics of all dharmas without attachment or obstruction, I bow my head to that which is like space, having no dependence.

The disciples of the Great Master adorn themselves by constantly upholding this verse. Within the great and most terrifying ocean of birth and death, when Muzhou was traveling on foot, he reached Mount Tiantai and encountered Hanshan and Shide;
for a moment he was utterly bewildered. Hanshan said: "Since parting from Vulture Peak..."

the ancients called such people "those who toy with their own spirits. Observe how the Sixth Patriarch instructed Yongjia—why do you not embody this?
"Non-arising. To realize that there is no grasping is to be swift. Yongjia said, "The essence is non-arising; to realize the original state is to be swift. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is.
What kind of spiritual eloquence and marvelous discernment! What kind of profound discourse on entering the principle!

After a long silence, he said, "When I was young, I recited the 'Chapter on Emptiness and Patience' from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and consequently, I was unaware of the existence of body, mind, or the physical world. Such is this realm."
It has been nearly ten days since then; yet every time I bring it up, I still feel a sense of exhilaration. To the assembly:
This one matter of cultivation can only be realized through self-acceptance. What is called the Way is not words or language;
it is simply the principle of the ordinary. Yesterday someone asked: "Not mind, not Buddha, not things—what is this?"
"Ma! The old monk raises his whisk and asks again, "Ultimately, what is this?
The old monk then lowers the whisk. Now I ask you all: that which the eyes do not see and the ears do not hear—what is this?
All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; do not let them pass you by right before your face. This matter is not...
This is a single utterance that exhausts the very bottom. Even if one were to speak with the utmost mystery and subtlety, it would have no connection at all.
Only by attaining it within the mind does one finally possess the handle. You people have been following after forms and chasing after sounds from beginning to end;

you have never for a single moment turned the light back to reflect upon yourselves. Therefore, day by day and month by month, you grow more distant. Although you have never set yourself right, its...
The ten stages are realized as they are; there is not a single hair’s breadth of increase or decrease. What, after all, is this? Strive with all your might to grasp it! Addressing the assembly:
In the past, Dàsui was at Mìoyán’s assembly for several years; his food did not reach satiety, and he sought no warmth in his sleep.
He refined his practice through austere asceticism, and his conduct was beyond the common. Master Shandao held him in high esteem.
One day, he asked him, "Upādhyāya, while you have been here with this old monk, you have never asked a single turning-word question. He replied immediately, "Where would you have me begin?"
Daguang said, "Why do you not ask, 'What is the Buddha? He then made a gesture with his hand and covered Daguang's mouth.
Daguang sighed and said, "You have truly attained the marrow. The assembly, look! Dasui said, "Where am I to apply my words?
Truly, it is like a needle that cannot pierce it; even Foyan could not peer into it. At such a time, Daguan—
Yet he was still unwilling to let the matter pass so hastily. He further instructed him to ask, "What is the Buddha? and immediately covered the other’s mouth. Baizhang then nodded his head.
Such was the thorough rigor with which the ancients helped others. O Great Assembly, why do you not reflect upon this?
If you can penetrate through this here and now, what Chan is there to study? What Way is there to learn? What more need be said? This—
All things are fully present within each person. Yet, alas, there are those who starve right beside their own rice baskets. If you seek it, you will know that it cannot be seen;
yet it never leaves its place, remaining ever-present and serene. Take heed.
He preached the Bodhisattva precepts to the assembly, showing that the mind itself is the Buddha, the mind itself is the Dharma, and the mind itself is the Sangha.
The mind itself is morality, concentration, and wisdom. Whether sentient or insentient, mundane or supramundane—all phenomena are devoid of any inherent nature.
That which is called the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is precisely your own mind. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "All phenomena lack the essence of a phenomenon;
it is taught that they are nothing but mind. Failing to perceive one's own mind, one gives rise to conceptual discrimination. Therefore, all phenomena are established in dependence upon the mind;
outside the mind, no phenomenon can be found, and outside phenomena, no mind can be found. This is what is meant by "mind."

The Dharma is one and suchness; there is no mind and no dharma. O Sons of the Buddha, that which is thus is the Vajra Jewel Precept, the seed of the Buddha-nature, the source of all Buddhas, and the root of Bodhisattvas. If sentient beings obtain this precept, they immediately enter the rank of Buddhahood.

As the Sutra says: "When sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas. Having attained a rank equal to Great Enlightenment, they are truly [enlightened]."

O sons of the Buddha, the essential meaning of the precepts lies solely in preventing what is improper and forbidding evil, thereby guarding and maintaining the inherently pure mind one possesses by nature.

If one realizes this mind, there is not a single dharma outside of it that can serve as a condition or an object of opposition. Since no such conditions or objects exist, [the mind remains unconditioned].

Thus, there is nothing transgressed. Since there is nothing transgressed, there is likewise nothing that can be maintained. To have neither capacity nor object is what is truly called upholding the precepts.

Alas, all sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamentally pure mind; consequently, phenomena such as the faculties and objects arise. Once these various phenomena exist, [transgression and maintenance follow].
Furthermore, giving rise to craving and grasping, one enters various realms of existence and sets in motion body and speech, thereby creating all manner of karma.
Since the cause of karma exists, how can its fruit be escaped? Thus, the retributive suffering of the three miserable paths and the cycle of birth and death have no end.

Yet, when one thoroughly investigates their ultimate source, they truly possess no root or origin. This delusion has no foundation; its nature is ultimately empty. Sentient beings do not know this and thus falsely undergo [suffering].

Bound by fetters, when my Buddha appeared in the world, he gave rise to great compassion. For those of superior faculties, he directly pointed out their original mind so that they might attain awakening;
for those of middling and inferior faculties, he used skillful means to uplift and encourage them, teaching them to cease evil and practice good—this is the Dharma of the Precepts.

Regarding what should and should not be done, what constitutes upholding and what constitutes transgression—regarding these various names and characteristics, how could a person of great power and strength casually take them as their own equipment?
Even the single word "Buddha" they would not like to hear; how much less would they call anything "precepts"?

Nevertheless, even though this is so, one must truly settle into practice before it can be achieved. Otherwise, one will paint a tiger and end up with a wildcat, wandering aimlessly and inviting disaster.
The calamities and misfortunes resulting from this are not slight; therefore, this precept cannot be neglected by those at the beginning of their practice.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* likens it to a life-preserving float, and the *Teaching Left Behind* (Śāriputraprakaraṇa) repeatedly and earnestly exhorts us to revere and cherish the *Prātimokṣa* as if the Buddha were still in the world.
This is because within the realm of arising and ceasing, one cannot suddenly transcend through expedient means;

if one does not directly attain a state of non-mindfulness, and lacks the goodness of the precepts, one will ultimately fail to achieve success and will inevitably fall. Even the retribution of humans and devas is difficult to expect, let alone the unsurpassed *bodhi* of all Buddhas.
Therefore, in returning from delusion to awakening, the precepts are truly the necessary provisions; in proceeding from cause toward fruit, the precepts serve as the foundation.
To begin with, protecting one's own mind within and avoiding reproach without, for the sake of both self-benefit and the benefit of others, constitutes the conduct and vows of a bodhisattva.
Since ancient times, those who study the Buddha have upheld these teachings upon their heads, receiving them as one who starved receives food or one who thirsted receives a drink.

It is like a poor person obtaining treasure, or a naked person obtaining clothing; it is truly not without cause. O Sons of the Buddha, you should conceive a sense of preciousness toward these jewels of the precepts and ensure that no transgression occurs.
Although it is said that if one is without intention (*citta*), there is no precept, you must know that it is precisely through being without intention that the precept can be obtained.

This is because those with intention constantly transgress the precepts; whereas those without [the intent to transgress] obtain the precept, and those who possess the precept [are free from such transgression].
Because the mind is constantly bound, the "mindless mind" is the true Buddha-mind; the "preceptless precept" is the beginning of the precept of nature (*dharmatā-śīla*).
This mind and this precept are non-dual and without distinction. The transmission from Buddha to Buddha and the succession from Patriarch to Patriarch consist solely of this secret.
It cannot be compared with the precepts and codes of discipline of humans, devas, or the other two vehicles. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"I establish all my children within the secret treasury. Within this secret treasury, the three virtues are fully present;

when these three virtues are perfected, the single mind is revealed. Thereby, the myriad practices serve as adornments, and the nature-ocean of the *Avataṃsaka* is infinitely layered and inexhaustible.

Nor is there any addition, even as small as a hair-tip, to one's own fundamental mind. Long ago, when the World-Honored One attained equal and perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, he exclaimed:
"How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata;
yet because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they do not realize it. If they were free from deluded thoughts, all-encompassing wisdom and unimpeded wisdom would be manifest."
The Master’s wisdom is immediately manifested before you. O Sons of the Buddha, you need only look at the single phrase "leaving delusion behind.
The World-Honored One earnestly brought this forth to teach people to directly and immediately be without mind. If you are without mind, what further matter could there be? Deshan said:
You need only have no concern for phenomena within the mind and no mind regarding phenomena; then you will be spiritual in your emptiness and wondrous in your voidness.
To speak of a beginning or an end, even by so much as the tip of a hair, is entirely to deceive oneself. The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"All dharmas exist only through the differentiation of deluded thoughts. If one is free from deluded thoughts, then there are no signs of any objective realms. Thus it is.
Within, there is no mind of one's own; without, there is no object of one's own. When both mind and object have vanished, from whom could precepts be established?
O sons of the Buddha, since there are no precepts to be obtained, what ultimately can they be called? After a long silence, he said: "Tsk! Go on and receive the precepts."
Tea Talk at Guanghui.
This mountain monk has arrived here and has received the profound hospitality of Layman Wang and others. This mountain monk has nothing to say;
if you have doubts, members of the assembly, please ask. When the assembly remained silent, the Master said: "This mountain monk, since..."
I have studied the Way for nearly thirty years, yet in truth, there is no dharma to be attained.

I have simply gained faith in my own mind and realized that outside of this mind, not a single dharma exists—this is what has been transmitted from Buddha to Buddha and handed down from patriarch to patriarch.

It is nothing other than gaining faith in one's own mind. Yet nowadays, as the Buddha-dharma declines, people everywhere constantly speak of "matters pertaining to the side of dharmas" and "dharmas..."
Regarding the matter of the body turning upward: here in my mountain monastery, there is nothing at all of the School of the Patriarchs; there is nothing with which to deliberate.

Having attained this, people today for the most part take their minds to study the Way and take their minds to seek the Dharma.

If one takes the mind to study the Way and takes the mind to seek the Dharma, even throughout kalpas and until the end of one’s life, one will ultimately never attain it. Why is this? It is simply because outside the mind there is truly no dharma to be attained.
If there were a dharma to be attained outside the mind, that would be called a non-Buddhist path (*tīrthika*). O Great Assembly, you must be extremely careful.
It is transformed by oneself; it is only when one turns back upon oneself that it is attained. After a long silence, he said: "The assembly has no question;
this mountain monk has no answer. It is even more wondrous than that. Take care."
A Tea Talk on Extensive Wisdom. One who recognizes the mind and reaches the original source is therefore called a śramaṇa. Does the assembly recognize the mind?
If you cannot recognize it, how will you evade the arrival of birth and death? Formerly, a monk asked Dongshan, "When cold and heat arrive, how can one avoid them?
Dongshan said, "Why not go to a place where there is no cold or heat to avoid them? The monk said:
"There is no place free from cold and heat; how can one avoid them? The Master said, "When it is cold, I will freeze you to death, monk!
When it is hot, I will scorch you to death, monk! "Great assembly, how do you understand this? If you can understand these words, only then will you have a way to respond and interact.
Physical vigor does not linger; it is like a galloping horse. Human life is impermanent, passing away faster than flowing water or moving mountains. Do not speak of the riches of the human world."
The pursuit of honor and fame does not endure for long. Even for one who has left the household life, there are no worldly ties; several decades will pass easily.
Why not, while your physical strength and vigor are still sound, seek a place of ultimate rest? You must turn the light inward to reach the fundamental source;
only when you have found the path of liberation can it be achieved. A monk asked: "I do not recognize my own mind; I beg the Master for instruction."
"Compassion. The Master said, "Compassion is right where you are. A monk asked, "Regarding the four-line verse of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, I do not know which four lines they are.

A monk asked, "The nature is fundamentally pure; why then do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?"
The Master said: "In my place here, there is neither the 'pure and original state' nor the mountains, rivers, and great earth.
Tonight, the head monk Guanghui Yinchu has invited this mountain monk for tea. Do you understand? The monk was at a loss. Another monk asked:

"Regarding the *ālaya-vijñāna*, the *manas-vijñāna*, and the six consciousnesses, I have not yet understood them in my own mind. I beg you to show me the place where one establishes one's body and life."
