You must truly resolve your minds and practice authentically for the sake of birth and death; only then will your stay on this mountain not be in vain.

As for the matters of the Zen school, it is extremely difficult even to open one's mouth. What need is there to speak of those of superior capacity? But as for those of middling or inferior capacity—"
The ancients did not fail to provide the expedient means of "dropping the hands. As soon as there is a phrase for practicing, in reality, what practice is there to be done?
The ancients said: "The two words 'Direct Pointing' are already a detour. As soon as one says "nothing to do," one has already done too much.
In such a state, where is there any opening for speech? Therefore it is said: "This matter is realized by myself alone."
Know this. Furthermore, it is said: "One must know that which exists, yet seek not to know it. Master Danxia said: "Every person has their own sitting mat;

when Buddhas and Patriarchs emerge, they do not increase it by even a single hair’s breadth. Right now, all you venerable monks and laypeople here have not decreased it by even a single hair’s breadth.
It is simply that, at this very moment, to hear once and awaken in a thousand ways is extremely difficult."
"One cannot help but rely on expedient means; the assembly must expend a measure of mental effort before it can be attained. After a long silence, he said:

"All you who have come together, you have traveled this road with hardship to reach this place. It is precisely now that you should settle your minds. Since you have taken up your duties, each of you must strive diligently.
If you have any doubts, do not hesitate to ask. A monk asked: "I do not ask about the restoration of Huashou Monastery; [I ask about] beholding [the Buddha] face-to-face..."
"Meeting face-to-face, what is your intention? The Master said, "Two eyes facing two eyes.

The monk asked further, "When the sea wind blows all night long and not a speck of dust remains upon the great earth, what then? The Master said, "Sitting alone on the Huashou Terrace. The monk bowed;
the Master spoke again, "This matter is not something that ends with mere words. If you truly wish to see your nature, you must truly realize it for yourself."
One must rest; one can rest or cannot rest. Try examining this for yourself. As for those who are able to explain it, they may have plenty of intelligence and wit;

it is not difficult for them to speak a chapter or two. If they read some records of the Zen "Passes" and the collections of Gao Feng and Zhong Feng, they need not even realize the Way themselves before they would know how to teach others. What connection does that have [to true realization]? To cite one example:
The Elder did not speak with the monks for an entire summer retreat. One monk sighed, saying, "I have truly spent this summer in vain;
even hearing the two characters 'Right Cause' (zhengyin) would have been good. The Elder said, "Reverend, do not speak so hastily. As for the Right Cause, there is not even a single character.
Having said this, he tapped his teeth and remarked, "It was not right of me to speak thus. A neighbor in the room...
An elder monk heard this and said, "What a pity—a whole pot of soup has been defiled by two mouse droppings.

The Master said, "If one sees the banner pole in front of Zifu Monastery from across the river and turns back immediately, one is already eight *ke* late; how much more so if one actually crosses the river?
This matter cannot be reached through a single blow, a shout, a single pivot or object, or even through one or two turns of speech."
"Once one has reached the other shore, it is truly a great difficulty, a great difficulty! O Great Assembly, you must resolve to transcend birth and death; only then will there be true realization.
When I was young, what did I know of Zen practice or the realization of the Way? I simply feared that birth and death would arrive and that the path ahead was vast and uncertain.
Later, upon seeing the *Platform Sutra*, I first learned that seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha. Alas, how regrettable!"
After deliberating for a hundred reckonings, he has only just managed to find peace of mind; this was by no means an easy matter. After a long silence, he said:

"In recent years, I, this mountain monk, have been plagued by many ailments and my physical strength has become too weak. I am unable to manage the affairs of the monastic community; we must rely upon all you venerable elders to work together with a single heart.
Only as for the Buddha-Dharma do I dare not leave it undecided. If there is any discussion, I shall not dare to fail you. As if...
Throughout the world today, everywhere is in a state of chaos and turmoil; yet this place remains peaceful and secure, like dwelling in quiet seclusion deep within the mountains.
It is excellent for everyone to train both body and mind here. Take care.
A Tea Talk on the Occasion of a Birthday. The Master said: "This morning, I raised the story of Old Teacher Wang regarding the time prior to the empty kalpa.
How do you all understand it? Old Teacher Wang also said: 'The Way does not belong to knowing, nor does it belong to not-knowing.
Knowing is deluded perception; not-knowing is indeterminate. How then do you all understand this? He further said it is simply non-existence..."

People perceive and understand through consciousness. Furthermore, it is said that the Way belongs neither to knowing nor to not-knowing. One who has attained it need not harbor doubt or deliberation;
if one harbors doubt or deliberation, one is ten thousand *li* away from Ya Zhou. Therefore, this mountain monk says: "To conceive of a thought is already an error.
O Venerable Ones, if you understand, you understand immediately; there is no further dharma remaining. An ancient also said: "One must clearly realize the matter of the other shore."
Yet you come to walk upon this side. The mountain monk says: there is no "that side," nor is there this side. If one attains it, one attains it;

there is no further waiting for a specific time. You need only realize what is before your eyes: that which existed prior to the empty kalpa is also right before your eyes, and all that will endure until the end of future kalpas is also right before your eyes.
Have you not heard it said: when the ancients spoke of "knowing and seeing," knowing and seeing are themselves the mind.
When the mind is present, there is knowing and seeing; that knowing and seeing is right here and now. Therefore, to realize it is simply to be thus.
If one does not understand what is before one's eyes, the myriad conditions will appear as distinct and separate. After a long silence, he said:

"Regarding this matter, there are those who know it by birth and those who know it through study. Ultimately, they are all the same. Those who know it by birth are truly rare to find. He sought them out.
Among the various patriarchs, those such as Danxia and Zhaozhou were individuals who possessed innate knowledge.
When Zhaozhou met Nanquan, Nanquan asked, "Are you a novice with a master, or a novice without a master? Zhaozhou replied, "I am a novice with a master. Nanquan asked, "Where is your master?
Zhaozhou bowed his body and said, "It is still cold in the early spring; I humbly wish the Master the ten thousand blessings of good health. All [the patriarchs].
Elder, had you simply turned over this news right then and there, at all times—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether moving, turning, bowing, or looking up;
whether welcoming guests or attending to visitors; even when defecating or urinating—there would have been nothing that was not the wondrous function of spiritual power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
When Zhaozhou was only fourteen years old at the time, how could he have ever expended the slightest effort? The next day, he asked Nanquan, "What is..."
Daoqian said, "Ordinary mind is the Way. Look at this: Nanquan did not require any special expedients;

he was simply like a person at home speaking of household matters. Zhaozhou asked again, "Is there still any need for directed effort? Nanquan said, "To intend to direct oneself is already to deviate from it.
Zhaozhou said, "If one does not intend it, how can one know it is the Way? Nanquan said, "Regarding what I just mentioned, how many phrases were raised?"
The Way does not belong to knowing, nor does it belong to not-knowing. Knowing is deluded awareness; not-knowing is indeterminate.
If one truly penetrates the Way that is free from doubt, it is like the great void—vast, open, and expansive. How could one forcibly impose distinctions of right and wrong?
O Venerable Elders, do not lightly dismiss these two phrases: "The Way does not belong to knowing, nor does it belong to not-knowing. You all eat your rice!
Satiated. When one wishes to walk, one walks; when one wishes to sit, one sits. Mountains are mountains; waters are waters; monks are monks; laypeople are laypeople.
At such a moment, even the Buddha-eye cannot see it. It is a pity that one has missed it right here and now.
I remember when I was young, seeing a Shaolin Dharma Master cite this dialogue: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "A student has newly entered the monastery;
I beg the Master for instruction. Zhaozhou said, "Have you eaten your rice gruel yet? The monk replied, "I have eaten my rice gruel. Zhaozhou said, "Go wash your bowl.
At that time, although I had not yet penetrated it thoroughly, hearing these words made my hair stand on end.
It was spine-chilling, like cold water being poured over one's back. Furthermore, I heard Master Wansong’s commentary: "Washing the face, you touch the nostrils;
pulling on the shoes, you rub the heels. At that moment, if you miss the pivot of the phrase (*huatou*), it is like digging in the earth to seek the sky.
This is why those who do not understand are pitiable; they have missed so much of their precious time.
When I, this mountain monk, speak in this way, you all listen and then immediately begin to deliberate, asking, "How can we know? This is merely adding a head atop your own head.
To seek the eye with the eye—ancient masters said that even if you study until you reach the very side of the Buddha, it is still a mixed application of the mind.
I, this mountain monk, constantly raise this discourse: why is it that reaching the side of the Buddha is still a mixed application of the mind? The *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says:
"Even to realize the pure nirvāṇa of a Tathāgata is still the mark of self. At this point, one must attain awakening before it can be achieved.
"Eh? Those who do not know have already missed many fine moments; those who do know have likewise squandered many fine moments.
The fault of those who do not know lies in their ignorance; the fault of those who do know lies in their knowledge. It is most difficult to find that which is exactly right.
Ultimately, how can one attain that which is exactly right? All you venerable ones, such a thing truly exists. If you believe it..."
And then it is finished. If you have faith that reaches this point, you must realize it with true substance; only when you have truly and completely mastered it will you attain it.
This cannot be compared to worldly achievements; it is simply the ending of birth and death in a single lifetime.
For us, who have come to this day after immeasurable kalpas, if we were to master it now, it would be forever unattainable [again]. You must exert great effort. Thus says the mountain monk.
To speak of it a thousand times or ten thousand times does nothing more than provide an aid to its awakening; the single word "directly" (qie) rests, however, with the person themselves.
Who else can exert effort on your behalf? A monk asked, "The moon's reflection is vast and shimmering; how is it that the Buddha saves sentient beings? The Master said:
"Wooden head. The monk asked, "When the moonlight is vast and shimmering, what is the Buddha who delivers sentient beings? The Master said, "A common brick.
The monk asked, "What is the Buddha who delivers as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges? The Buddhas have never been different from ordinary people.
The Master said, "Regarding those two previous phrases, how do you understand them? The monk was at a loss. Another monk asked, "A Taoist sells a spirit..."
Fú said, "Why is it that everything is auspicious everywhere? The Master said, "What are you doing, flapping those two pieces of skin back and forth?

Fú replied, "The Master does not know good from bad. The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment that this mountain monk does not know good from bad, how about you, Upādhyāya, who do not know good from bad?
What then? Fú replied, "A single perfect sphere; wherever it goes, all is in harmony."
The Master said, "This is the stolen goods. The monk stepped forward and asked, "And what about you, Preceptor? The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, have no place to hide my shame.
The monk bowed and rose, intending to offer further words, but the Master said, "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak," and immediately returned to his quarters.

Tea Talk. [The Master] cited the verse by the scholar Zhang Zhuo: "Brilliant and silent illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges; Ordinary beings, sages, and all living creatures are of one family. When a single thought does not arise, the whole body is revealed; As soon as the six sense organs stir, they are obscured by clouds. To try to eliminate afflictions is to increase the illness; To strive toward True Suchness is likewise a deviation. Accord with worldly conditions without attachment or hindrance— This is Nirvana. Nirvana. Birth. Death. Transmigration. The cycle of birth and death. The wheel of rebirth. Samsara. The ocean of suffering. The path of delusion. The realm of ignorance. The prison of the five aggregates. The thicket of views. The net of craving. The darkness of ignorance. The fire of passion. The river of birth and death. The mountain of pride. The forest of doubt. The pit of greed. The abyss of anger. The whirlpool of attachment. The storm of aversion. The fog of delusion. The fetters of the three poisons. The shackles of the four bonds. The chains of the five hindrances. The yoke of the six sense objects. The snare of the seven consciousnesses. The trap of the eight worldly dharmas. The cage of the nine dwellings. The snare of the ten realms of existence. [The Master continued: "If you can understand this verse, you will see that from the very beginning there has been nothing to attain, and from the very beginning there has been nothing to lose. It is like the great void of space—vast, open, and unobstructed. It is like the bright moon in the sky—clear, cool, and luminous. It is like the vast ocean—deep, calm, and boundless. It is like the great earth—firm, stable, and supporting all things. It is like the great sun—shining universally upon all without partiality. It is like the great wind—blowing freely through all directions without obstruction. It is like the great fire—burning away all delusions without residue. It is like the great water—washing away all impurities without exception. It is like the great mountain—unmoved by the winds of the world. It is like the great tree—providing shade for all who seek it. It is like the great jewel—fulfilling the needs of all who behold it. It is like the great drum—resounding throughout the ten directions. It is like the great bell—awakening those who sleep. It is like the great mirror—reflecting all forms without distortion. It is like the great lamp—illuminating the dark night. It is like the great cloud—raining down the Dharma rain. It is like the great thunder—striking the ears of the deluded. It is like the great lightning—revealing the true nature of reality. It is like the great rain—nourishing all seeds of goodness. It is like the great harvest—bringing forth the fruit of liberation. It is like the great feast—satisfying the hunger of all beings. It is like the great medicine—curing the disease of suffering. It is like the great physician—diagnosing the ailment of ignorance. It is like the great surgeon—removing the tumor of the ego. It is like the great chariot—carrying all beings to the city of Nirvana. It is like the great bridge—crossing over the river of birth and death. It is like the great boat—sailing across the sea of samsara. It is like the great palace—dwelling in the bliss of the Dharma-realm. It is like the great garden—blooming with the flowers of wisdom. It is like the great grove—filled with the fragrance of virtue. It is like the great stream—flowing toward the ocean of enlightenment. It is like the great river—uniting all waters into one. It is like the great ocean—containing all jewels of the Dharma. It is like the great treasure—granting the wealth of liberation. It is like the great king—ruling over the kingdom of truth. It is like the great minister—assisting in the governance of the Dharma. It is like the great general—defeating the armies of Mara. It is like the great warrior—conquering the enemies of the passions. It is like the great hero—protecting all beings from harm. It is like the great sage—living in peace and harmony. It is like the great saint—attaining the ultimate goal. It is like the great Buddha—manifesting the supreme enlightenment. It is like the great Dharma—turning the wheel of the teachings. It is like the great Sangha—maintaining the harmony of the community. It is like the great assembly—gathering together in the Dharma-hall. It is like the great banquet—sharing the feast of the Dharma. It is like the great dance—performing the dance of liberation. It is like the great song—singing the song of the Dharma. It is like the great laughter—laughing at the folly of the world. It is like the great weeping—weeping for the suffering of others. It is like the great joy—rejoicing in the attainment of the Way. It is like the great sorrow—sorrowing for those who have not yet awakened. It is like the great compassion—embracing all beings with love. It is like the great kindness—benefiting all beings without limit. It is like the great patience—enduring all hardships with equanimity. It is like the great diligence—striving tirelessly for the sake of others. It is like the great meditation—abiding in the stillness of the mind. It is like the great wisdom—penetrating the nature of reality. It is like the great emptiness—free from all conceptualizations. It is like the great signlessness—beyond all marks and characteristics. It is like the great wishlessness—free from all desires and attachments. It is like the great non-arising—unborn and undying. It is like the great non-extinction—neither coming nor going. It is like the great non-duality—beyond all distinctions. It is like the great non-discrimination—beyond all judgments. It is like the great non-attachment—beyond all clinging. It is like the great non-obstruction—beyond all barriers. It is like the great non-dwelling—beyond all resting places. It is like the great non-abiding—beyond all foundations. It is like the great non-grasping—beyond all seizing. It is like the great non-releasing—beyond all letting go. It is like the great non-taking—beyond all receiving. It is like the great non-giving—beyond all bestowing. It is like the great non-doing—beyond all actions. It is like the great non-non-doing—beyond all inactions. It is like the great non-being—beyond all existence. It is like the great non-non-being—beyond all non-existence. It is like the great non-both—beyond all duality. It is like the great non-neither—beyond all extremes. It is like the great non-middle—beyond all centers. It is like the great non-center—beyond all peripheries. It is like the great non-periphery—beyond all boundaries. It is like the great non-boundary—beyond all limits. It is like the great non-limit—beyond all measurements. It is like the great non-measurement—beyond all scales. It is like the great non-scale—beyond all weights. It is like the great non-weight—beyond all balances. It is like the great non-balance—beyond all comparisons. It is like the great non-comparison—beyond all analogies. It is like the great non-analogy—beyond all metaphors. It is like the great non-metaphor—beyond all symbols. It is like the great non-symbol—beyond all signs. It is like the great non-sign—beyond all indications. It is like the great non-indication—beyond all pointers. It is like the great non-pointer—beyond all guides. It is like the great non-guide—beyond all leaders. It is like the great non-leader—beyond all followers. It is like the great non-follower—beyond all disciples. It is like the great non-disciple—beyond all students. It is like the great non-student—beyond all learners. It is like the great non-learner—beyond all trainees. It is like the great non-trainee—beyond all practitioners. It is like the great non-practitioner—beyond all seekers. It is like the great non-seeker—beyond all aspirants. It is like the great non-aspirant—beyond all devotees. It is like the great non-devotee—beyond all believers. It is like the great non-believer—beyond all faithful ones. It is like the great non-faith—beyond all trust. It is like the great non-trust—beyond all reliance. It is like the great non-reliance—beyond all dependence. It is like the great non-dependence—beyond all support. It is like the great non-support—beyond all bases. It is like the great non-base—beyond all grounds. It is like
"Death and the like are like flowers in the sky. The Master said, "All you venerable elders, you must firmly plant your feet upon the solid ground before you can succeed.
When the ancients tested people, they would know whether one had realization or not by a single word or half-sentence. Therefore, people probe with words;
if one has realization, it will naturally be distinct and extraordinary, just as when masters meet, it is like two mirrors reflecting one another. At last—
Do not be confused. If you merely engage in one sentence after another, seeking only verbal fluency, what use is there?
Do not say this is a modern phenomenon; even in ancient times, this malady already existed. As Mahamati said: "Lately, the monastics..."

He was unwilling to apply himself to the practice where effort is saved, but instead busied himself in a frantic manner, presenting his intellectual views and composing verses on ancient cases (*gong'an*).
Yunmen told him, "This is not the principle," and immediately seized him, refusing to let him go.
Let me ask you this: have you yet been able to let yourself go? Each of you, venerable elders, must know shame;
do not allow those who understand to mock you. Tonight, I, this mountain monk, shall pierce through your delusions for you. If you are one who has attained realization—
Lift it up and you know it at once; as the silk comes and the thread goes, they naturally and elegantly harmonize. Look!
Layman Pang visited Master Songshan, and just as he arrived, the Master was walking back and forth. The Layman asked, "What is that in your hand?
Songshan held up his staff and said, "I am an old monk; I cannot afford to miss even a single step. The Layman said, "Though this may be so, one must still have the strength of a youth."
It still exists. When those who have attained it meet one another, they naturally fit perfectly.
This is what is meant by "having ice in one's mouth, yet never uttering a single word of 'water.

It is not like people nowadays, who do not even know where their own footing lies, but merely stuff their bellies with remembered phrases, vainly displaying cleverness. What connection can there be? Xuedou called this—
Following the current until one reaches the source—tell me, where does his sickness lie? His sickness lies in not taking this as his primary concern, but merely seeking to look impressive.
If one were truly a person dedicated to the Way, they would take a true *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend) as their own self.
You have never reached the ground of great rest, nor do you yourself admit it. Let the assembly observe for themselves:
amidst the gates of sound and form, and through all circumstances—whether favorable or adverse—at every moment and in every matter, are you truly able to remain without a single thought arising?
Is the mind like wood or stone? It is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves; one cannot deceive oneself.
Even if one could deceive oneself, it would ultimately not concern anyone else’s affairs. I have just raised the point that "severing afflictions only increases illness. Now tell me: how is this so?
Are afflictions within? Are they without? Or are they in between? If, when seeking afflictions, they cannot be found, what is the point of further wishing to remove something else?
Would that not be a superfluous expenditure of effort? To strive toward True Suchness (tathatā) is itself a deviation.
What is the actual face of True Suchness? How do you intend to strive toward it? Venerable elders, as soon as you intend to do so—
That is not it at all. As for this ground: from beginningless time until today, and further from today to the end of the future—has it ever been moved? Why do you not awaken directly?
It would be far more straightforward; why undergo all this hardship?
Question and Answer:
A monk asked, "Present before me now, tell me: by whose power of grace do you receive this? The Master said, "The Senior Monk also understands how to ask such a question.
The monk pressed further, saying, "Setting aside the gate of building and transforming, bring forth a single phrase from before anything had even sprouted. The Master said, "Right now."
"What is it? Jin said, "A staff with rabbit horns. "Why can it pierce through a film? The Master said, "The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion.
A monk asked, "In the case of the 'Soul-Separation of the Beautiful Woman,' which one is the real one? The Master said, "Everyone, look! This monk also understands."
[The Master] asked thus.
A monk asked, "What is it like when the Great Matter has not yet been clarified? The Master said, "One, two, three. [The monk asked,] "What is it like after it has been clarified? The Master said:
4, 5, 6. Lingmi asked, "How is it when the lotus has not yet emerged from the water? The Master said, "Brewing tea beneath the crags, burning tree leaves.
He asked, "How is it after it has emerged from the water? The Master said, "Flowing waters by the ravine scatter peach blossoms."
A monk asked, "Since I began my studies under you, I have struggled without finding any point of realization. The Master said, "Why do you want to see?
The monk pressed further, "But there must still be some genuine place of realization. The Master said, "Fortunately, you are still quite pitiable. The monk was at a loss.
During the Master’s time in the seat, after a monk had finished asking about the principle of non-self (*anātman*), the monk asked again: "What is this very one who is able to be without self?
The Master said: "There is a person with an eye disease; please ask a physician to treat the cataract. Once the cataract is cured, the physician asks:
'Your cataract has already gone away—what is it [that remains]? The monk was speechless."
While seated, the Master pointed to a bronze cauldron and asked a monk, "If someone asks you what this is, how would you answer?
The monk said, "A bronze cauldron. The Master said, "Do you still have any doubts? The monk said, "I have no doubts. The Master then questioned another monk, who did not respond.
The Master pointed his finger and said, "There is Zen within your belly."
A monk asked, "What is the guest within the guest? The Master said, "Vast and boundless is the consciousness of karma, with no foundation to rely upon;
alas, in broad daylight one loses one's true nature. "What is the host within the guest? The Master said, "To know how to live while on the road;
there is nothing one cannot accomplish. "What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "Skillfully applying compassion and expedient means, one is adept at wielding the office."

[The monk] tested right from wrong: "What is the Lord of Lords? The Master said, "The Buddhas and Patriarchs have hidden their tracks; the common people have cut off all traces. The monk pressed further:
"When the Buddhas and Patriarchs have hidden their tracks and the common people have cut off all traces, what then? The Master did not answer. The monk bowed.
Lizhong asked, "In principle, there is sudden awakening; in practice, there is gradual elimination. Is there also a gradual awakening to principle? The Master said, "There is.

[The student asked], "Is there also a sudden elimination of phenomena? The Master said, "There is. He further said, "If there were no gradual awakening to principle, then Buddhas and sentient beings would not arise through dependent origination. If there were no sudden elimination of phenomena, then all dharmas would possess roots."

[The Master] said, "Fundamentally. He asked again, "Even the single word 'awakening' is not established. May I ask: is it that it is not established before awakening, or is it that it is not established after one has awakened?
The Master said, "Moon. [The student] bowed.
A monk asked, "To which school do you belong, Master? The Master said, "When hungry, I eat; when tired, I sleep. The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "Tell me, to which school do you belong? The monk said, "I do not know. The Master struck him.
The monk said, "Is it not the Linji school? The Master said, "You are quite clever."
Daicong opened his mind and asked about the general principle: "All the sutras speak of 'no-self'; why does the *Nirvana Sutra* alone speak of 'having a self'?
The Master said: "It is like a physician treating a patient: first he uses rhubarb to eliminate the fever of the pathogenic factors, and later he uses ginseng to replenish the primal qi."
Yang Weilian asked Master Sima, "Your disciple has long abstained from killing. Lately, I have devoted myself exclusively to recitation; is this sufficient?
The Master said, "This belongs to the realm of meritorious practice. If you have not yet resolved the matter of your own fundamental nature, it is all merely a vast expanse of karmic consciousness."

The student asked, "What is this fundamental matter? The Master said, "An ancient said: 'Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a single treasure, hidden within the mountain of form.
Layman, do you recognize it? The student replied, "I do not recognize it. The Master said, "Why do you not look into that very place where you do not recognize it?
The student was at a loss. The student continued, "In my daily life, I often sit for long periods without even realizing it."
When encountering an unfavorable circumstance, one is unable to strike back; this is because one does not know where the root of the ailment lies. The Master said:
"The Goddess of Fortune and the Woman of Darkness—a wise host will accept neither. What is there that cannot be struck down? After a long silence, he spoke again:
'If you cannot resolve it directly and immediately, then for now, examine and penetrate it from the perspective of worldly convention. For instance, as for dwelling...'"
When a man reaches his sixtieth year, reflecting upon his past experiences, tell me: where is he now? Not only at sixty years, but even after another six kalpas have passed, it remains just this way.
It is a phantom and a delusion, like a flower in the sky; all efforts to grasp it are in vain.
If one can discern this here and let go, then as days and years pass, that one fundamental point prior to the birth of one's parents will naturally manifest.
"Right on the mark. The student said, "I have heard your supreme discourse from the side, and my hair stands on end with awe.
I do not know how to apply myself to see that one stroke prior to birth. The Master said, "This very thing is the application. The student prostrated himself.
Yan Chunling asked about the duties of a district magistrate: "As a disciple who presides over punishments, the lives of the people depend upon me.
How can I ensure that they have no hidden feelings and that I do not wrongfully apply the law? The Master said: "Simply seek a clear understanding from the very source of your own self."
Naturally, the handle is in your hand; life after life, death after death—there is nothing that is not its wondrous function. [The student] further asks:
"I venture to ask where my own fundamental source is clearly situated. The Master says: "If I were to speak of it, it would be mine. [The student] replies: "..."
