How can one cause the snow to melt and the mist to disperse? The Master said, "Everyone suffers from the heat; I love the length of summer days.
The monk asked, "In winter one drinks hot broth, while in summer one drinks water. How can one avoid being out of step with the seasons? The Master said, "The mind..."
[The monk] was defeated; his face showed no sign of shame. [The monk asked: "The water flows cold from the edge of the rocks; the wind comes fragrant from within the flowers.
How can one achieve the harmony between ruler and subject? The Master said: "Nine times nine is eighty-one. [The monk asked:

"Thrusting through the sunlight in a thicket of thorns; ripples of clouds and mists upon the waves of smoke and mist. What is the matter of 'lowering the hand' when entering the marketplace? The Master said: [Silence].
[The Master] said: "I shall answer what you ask.
The layman asked: "Regarding Baizhang’s wild fox—why does he fall when he does not 'miss,' yet escape when he does not 'delude'? The Master said:
To grind flour, one must use the wheat of his own province; to sing a song, one must be a native of the imperial capital.

The student said, "If that is so, then those who have escaped have not yet escaped, and those who have fallen have not yet fallen. The Master said, "They are blown by the wind once again into another tune. The student said, "..."
"What was the meaning of Huangbo’s single slap? The Master said, "An mute person asking a deaf person.
A monk asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "When hungry, eat; when tired, sleep.
[The monk] asked, "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind do you succeed? The Master said, "Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch did not..."
He traveled to the Western Heavens (India) and asked: "What is the place where a student-practitioner travels on foot? The Master said: "Wearing tattered straw sandals, walking barefoot.

"What is the place where a student-practitioner does not give rise to deluded thoughts at any time? The Master said: "It has already arisen. "What is the place where a student-practitioner is intimately intimate?
The Master said: "Do not bring your questions to ask. "What is the place where a student-practitioner does not rely on [external conditions]? The Master said: [The text here is incomplete].

Regarding the point of awakening, the Master said, "Ugh. [The student asked: "What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? The Master said, "When one house has business, a hundred houses are busy.
[The student asked: "What is the matter personally transmitted by the Master? The Master said, "There is a question and there is an answer."
A monk asked, "Apart from all speech, staff blows, shouts, raising the eyebrows, and blinking the eyes, I beg the Master for a direct pointing.
The Master said, "You have already exhausted it yourself. The monk was at a loss; as he rose from his prostrations, the Master asked, "How do you understand this?
The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Not understanding is even more wondrous. The monk asked, "Is there still a fundamental meaning or intent? The Master—
[The Master] said: "Furthermore, this is the emergence of the head and horns.
A monk asked: "What is 'the former thought not arising is the mind'? The Master said: "The whale swallows the ocean until it is exhausted. [The monk asked:
"What is 'the subsequent thought not ceasing is the Buddha'? The Master said: "The coral branches are revealed."
A monk asked, "When the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is like losing one's parents; when the Great Matter has been clarified, it is like losing one's parents.
What is this Great Matter? The Master picked up his bamboo staff and said, "This thing of mine is simply a bamboo staff.
The monk asked again, "It is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing. Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "You yourself provide the answer."
The formal report was completed.
The layman asked, "Are Mañjuśrī, Wǎngmíng, and the woman one or three? The Master said, "Two colors, one match.
The layman pressed further, "And who is Wǎngmíng? The Master said, "And who is the woman? He then said, "This is certainly settled."
Even Gautama could not emerge from it. Even now, the sentient beings of the great earth have likewise never emerged from this samādhi.
Therefore it is said: "All sentient beings have already attained Buddhahood; they have already delivered all beings; they have already entered nirvāṇa. [The questioner] further asks:
In the end, he did not understand this. The Master said, "This is like adding eight more strokes to the eyebrows.
A monk asked, "Why does a precept-breaking bhikṣu not enter hell? The Master said, "An iron hammer without a hole.
"A pure practitioner—why does he not take birth in heaven? The Master said, "A stone lion."
A monk asked, "What is the single phrase that directly points to the source? The Master held up his whisk. After a long silence, he said, "How do you understand this?
The monk replied, "I see the Master’s function. The Master said, "Where did you see it?
The monk replied, "I saw the Master raise the whisk. The Master said, "Before I raised the whisk, how did you understand? The monk was speechless.
A monk asked, "I do not ask about hearing the wind from a thousand miles away; what is the news of Hai-tang these days? The Master held up his whisk.
The monk stepped forward and said, "Apart from this, how is it? The Master lowered the whisk. The monk bowed.
The Master said, "How do you understand this? The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "A fine shout! Shout again and see. The monk said, "It has already been shouted past."
"It has been a long time," [the Master] said. "This is merely a cliché. He asked again, "When Zhigong ate the pigeon, he never moved a single hair on its body.
I ask you: where was the pigeon? Where did it find its place and establish its life? The Master replied, "What kind of talk is being held in the kingdom of Silla today?
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
A monk requested instruction. The Master held up his whisk and said, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Do you even know that which you do not understand? The monk spread out both hands. The Master said, "This is something learned.
The monk asked again, "What is the single phrase of direct, unconditioned presence? The Master said, "It is already too late."

The two lay practitioners Zhang Yue-lu and Huang Tang-ting came for an audience. Zhang said, "Since I received the teachings from Mount Lu, I have gradually felt that I am no longer greatly burdened by worldly dust.
Whenever I recite the Heart Sutra, reaching the passage 'the mind has no obstruction,' I believe it with deep conviction and without doubt.
Yet, I cannot let go of it in the present moment; ultimately, I cannot put it down myself. The Master said, "Is it still..."
If you can see through the present moment, how could there be anything that cannot be let go? As the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says:
"One falsely identifies the four elements as the characteristic of one's own body, and the reflected images of the six sense-objects as the characteristic of one's own mind.

One does not know that all these various things arise from conditions; they are born when conditions gather and perish when conditions disperse. They are like dreams and illusions, like bubbles and [foam]."
Ying said, "The fact that this mountain monk and you, layman, are conversing here at this very moment is also a matter of coincidental conditions;
neither is obtainable. Zhang asked, "I clearly know that all things arise from conditions; is there anything that does not arise from conditions?
The Master said, "It is fortunate that you, layman, have asked this question. Huang said, "That which does not arise from conditions—is that not [the case]?"
[The student] asked about the mind. The Master said, "The mind arises from conditions; from morning until evening, thoughts arise and cease. Is this not arising from conditions?
Zhang said, "Apart from this arising from conditions, where else could one seek the truly real? The Master said, "There is not a single moment when it does not receive its power from that [source].
Thus, these very arisings and ceasings both originate from it; yet, though you seek the place where it originates, you cannot find it. He dwelt there.

A practitioner must apply a full measure of genuine effort; only through such investigation can they attain realization. Zhang said, "Whenever I reach this point, it becomes difficult to apply effort.
The Master said, "It is fundamentally manifest and majestic; if you do not take it up for yourself in the present moment, the more you seek, the further away you go.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says, "The continuous cycle of birth and death for all sentient beings arises entirely from their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind. Zhang said, "In this regard..."

"How can one now know the eternally abiding true mind? The Master said, "Layman, as for what you usually call benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and good faith—these various principles, are they eternally abiding?
Zhang replied, "When this person exists, these principles exist; how could they ever fail to exist for even a single moment?
The Master said, "If that is so, then in the end, principles are manifested because of the person. Yet if the person does not exist, where would the principles abide?"
Appendix. Huang said, "I truly know that all things in Buddhism return to emptiness. The Master asked, "Tell me, where does emptiness return?

Fotuo Dashi said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; Formless, it is fundamentally still and vast. It can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, Yet it does not wither along with the four seasons.
Is this emptiness non-empty? Is this permanence not permanence? Zhang said, "Although I am not..."
To know the eternally abiding true mind, one must simply verify it for oneself; there is indeed a point where one gains efficacy. It is simply these two words: "no-seeking.
In the affairs of worldly people, every entanglement arises because of seeking. If one can be without seeking, what entanglements could there be? The Master said:
"If you wish to be thoroughly without seeking, you must also be thoroughly able to see through things. It is like the light of a lamp, where the flames continue in succession."
The fool would think that the light of a lamp remains constant, not realizing that the subsequent flame is already different from the preceding flame.
It is like flowing water, which never ceases for even a moment; yet when a fool sees the water, he says the water is constant. It is also like the people coming and going within a single city.
It is thus for one year; it is thus for a hundred years. How can you know that the dead are dead and the living are living?
While people and things remain as they were, they are no longer what they once were. It is like a single person whose body today is already not the same as it was yesterday.
The Buddha said: "As soon as there is birth, there is cessation. This is not spoken for the sake of the foolish. Here, how could you allow yourself to grasp and cling? How could you allow...
"You have attained the capacity for reflection and discernment. Now, however, you grasp that which cannot be grasped and abandon that which cannot be abandoned;
how can this be right? Zhang Ci requested a single word that he might practice throughout his life. The Master said, "Commit no evil; perform all good. Zhang said, "I pray for further progress.
The Master said, "One should purify the mind," and then recited a verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "If..."

If one wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, one should purify the mind so that it is like empty space, remaining far removed from discursive thoughts and all forms of grasping, such that wherever the mind turns, there is no obstruction.
Zhang said: "Is the purification of the mind not precisely the realm of neither arising nor ceasing?"
Huang said, "Is there still any room for effort? The Master said, "When you do not understand, investigating right here is itself the effort.
Huang said, "Nowadays, whenever an event or an object arises, I respond to it as the moment demands and let it pass without leaving a trace.
How is this? The Master said, "That state is also very difficult. Huang then related this again [to another].
The Head Seat said: "To reach that state, one must first recognize the mind.
Regarding the phrase, "Cuiyan truly saw Ciming," when Ciming asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Zhe replied, "A probe-staff."
Yingcao said: "No clouds arise upon the ridge; the moon descends into the heart of the waves. Zhen remarked: "The small month has twenty-nine days;
the large month has thirty. Zhao said: "With hair white and teeth yellow, you still hold such a view. Zhao remarked: "..."
Zhen was weeping with tears streaming down his face, not daring to lift his head. Zhe said, "Your eyes have been swapped out by someone.
Jin asked, "Ultimately, what is it? Zhe said, "A lion bites a man; a hunting dog chases a clod of earth. Ming said, "No clouds arise upon the peaks;
the moon descends into the heart of the waves. Zhe said, "Ultimately, you still cannot get out of that ghost cave. Zhen.
Upon hearing these words, he attained great enlightenment. He remarked, "Furthermore, my eyes have been plucked out by another.

When Yongjia Xuanjue went to visit the Sixth Patriarch, he circumambulated him three times, shook his mendicant’s staff, and stood there. Zhe said, "You have come from a thousand miles away specifically to show your old face.
The Patriarch said, "Now, a śramaṇa possesses three thousand dignified deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices. You, Great Virtue..."

"From where have you come? [Zhaozhou] gave rise to great conceit. Zhaozhou said, "People probe with words; water is probed with a staff. Zhaozhou asked, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift.
Zhaozhou said, "It is like tying up one's hair and rushing to the yamen. The Master said, "Why do you not realize non-arising? Why do you not understand that there is no swiftness?
Zhaozhou said, "It has already come; it has already come. The Master said, "If you realize it, it is non-arising; if you understand it, it is fundamentally without swiftness."
Zhaozhou said, "Indeed, indeed. The Master said, "So it is, so it is. Zhaozhou said, "It cannot yet be relied upon. After a short while, he took his leave.
Zhaozhou said, "If you can simply go when you have finished, what is there that is not permissible? The Master said, "Is it not returning too soon? Zhaozhou said, [and departed].
[The Master] repeatedly pulled [the monk] out and examined him, saying, "Fundamentally, it is not moving; how could there be speed? Zhaozhou said, "It is still as before:
'Early spring is still cold. The Master said, "Who knows it is not moving? Zhaozhou said, "Deeply entering the tiger's den.

The Master said, "The benevolent one creates distinctions for himself. Zhaozhou said, "A true lion cub. The Master said, "You have thoroughly grasped the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Zhaozhou said, "A precipice."

Yunmen pushed him once and said, "In the state of non-arising, how could there be intention? Xuedou commented: "What a somersault! The Master said, "If there is no intention, who is it that makes distinctions?
Xuedou commented: "The first arrow was light; the second arrow is deep. The Master said, "Even making distinctions is not intention. Xuedou commented:
"In a great furnace, even refined gold does not change its color. The Master sighed in admiration, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! Stay for one night."
The commentary says: "Equal meeting, equal meeting.
Regarding Dongshan Liangjie’s verse, "Utmost care not to seek it from another," the commentary says: "As soon as it arises, one bites; naturally there is nothing to do."
"Far, far away, he is distant from me. [Zhaozhou] said, "Wrong. "Now I go all alone. [Zhaozhou] said, "Majestic and dignified. "Everywhere one meets him.
[Zhaozhou] said, "In brothels and wine shops, one meets Maitreya. "He is now precisely I. [Zhaozhou] said, "Wrong."
"Old and decrepit, you speak such words. [The Master] said: "I am not he now; this can be called 'saving half. [The Master] said:
"One must understand it in this way. [The Master] said: "How thick is your face? [The Master] said: "Only then can one accord with Suchness. [The Master] said: "Bury them all in one pit."
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chángqìng Zōngbǎo, Volume Three:

Phonetic Explanations *Shěng* (pronounced *suǒ jǐng*; *shēng* in the third tone; a disease of the eyes in which a film or cataract forms). *Lí* (pronounced *lǐ*; the name of Pénghǔ Lǐ, a marsh). *Zòu* (pronounced *zuòu*; the sound of *zhòu*; cloth; fine texture; gathered).
*Wenyi*: *The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zongbao of Changqing*, Volume Four.
Re-edited by Jinshi, a Dharma-grandson of Danxia.
Regarding the "Three Mysteries and Three Essentials" of the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, it is said in the verse-commentary concerning Zhang Bie,
the *Xiaolian* (Imperial Scholar), that Baizhang attained the Great Function (*da ji*) and Huangbo attained the Great Utility (*da yong*), while all others were merely [partial].

Regarding the master who leads the chanting, Linji said: "In general, when proclaiming the Dharma of the school, a single phrase must embody the Three Mysteries, and each Mystery must embody the Three Essentials.
Fenyang deeply grasped this essential meaning and was only then able to express it in verse.

In truth, they are not divided; yet, neither are they a mere undifferentiated whole. The ancient Tower Master’s division into "essence," "phrase," and "mystery within the phrase" has already lost the intent of the ancients.
When people of today fabricate their own systems, they further confuse "wu" for "an" and "an" for "ma."

The first mystery: The wildcat and the white ox understand how to transmit it; the blue-eyed old barbarian steals a glance and sticks out his tongue, holding his breath and swallowing his voice, not daring to speak.
The second mystery: Left and right, one encounters the source everywhere; the karmic enemy is difficult to untangle—quickly fix your eyes upon it!
The third mystery: the vast expanse of the universe in its myriad forms; every single thing is a living expression—how could it ever require the expense of straw sandals?
The first essential: the light of heaven does not announce the dawn; Śākyamuni and Maitreya do not know its name—it refuses to leave even a trace in the human world.
The second essential: The songs of woodcutters and the chants of herdsmen are truly marvelous. Yet, alas, those on the road have not yet opened their eyes;
they have wasted so much salt and sauce. The third essential:
All living beings of this great earth share this same tune. In every turn, step, bow, and gesture, they cannot leap out; their karmic consciousness remains vast and unbounded.
How truly laughable!

The general verse on the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) holds that attaining the essence within function is termed "Mystery" (Xuan). A single phrase, brilliantly clear, cuts through all triviality; its transformations are spontaneous, bringing forth life.
Consider this: the iron wall and silver mountain stand before one’s face.
The "Essentials" (yāo) refers to the manifestation of function within the essence; it values nothing more than the student’s true eye opening. A single phrase, clearly manifest, is fully complete.
Sufficient. When the occasion arises, one should employ skillful artistry as the Master fashions it.

Among the "Three Falls" of Caoshan, the matter of the water buffalo is most refined: "Knowing only to graze on grass, it is devoid of all other sentiments. If people of this age can understand this, they will be able to fully assimilate it.
Resting. Whether drinking when thirsty or eating when hungry, all is spontaneously present (Falling into Categories).
Moving freely and naturally amidst sounds and forms, emotions forget their preferences and the object and mind merge. It remains as it was before, without effort;
this is truly the empty void that does not dwell in emptiness (Falling into Accordance).
He cannot remain within the rank of Buddhas and Patriarchs; following conditions, he acts as a mountain-dwelling elder. Within the mountains there is naturally the unique flavor of the mountains;
imperial delicacies and rare delicacies are never encountered here. (The Noble and Precious Fall)
The wind and the banner are neither wind nor banner. Passports and mountain passes block the way, making travel difficult. People of this age merely hasten along their journey;
who understands that the whole body is right here?

The wind and banner do not move; it is the benevolent mind that moves. From antiquity to the present, this is truly convenient. If one were to discuss the "Plucking of the Flower" as a further commentary, even the Patriarch would still be occupied with the initial spark.

It is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind; when the Patriarch reached this point, all who could understand him were cut off. People say that possessing a thousand pieces of gold is good, but how does that compare to a man of middle means sitting amidst the bamboo grove?
It is neither wind nor banner; it is precisely the mind. Charge straight ahead and do not linger in silence.
If one can recognize the face of the Eastern Lord, the myriad purples and thousands of reds are at the height of spring.

When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, the cold of the three winters was difficult to endure. He brought the wooden Buddha back and split it into firewood; his body warmed, the cold vanished, and there was nothing else to say.
Let practitioners cease their further confused doubts and speculations.
"Rice-ear sickle, rice-ear sickle! Thirty coins—everyone knows this, yet when questioned, they are at a loss.
Nanquan beheads the cat.
The cat presses down upon the *yǒufēnná*; alas, these Chan practitioners are not true masters. Once the King’s command has been issued, it is difficult to evade;
the General may boast in the lands beyond the frontier, but in vain.
The assembly of monks in both halls stirs up wind and waves; how extraordinary is that one stroke beneath Nanquan! Whether they were saved or not, let there be no discussion;
display your heroism where heroism is not yet manifest.
A live cat bites a dead cat. I ask you, followers of Zen, do you know this or not? This is a dignified man of no affairs;
whether he charges straight ahead or takes a diagonal course, it is entirely up to him.
Holding a cat in his hand, he strikes a single blow; why must Zen practitioners prattle on so much? Only the old man Zhaozhou truly knows this;
with straw sandals upon his head, he sells his own eccentricity.
Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman:
the main road to Mount Tai is as straight as a bowstring. The monks who come and go have truly completed their training. The old woman and Zhaozhou’s true character were revealed;
yet this only causes people to feel all the more ashamed when they see it.
An old man who has become a refined spirit is Old Zhaozhou; he assists his wife in doing evil, raising spears and lances. The main road to Mount Tai remains as it was;
it simply requires the traveler to be willing to nod their head in assent.
Linji’s Three Mysteries stir up snow-waves in a vast furnace; dust and smoke rise from the bottom of the sea. Since humans and devas do not understand, even Buddhas and Patriarchs fall silent.
When Hanshan meets Shide, they clap their hands and laugh uproariously; bystanders do not understand at all, yet they say it is madness.
The warm spring spreads its virtuous grace; it is the clear and bright sky of the third month. The haggard-faced woman weaves through the long nights; the plowman busily sows his fields.

When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed to heaven and pointed to earth, alone claiming supremacy. These words were spoken out of compassion for all living beings. Fortunately, Yunmen knew how to adapt.
Otherwise, it is merely a waste of the "Old Lady’s Zen.
If you do not treat a strange thing as strange, the strangeness will vanish of its own accord. Yunmen was adept at discerning the opportune moment; he eliminated disaster the very instant it arose.
How extraordinary! Better that such a "good thing" had never happened at all.
After the World-Honored One realized the Way, he sat alone in the frosty sky; upon seeing the morning star, he suddenly struck the spark.
Had he known earlier that the lamp was fire, he would have found that the rice had long since been cooked.
The World-Honored One’s questioning of the piglet was clear and distinct, right before one's eyes; why need one move the tongue to initiate words?
Though it is said that the Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom, he still required us not to be deceived.
The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū dwells solely in this one mind, the mother of both ordinary beings and sages; when the ten stages are fully perfected, there is nothing else to seek.
Should one speak of whether he has attained Buddhahood or not, such views are entirely caught within the gate of the temporal present.
The old woman east of the city was originally a naturally manifest Buddha. For what reason did she act so peculiarly? Space may come to an end, but she is inexhaustible;
how could five fingers ever conceal her?
Zhaozhou has no person;
he has a pair of hands that have nothing to do. According to his capacity, he plucks flowers and breaks willows.
If someone asks where his hands are, he simply points to the flowers and willows and does not speak of the hands.
When asked about the nature [of reality], answer only with the word "no. Do not seek it through words; quickly turn back your head.
Suddenly, when you tread upon the path from whence you came, you will finally know that man understands how to ride a cow backward.
Zhaozhou said, "No. Within these words there is resonance; look with an urgent eye. This very skill—when asked whether a dog has Buddha-nature, Zhaozhou the Old One says "Yes" and "No.
Why do you Chan practitioners not examine the underlying principle? Alas! It is like weeping for a lost sheep on the road.
All of these linger within the realm of non-existence.
Looking at the mountains throughout the day:
three times three is nine; four times four is sixteen. When there is rice, one cooks it into rice; when there is no rice, one cooks it into gruel.
The great fish has swallowed the bamboo hook;
its intestines are already pierced by the barb. It leaps wildly in the clear ripples, yet the line remains firmly in hand; there is no further need for sword or spear.
I raise this bamboo staff—its back and its touch—for you to see: meeting on a narrow path, there is nowhere to hide. A truly majestic man!
Child, when you have the spirit of aspiration, let that aspiration increase.
I shall speak directly for you with this bamboo staff; truly, it is like a turtle that does not escape from its jar. There is no need for "how" or "what if";
the ignorance of kalpas will cease from this moment on.
The old monk raises his bamboo whisk. As soon as a Chan practitioner opens their mouth, they are already wrong. Neither turning one's back nor touching it is permissible; do not move.
Hurry, let go of your grasp, and return home.
The old woman burns the hermitage.
Host and guest strike one another; there is the mechanism of the coming. A golden hammer behind the head—how truly extraordinary! No signs or omens remain; all is empty and level.
On the cold crag, the withered tree is lush and green.
The old woman burning the hermitage is a most extraordinary matter; the accounts transmitted from all quarters are entirely inconsistent.
Everyone understands the clear construction of the plank road, but how many know the secret crossing at Chen Cang?
The mechanism of killing and enlivening, of letting go and seizing, is纵横 (zōnghéng) and 縱奪 (zòngduó); it harbors the springtime in secret, causing people to doubt.
When the blind donkey extinguishes even a trace of it, he returns to the ancient patriarch for ten thousand ages.
At such a time as this, what is the meaning? A withered tree in a cold cliff dwells in solitude;
to drive it away to burn its hut is too cruel a sentiment, yet it causes people to see all the more confusion.
Without leaving Tuṣita he has already descended into the royal palace; without emerging from his mother’s womb, his work of saving beings is already complete.
Without leaving Tuṣita he descended into the royal palace, and the cycle of his Buddha-activities is fully consummated. It is not only Gautama who is thus;
the nostrils of all people are exactly the same.
Greatly following the destruction, the stones and clods of earth are shattered; following each bird’s cry, the flowers fly. In the clear pool, the shadow of the azure dragon is not seen;
one need only observe the moment when clouds arise and mists are spread.
Jiufeng refused to assent;
as soon as the incense smoke rose, the Head Seat departed. This man was a veteran master of the monastic community.
Yet, were one to discuss the final intent of our former teacher, even Jiufeng had not yet glimpsed its depths.
No seeing, no hearing. Where does the master reside?
Does the master not reside in this state of no seeing and no hearing? Even if you follow along, what can be done? At whose door is there no bright moon?
It is unbearable that wayfarers are even more numerous at night.
Xuan Sha’s three types of patients—the blind, the deaf, and the mute—are most intimate; hearing, seeing, sensing, and knowing are no different from one another.
Old Man Shao Yang is far too eccentric; he has emptied out all the family treasures.
Meeting at Wangzhou Pavilion, Wushan Ridge, and before the Sangha Hall—bringing the entire earth forth is like holding a grain of millet. This meeting and this presentation are likewise coincidental.
If one discusses the secure ground of returning home, Gehu and Baofu both understand the shifting flow.

The large stone in the house of Grandee Lu Xing and the boat sailing upon the water both depend entirely on the person at the tiller. Picked up with the hand as it falls, every move is personal. Clouds, mountains, water, and moon have all been traversed;
with whom can one discuss the affairs of this full heart?
Lu Zu faces the wall;
the wall stands ten thousand fathoms high, connecting with the ultimate pivot. Why labor with the lips and skin of a winnowing fan?
Had it been Old Gao Ting at that time, he would have truly surpassed Master Nanquan Wang.
Fayan drew back the curtain—once gained, once lost. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*! Raise your eyebrows and be wide awake:
what is this "once gained, once lost"?

When Deshan arrived at Longtan, he saw neither the pond nor the dragon; only when he blew out the lamp did he realize he was right within it. Although he no longer harbored doubts regarding the elders of the world, he remained the same as before, in a state of non-awakening.

Ten million streams and a thousand currents are all but water; the seven golden mountains and five sacred peaks are all Mount Sumeru. Whenever meeting people or encountering objects, he raises a single finger;
in this dusty world, there will surely be a Ziqi.
One coin, two coins, or three coins for Shushan’s stupa; a single inch of tortoise hair weighs nine catties.
Master, you shall not have a stupa in this life, even if you lie in disarray upon the desolate peaks.
Mazu’s single shout left Baizhang deaf for three days;
when the Golden-Winged Bird King soars through the universe, who among them can transcend the crowd? A single blow of the lethal poison—those who hear it all perish;
were it not for a grieving heart, even the soul would be severed.
Majestically sitting alone upon the Great Hero Peak, his life’s journey exhausted and his traces vanished. Fortunately, he has inherited the ancestral fields;
from now on, his descendants shall revitalize the ancestral tradition.
Touzi’s oil-flask is full of oil.
Is it not Touzi himself? "The mandarin ducks are embroidered; let you behold them from afar, but I do not hand the golden needle to anyone."
National Teacher Yan had an awakening when Xuefeng grabbed him by the chest;
he thought, "What is so extraordinary about this? It turns out it is simply like this. Where did he go in years past? Now, too, there is not much difference.
The old woman casts her child away;
the dream of Nanke awakens, and the spirit becomes clear and expansive. Within this, why bother to distinguish between the distant and the near?
Cease boasting of your skillful rowing and paddling; you head toward Xiangxiang while I go to Qin.
The ten knowledges share the same truth;
the one and the same are of a single substance. Meeting Maitreya at the brothel and the tavern, the old woman east of the city could not avoid him.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
2. Identical in the Great Matter: Whatever the hand grasps is all it. From now on, do not lament the poverty of your house; when you have the will, augment that will.
3. All are equally fellow-students:
The plowman and the weaver bow in greeting. Each is truly natural and wondrous; why must one travel south in search?

Fifty-three. These four are identical to true wisdom; from of old, they have not been permitted for others to know. The blue-eyed old barbarian did not recognize them; the white ox and the tabby cat knit their brows.

5. Identical in Pervasiveness and Universality: When the neighbor to the east beats the drum, the neighbor to the west dances; with songs of the Ba region and wine of the village society, they laugh and frolic.
They find joy within it, yet others do not know. 6. Identical in Fullness:

Encompassing heaven and wrapping around earth, there is nothing left outside. If one wishes to advance, there is no door through which to enter; if one wishes to retreat, there is no place to withdraw.
It is obtained.
The seven [points] share the same gains and losses. Left wall, right wall; success is Xiao He’s, failure is also He’s. Swallow your breath and stifle your voice;
do not cry out your grievances.
Eighth is "killing what is born together. Whatever is grasped by the hand is medicine; sometimes it is pearls, jade, and the eight delicacies, and sometimes it is a dung heap or a refuse basket.
9. Same Sound Roar. The sounds of the stream and the colors of the mountains are complete. Guanyin buys a sesame cake with money;

it turns out to be a steamed bun. 10. Same Attainment Entry. The transformation city provides a temporary rest. Not knowing what lies outside the hermitage within the hermitage; moss grows upon the jade palace.
The power of the red bones arises.
A general verse on the ten knowledges being identical with reality is clearly presented here. Do not attempt to deliberate upon it further.
The Five Ranks: The Sovereign and the臣 (Minister) in the Center and the Deviation. A chaotic indistinguishability before the empty kalpa. Majestic and vast, the universe—no one recognizes it.
Vague and elusive, it is not easily described.

Correctness within partiality: there is not a single thing that can be grasped by the intellect. One who understands how to sing the song of returning home while on the road is willing to exchange their profound interest for empty fame.
Coming from the very center: look at him, how brilliant he is! Not involving either of the two paths, what need is there for any contrivance?
"Simultaneously Reaching the Center": Here, all distinctions between self and other are utterly forgotten. When self and other are forgotten, letting go and gathering back proceed with perfect ease.

"Simultaneously Arriving at the Center": From ancient times to the present, no one has understood this. Among them, who is the person who emerges? All who come try to be clever, yet end up being clumsy.
A verse in response to the questions of Provincial Education Commissioner Qian Wuxin:
When the stomach is hungry, one inevitably thinks of food; when the body is cold, one inevitably longs for clothing. Since arising and ceasing have not yet ceased, how can you say [there is no self]?
Cease the workings of the mind.
When hungry, think of food; when cold, think of clothing. Who is it that stirs and ceases in such confusion?
From this moment on, let all conditions come to rest, even if there are needles and awls in disarray outside your gate.
Question: Stillness and concentration are called *dhyāna*; movement by wind is called waves. If stillness and concentration are like a clear pool, from where do the winds and waves arise?

The inherently pure original mind is fundamentally still and concentrated; as soon as a single thought arises, it becomes turbid and confused. Observe this thought closely—it is originally non-existent.
There is. From here, the clear pool is cut off from waves and ripples.
Question: The examination hall period is seventy days; thirty remain of the hundred-plus days. Having passed away and then revived again—whose blood flows?

One must know that within the Dharma-hall day after day, it is only upon passing away and reviving again that one truly perceives the efficacy of the practice. The old father has never lent anything from the start;
yet his descendants display their prowess outside the gate.
Question: Arising and ceasing occur at every moment; perfect clarity is attained according to one's stage. I ask you practitioners of Zen: who among you does not suffer humiliation?
Arising and ceasing are fundamentally non-existent; perfect clarity is something that cannot be attained. Every man of noble character—when his will and spirit are present, they increase.
Zhigui asked:

"When the mouth opens, it becomes discursive thought; when there are no words, it is still a dead phrase. Since both existence and non-existence are unestablished, where is the place for going or staying?"
Opening the mouth is not thinking; silence is not a dead word. Whether horizontal or vertical, it is all me; as for going and staying, who else could it be? Question:
Sudden enlightenment is called "seeing and attaining. Does the original nature have form? It is said that emptiness is not emptiness, and that what is called existence has never existed.
It is said that emptiness is not empty, and that what is called existence is also not existent. To gaze upward, bore into it, and contemplate it is merely to waste one's effort.
If you have no mind, I too shall rest.
Question: Where did you go last year? Where do you come from this New Year? If you say there is no place from which you come, then [the answer is] "The hundred grasses..."
The Evidence: Last year there was nowhere to go; this New Year there is nowhere to come from. How marvelous! This is the ultimate meaning: the myriad plants turn toward spring and bloom.
Question: Deshan had his single blow; Linji had his single shout. These are but minor matters of the world. When meeting [the masters], if...
This accords with Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout— meeting face-to-face, the function is swift. Nevertheless, if you encounter a rogue monk,
you must hide yourself and retreat before you can succeed.
Verses on Distinguishing the Real from the False:
The true nature of dharmas is fundamentally pure; it is simply that people do not know this. This ignorance and the pure nature are neither one nor two.

Reality and falsehood originally have no inherent nature; they are all the dependent origination of dharmas. When awakened, one accords with True Suchness; though without end, it seems to have a beginning.
When deluded, one violates true nature; there is an end but no beginning. Since both delusion and awakening are empty in their nature, there is neither end nor beginning.

It is not that the real gives rise to the false; rather, by deluding oneself regarding the real, the false subsequently arises. Once it is realized that the false has no substance, how could it not be brought to rest?
Because the nature of causes and conditions is empty, what is born and what dies? In the verses of the "Poor Son" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said:

for many years he wandered abroad in foreign lands; the mountain passes were steep and perilous, and the roads were vast and desolate. For more than fifty years, he was occupied with the affairs of men.
Separate. Upon returning, it is fundamentally the old practice of concealment.
Holding the staff and chanting the verse, he restrains and releases; he relies on me. Ascending heights and descending precipices, I am guided by him. He has no self—how could he [otherwise] act?
Alive! I have obtained him for use, free to extend and contract as I wish. He and I have been fundamentally no two; how could there be intimacy or estrangement between me and him?
From this day forward, let there be no discrimination; hand in hand, we shall forge a noble plan together.

The verse by Changqing for hanging the bell-board—whether there is a phrase or no phrase has been transmitted through ancient and modern times. Since the tree fell and the vines withered more than a hundred years ago, today the ancestral wind is restored;
come along with me, everyone look!
The Verse on the Precept-Robe:
At midnight at Huangmei, it was stolen away and transmitted; it has caused descendants throughout the world to toil in haste.
When driven to the crest of the ridge with no place to hide, he flung it out before one’s face for all to see.

The transformed bell’s verses clarify light and darkness; Mañjuśrī perceives them. Avalokiteśvara responds to the mechanisms of movement and stillness. Its resonant, ringing sound deafens the ears—tell me, who is it?
Answer: Layman Sengmo.
A single phrase facing the sun is difficult to utter; before a word is spoken, one has already fallen into the stream ahead. This mountain monk does not understand idle lamentation;
why must you, Layman, speak of awakening and delusion?

Showing the bear’s heart, he opens the mind to realize that the holy and the ordinary are without distinction—a single awareness pervading all. You and I share the same source and nature of mind; how joyful it is that our karmic conditions from past lives have coincided.
With a girdle of gold, you ride the crane, fulfilling the tenet of my school.
Occasionally I wander through the southern hills, trailing water and mud; I know not where my native mountain lies.
A thousand-year-old permanent resident, yet a guest for but a single morning—the rustic elder constantly contemplates things thus.
Bestowing Dharma Words:
"In my Way, no one recognizes it; rely on you to pass through its single thread. Your mind and my mind merge; thus one arrives within it."—Presented to Li Zhong.
The single verse on the wind and the banner resolves the matter as it meets the occasion; the fact that "the same breeze blows for a thousand miles" is also extraordinary.
Having gone three times to Huangyan to inquire about the ultimate point, he truly knows that the village elder does not deceive him.

Manifesting the two adornments at the threshold of the gate of arising and ceasing, with a single thought turning back, the King of Emptiness transmits his command for the son to return. All together, gather to discuss the ancient and the modern;
do not feel ashamed that your eyes were previously unopened.
The son, Yuanshi, is shown returning to his father to communicate news; the father, believing his son’s words, gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
All merit belongs entirely to the son, yet one must know that the old father never leaves the gate.
To the two attendants, Fawei and Fashu, he said: "Return to Mount Kuang and make your living through practice.
My son has nothing else; there is only 'no-mind,' so do not add anything further. If the mind does not arise, there is not a single thing;
when the mind arises and thoughts stir, affairs are like hemp seeds."

Furthermore, although the afflictions of worldly dust have no inherent nature, they are difficult to endure as they seem to arise in continuous succession. Be diligent in mindfulness and cease all indolence;
what then of the two eyes of Great Penetration?
Shishi said, "Lady Nengsu Han does not think of good, nor does she think of evil. What is this 'not thinking'?
Do not say that we have not known each other for many years; it is still just the old woman."

To the Chan practitioner, it is shown that in the four directions and eight corners there is no path at all; one simply prizes the teacher’s having eyes to see. The fishing rod is already in the fisherman’s hand;
there is no need to greedily pursue the journey across distant mountains.
Having heard the news of Qiaoyun’s passing, I have not engaged in worldly sentiments for some years. I was most pleased that while dwelling in the mountains, my door remained half-closed;
yet hearing this report, it causes my mind to become even more tranquil, for you have long been established within the ground of your own heart.

The Teacher of the Way has always said that there is not much to this Buddha-dharma: as soon as it is thus, it is not thus; once you step upon the pivot of the highest gate, hundreds of thousands of samādhis are excreted all at once.
I show the assembly that day after day the sun rises from the eastern side, and morning after morning the cock cries at the fifth watch. If, within this, one possesses the adamantine eye,
then the sister-in-law is originally the elder brother’s wife.
The chief seat, Yeo-jeong, who resided at Heolin, dispatched the official Kadoji to deliver a fly-whisk as a token of his faith, with this verse to express his sincerity:

"The patriarchs have transmitted from one to another nothing but the One Mind; Qingyuan and Nanyue need not be divided. The three mysteries and their illumination and function are none other than this."

Standing, the five ranks of ruler and subject are arrayed herein. Under the blow of the staff, there is no birth; ordinary and sage are cut off. In the moment of action, not even a single monk is to be seen.
The debate on the wind and the banner is firmly re-established at Heli. Fortunately, our school has people who carry on its lineage from generation to generation.
The Elder of the Established School has come from afar to beg for a verse:
"Cutting iron or biting a nail is an easy matter; severing the lotus fiber is a task of even greater length. People do not anticipate the strategies of Zhang Liang;
I fear you may fall into our salt-and-soy sauce vat.

Furthermore, the waters of Chu and the mountains of Qin are difficult to traverse from afar; do not regard them as trivial matters, O *śrāmaṇera*. With earnest urgency, apply the hand that seizes the King;
examine the unmoving wind and banner with meticulous care.

When Yuan Chan returned to Huashou, it was thought that the Gate of the Patriarchs possessed a secret transmission; who would have known that Kongyin remained entirely silent? Now, he takes up his staff and departs for Luofu;
there, by the side of Huashou, he shall live by fire-seeds and blade-plowing.

Revealing the Patriarch’s mind, one returns to the Flower-Crested Peak atop Flying Clouds to gaze upon the bright moon; this is precisely the moment Guizong rubs his forehead in anticipation. North, south, east, and west share this same intent;
heart-mind after heart-mind, it is permitted only for the Patriarch’s mind to know.
Again,
he slung his staff across his shoulder and, heedless of others, went straight into the ever-deepening depths of Mount Luofu. He made a record of gathering yellow leaves and vegetable roots,
fearing they might drift away with the current and lose their resonance with those who understand.
Demonstrating diligent exertion, he went to Huashou;
having finished his studies under the masters of the various quarters, he realized that the "five flavors" of Chan reside solely at the edge of the mattock.
If anyone comes to inquire about its inner meaning, he strikes them with one or two punches right on the jaw.
To Zen practitioner Xishui:
To grasp the meaning before the words are spoken is still a moment too late; to turn one's body beneath the phrase is not yet sufficient. A true man of great character must resolve this for himself;
do not let the word "Zen" deceive you for the rest of your life.
To Zhang Yushu, Prefectural Governor:
A true man of great character must be fierce and resolute. Transient splendors are like the moon reflected in water; how could the flickering waves of a mirage be worth mentioning?
How much less can one speak of empty flowers casting their shadows? There is only the supreme jewel of True Suchness (Tathatā), which remains eternally constant from antiquity to the present.

Thoroughly! Since it does not follow from conditions, how could it ever be extinguished? At the gateways of the six sense organs, true clarity is pristine. Bodhidharma did not bring this from the Western Land;
the Patriarch Ke said there is nothing to attain, so simply rest. I know you have planted many spiritual roots under the Buddhas; be earnest and do not fail this auspicious season.

It shows the practitioner that both sin and merit arise from conditions; the nature of what arises from conditions is fundamentally empty. If one knows this principle of the absence of intrinsic nature, one shall immediately escape the cage.
This teaches the precepts to the practitioner.

Like fish in water or birds in flight, coming and going, circling within this realm; if you deliberate upon it, you will know that You cannot be seen—without a mind, one enters perfect penetration everywhere.
To the Chan practitioner Yinping, who has attained direct realization: there is no second person. "Where there is a path that can be ascended, those of higher capacity will also walk it.
This is the posthumous pen-inscription on Lingmi’s *Songgu* (Verses on Ancient Cases).
Lingbi has gone away and left no trace; there remains only Lingbi’s legacy in his calligraphy.
From the brushstrokes, I know he is not the man of former days; I have kept them to comfort my heart. That you and I are both empty—I have known this for a long time.
Not only have I known it for a long time, but I have contemplated it deeply. Having attained this samādhi of emptiness, I am thus detached from the sentiments of birth and death. Lingbi! Lingbi!
Thirty-seven years pass like a dream from yesterday; another hundred years will be just the same. Alas! This world dwells like an illusion;
you and I have never existed from the beginning.

I pay homage to the Golden Wheel Stūpa, towering and solitary as it soars into the void. It does not dwell as a neighbor among the multitudes; from all four sides, the paths for climbing are cut off, while ten thousand peaks wind and turn in new patterns.
Every point is a true śarīra; everywhere is the body of the Original Teacher. Today I behold him in person, yet I look back with longing upon those who bore the iron [to build this monument].
In response to Mr. Zhou Yuanliang, Minister of Agriculture, on his birthday, four verses:
I am ashamed that my merit and wisdom are meager; To transcend the world would surely be difficult for me. The lotus leaf may serve as clothing; The yellow jing root can be used for food.
For what reason does the eventless patch-robed monk encounter an official in this present life? It is a single tune on a stringless lute; only those who know the music can play it.

Furthermore, phenomena abide in their own positions, for all things are fundamentally non-transmigrating. Since the faculties and objects are free from fault, one may find peace in dhyāna amidst sounds and forms.
Seeing the horns, one knows the ox is there; observing the smoke, one recognizes the fire is burning. When this is clearly and personally witnessed, how could there still be center or periphery?

Furthermore, having entered the Gate of Emptiness, one has sought and contemplated for years without counting. One loves the ground of withered dry-wisdom; the flowers fall from the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens.
When the sentiments of acceptance and rejection are forgotten, one stretches out both legs and sleeps. Sitting alone in a thatched hut, the grass outside the door grows lush and green.
Furthermore, becoming a Buddha is fundamentally easy; as soon as there is doubt, it is not accomplished. Do not boast of Linji’s shout; have you ever recognized the sound of Yanxi?

The Way is straight, yet it appears crooked; to speak of emptiness is but a forced designation. Having happened upon this dusty world, how many years have passed? In response to Master Qihexi’s inquiry regarding our parting at Jinyun Temple:
more than twenty years have passed since counting the fingers; worldly affairs are as if they never existed, while the true mechanism remains right before one's eyes.
I am like the shadow of a wild goose; you enjoy the karmic affinity of water and clouds. May we meet again on another day at the highest peak of the celestial lake.
Praise to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The eye can see, the ear can hear; the celestial nature is luminous and wondrous, requiring no seeking.
When the eye sees form, form is not form; when the ear hears sound, sound is not sound. This innate, true Buddha-nature has reached the present from beyond the limit of Vipaśyin Buddha.
Great men, cast your eyes upward: the original, ancient Buddha seeks to become new. Guanyin and I are fundamentally...

They are of the same substance; it is only because of defilement and purity that they are distinguished. If one can, in a single thought-moment, turn the light back to illuminate, the entire body is the sacred mind—there are not two people.
When the eyes see forms, one is turned by form; when the ears hear sounds, one is submerged by sound.
From vast eons until now, one has been deluded and failed to return, thereby forming the very root of birth and death. If one can call upon the power of Avalokiteśvara, this delusion...
Without inherent nature, originally empty; nature is primordially empty. Shackles and fetters are naturally liberated; the cauldrons, boiling water, furnaces, and coals are instantly melted away.
Furthermore:
I have heard that the Great Being does not perceive by means of the "observed" (the object), but rather perceives through the "observer" (the subject).

Therefore, he enables sentient beings to obtain benefit through seeing and hearing, pulling them from suffering and granting them joy. Like an echo in a valley responding to objects to produce sound, he appears in every eye as seeing and in every ear as hearing;
he manifests in every instance and divides his body everywhere. The Great Being and I are no different from one another; yet though I seek him, I do not find him.

To see [with doubt] and to not see [without doubt] are as far apart as heaven and earth. If one does not doubt and does not seek, Avalokiteśvara appears before one. Those who wish to see the Great Being should contemplate in this way.
As the Sūtra says: "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same manner."
Eulogy on the Portrait of Master Boshan:

The clay ox enters the water, leaving no trace; Heavy snow and thick frost block the path. If you wish to know the true countenance of our Master, The peach blossoms still smile at the spring breeze as before.

Self-Praise (Requested by Huanshi): Buddha to Buddha, only the fundamental substance is transmitted; from teacher to teacher, the original mind is secretly entrusted. It relies entirely upon this one point;
you, my disciple, must exert yourself with earnest diligence. You must know that there is yet another level above this. *Ei!* Before your eyes there is no *śrāmaṇera*; here there is no old man.

Monk: Furthermore, as for those who say "one may request [instruction from] the Casket," this is the great emptiness of Han. Since he himself has not even a place to plant a single awl, where else could another find a way to communicate?

Throughout my life, I have trusted only in myself and have not conformed to the ways of the people of this age. That "the very mind is Buddha" is a conviction that has penetrated to the very marrow of my bones.
Originally, I intended to hide deeply in mountain valleys and not allow others to know of it. *Ei!* Who would have expected that you, Keshan, would emulate Xiong'er?
Furthermore, as for this fellow (invited by Hanzhi), at first glance he seems honest, yet his inner thoughts are difficult for others to discern. Ultimately, he has no other talent;
it is simply that he has been infected by the lingering poison of Master Bodhidharma. While it might be forgivable if he had merely deceived himself, it is truly intolerable that even his speech...

He does not practice self-restraint; every time he is before others, he proclaims with every word and every voice that "the mind itself is Buddha," thereby inciting slander in others while his own mind remains undisciplined.
Furthermore, (Huan-wan-qing) it is just so, yet immediately it is not so. Tell me: is this "I" or is it "not-I"? If you say it is "I,"...
I am not like that. If you say it is not me, I am not "not like that. "Not like that" is not "not like that. Ultimately, how is it?
In the language of Tang, he is called a *qishi* (alms-seeker); in the language of India, a *bhikṣu*.
Furthermore, [with the *han* seal held and the *man* seal standing by his side], he said:
"The mind itself is the Buddha; the mind itself is the Dharma; the mind itself is the Sangha. This old fellow has spent his entire life with nothing but this skill, enjoying it himself without end.
Lately, there have been those who understand him; when two hearts are of one accord, their strength is such that they can cut through anything.
Gold. How much more so for three people? *Ei!* Everyone, exert your strength together! To repay the Buddha’s kindness and the Patriarchs’ kindness, one must not seek only to perfect oneself;
one must become a meritorious subject of Prajñā.

Furthermore, as for the teacher whom [Hanyin] requested, his face was sallow and his eyes large; scarcely had he emerged from his mother’s womb when he began acting strangely, seeking only to see his nature and become a Buddha.
In human affairs, there is nothing one truly loves; forty years have passed in weary toil. Now, it is not worth even half a coin.
I often pondered where my own heart’s content lay, thinking that no one would recognize it. Little did I expect Master Yin to exhaust himself in his efforts.
Three feet of snow before the gate.
Furthermore, as for this "Old Man" [invited by Huashou]:
he has been dull-witted and simple-minded throughout his life and is incapable in all things. As for your own meager skills, they amount to nothing more than mere recognition.
Having attained a single mind, as the years and seasons have passed, it has grown ever more refined with age. Yet you come to entice the people of this world;
you possess no literary elegance, nor do you offer anything sharp or novel. Everyone everywhere laughs at you; you have nothing but this single scroll of the *Platform Sūtra*.
People speak thus, and I know you would accept it with equanimity. Aha! Who is right and who is wrong? It is like rice and wheat—hard to distinguish. Nevertheless, people do not...
Consciousness. You also have those who understand this.
Furthermore, [as requested by Sāgaradhvaja]:

above, there is no reaching up or looking toward; below, one cuts off the self-body; externally, one is detached from the marks of detachment; internally, one subtly detaches from emptiness. Within the rank of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—
He cannot be detained. From the beginning, this venerable mountain-dweller has been a teacher of profound depth;
his disciples are but common children. Behold how truly carefree he is: with tattered robes and straw sandals, he is solitary and detached amidst the bustling crossroads of the city.
East *pao*, west *pao*. One’s own person has nothing to seek; it is only for the sake of others that one seeks peace and happiness.
Ehi! Suddenly bumping into the man within—how wonderful this much grappling and searching!
This inscribed staff was originally yours, Elder Shengren;
I now return it to you. We speak only of realizing one's nature, not being bound by words and texts. Heh! Unfold it right before your eyes.
I leave it to you to decide. The tradition of the Upper Cavern (Dongshan) now rests solely with you.
*Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zongbao of Changqing*, Volume Four, Phonetic Glossary.

Jiā (cut with zhāngguā; sound zhā. To strike a drum). Tiē (cut with tāxié; sound tiē. To settle and stabilize). Háng (cut with húguāng; sound huáng. The sound of bells and drums. *Háng-háng* is the sound of music).
Yuán (ancient form of yuān. Things sprout from the *yuán*. A description of depth and vastness). Bào (cut with pījiào; sound pào. The sound *bào-rán*).
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chángqìng Zōngbǎo, Volume Five.
Compiled by the Dharma-grandson of Danxia, the present-day monk Zhong,
based on the correspondence between Zhang Bie-gong, a licentiate (Xiaolian), and his inquiries (with the original letter appended).
Dajian [Huineng] possessed but a single eye; Datong [Xuanze] had both eyes perfectly clear and bright.
The Elder Yongming may truly be called one who most thoroughly protected the True Dharma, not permitting those of "mad Chan" to peer beyond its boundaries.

These were merely men carrying a single plank, who spent their days suppressing delusive thoughts in an attempt to achieve the non-arising of a single thought. Often they conformed to his teachings, yet among them there were distinctions.
I humbly beg for your instruction.
Master Bodhidharma said, "When practice and understanding correspond, one is called a Patriarch. Is this not the state of both eyes being perfectly clear?
Yongquan said, "People of the present day must completely exhaust the present moment before they can achieve realization. He further said, "One must..."
"Consciousness is dry. If consciousness were not dry, how could one dare say that there is wandering in saṃsāra?
How could one dare say that there will be days of weeping? Is this not placing emphasis on practice? Miaoshan said, "I value only that your eye be correct; I do not speak of your practice.
Is this not placing emphasis on the ground of realization (dṛṣṭi)? One who has attained it knows the time for himself. To cultivate or not to cultivate—these are two extremes."
To speak: there is no practice apart from the ground of insight, nor is there any ground of insight apart from practice.
This statement by Daotong Shuangyan Yuanming was intended to remedy the defects of his time;
how could it be compared to those who engage in blind cultivation and reckless refinement, merely suppressing their discursive thoughts?
Reply to Master Zengzhai Xiaolian (with attached letter):
The single school of Bodhidharma takes direct pointing as its title and the gate of awakening as its ultimate goal.

It is appropriate that those who have realized their true nature should employ the ready-made function; all measures of stages and gradualism are merely superfluous doctrines. Thus, the ancients said:
Baizhang attained the great capacity; Huangbo attained the great function. All others were merely teachers of exhortation.
As such, each has their own measure. Shushan said: "Before the Xiantong era, I realized the affairs of the Dharma-body;
after the Xiantong era, I realized that which is above the Dharma-body. This still belongs to gradualism. Since there is a measure, there is gradation.
Next, one might think that a single awakening is not ultimate. What is meant by "direct pointing"? This is why people whose own eyes have not yet opened harbor doubts because of it.
Even those who have attained some degree of realization still have their wild minds unsettled.
Have you not seen how Gaoteng beckoned from across the river and then hurried away, or how the Boatman capsized his boat to show that there was nothing else?—Mahamati.
The reply to Li Hanlao states: "In the midst of a single laugh, you have attained release. Is there any further extraordinary principle?

If there were, it would be as if you had not yet attained release. It further says: "If you wish to clarify the Great Dharma so that your responses to circumstances are unimpeded, simply continue as you have been;
there is no need to consult others. After a long time, you will nod your head in understanding yourself."

Although human sentiment is difficult to dispel, have you not heard that the matter of life and death is of great importance and that impermanence is swift? Among those in this world, even the longest lifespan is but one hundred years.
As for the lifespan, the shortest is ten years; once a hundred years have passed, neither the longest nor the shortest can be found.
What is called "Peng" (the long-lived) and "Shang" (the short-lived) are merely different by name; in birth and death, there is ultimately no distinction.
Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "How does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings? Vimalakīrti replied, "It is like a magician seeing his own magical illusions."

like a mirage in the heat; like an echo in a valley; like the tracks of a bird in the sky; like bubbles on the surface of the water.
Like the son of a barren woman; like the solidity of a plantain tree; like lightning remaining for a long time—thus does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī asked, "If a bodhisattva contemplates in this way, how does he practice loving-kindness?
Vimalakīrti replied, "Once a bodhisattva has made such an observation, he reflects: 'I shall preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. This is the true [practice of loving-kindness]."

Would it not have been more definitive to say, "This very mind is precisely Buddha"? I beg you to question the one on the high seat and hope for a thorough explanation.
"This very mind is Buddha" is an affirmative statement; "neither mind nor Buddha" is a negating statement.
People today mostly value the negating statement, claiming it leaves no trace, while they neglect the affirmative statement, failing to realize that "this very mind is Buddha.

Furthermore, this matter must be seen face-to-face. If one merely continues to discourse on principles, when will there ever be an end? As the ancients said:
"Understanding belongs to the realm of emotion; when emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed. Your letter states that the "original face" is simply one...

You always misunderstand the method of practice. It is not like that. To perform this work in such a manner is by no means easy;
even those of immeasurable capacity cannot manage it, so how could a mere practitioner find it easy? Suppose, for instance, that birth and death were to arrive this very instant;
at once, the mind and consciousness would grow dark and obscured, and the suffering would be immeasurable. What you have perceived during ordinary times would then become utterly empty and hollow.
As for these principles, will they ultimately prove useful? I dare say they certainly will not.
Therefore, please cast aside entirely all these things seen with the eyes and heard with the ears, as well as the principles you have mastered from books.
Continue eating and resting as before; continue rising and sitting as before; continue reading and working as before. Only—
Throughout the two periods of six hours each day, do not let go of this thought; constantly bring it forth and examine where there is doubt:
before one's parents were born, where did one establish a dwelling and sustain one's life? When a single breath does not return, where does one go? One cannot help but have doubt; doubt right here.
For example, a monk asked Zhaozhou: "Does a dog have the Buddha-nature? or "Does a dog not have the Buddha-nature? [Zhaozhou said: "Wu. (No. It is precisely at this point that one must doubt.
"Is there Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, "No. Is there a principle here? Is there a point to be understood?
If you have no place to apply yourself, then apply yourself right here. Meditate by day and meditate by night; what, after all, is this principle?
You must strive to see through the old man Zhaozhou’s standing ground, only then will you reach resolution. Part One.

When practicing the mind, the greatest taboo is being unwilling to doubt the critical phrase (*yánjù*). The ancients said that having no doubt regarding the critical phrase is a warning of a grave illness.
The "Mu" (No) koan is the very marrow of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Once this doubt is shattered, the work of study is complete.
The reason why the Bear-Hearted One and the Prime Minister were identical to the Sages was their *xin* (mind). The reason why ordinary people differ is their *qing* (sentimental passions).
This mind is pervasive and pure, admitting nothing else within it; it fills the world and pervades space like ten suns shining simultaneously, manifest and majestic before one’s eyes.
Facing a precious mirror, one’s eyebrows and eyes appear distinct and clear. Though they are distinct and clear, if one seeks their essential substance, it is utterly unobtainable.

Yet, though unobtainable, the great function manifests before one: every movement of turning and bowing, every act of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is individually and naturally authentic, without a moment’s rest or cessation.
To realize and enter this directly is called attaining the Way. At the moment of attainment, one is not a saint.
Before realization is attained, one is not yet an ordinary person; yet it is precisely these ordinary people who pass the truth by right before their faces.

Within, they perceive a mind; without, they perceive objects. Day and night they are in turmoil, creating karma according to their emotions. When one investigates the root and traces the source, there is truly no foundation.

If one is a high-minded gentleman who has realized the Mind, he wields the Vajra King’s precious sword; wherever he encounters [delusion], he cuts it off immediately—this is not a matter of suppression.
Suppress discursive thoughts and eliminate sounds and forms. At all times and in all matters, let nothing interfere with this.
It is simply that when things arise, one is not deluded; when things pass away, one does not retain them. As the ancients said:

"Not allowing even a single hair’s breadth of internal thought to arise, and not allowing even a single hair’s breadth of external objects to enter. This is not a matter of forced effort; it is because the internal mind has never existed from the very beginning.
A single hair arises; from the beginning, external objects have never entered even by a hair’s breadth.

"To see one's nature and study the Way is difficult. Throughout an entire lifetime of cultivation, those who succeed are as few as hairs; those who see their nature are as rare as horns. As for those studying today...

Sentient beings. All dharmas fundamentally do not arise. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The continuous succession of birth and death among sentient beings is entirely due to their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature.
By employing various deluded thoughts, and because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic wandering.
What is called the "eternally abiding true mind" is precisely one's original face. What is called "deluded thought" refers to you— [the text continues].
In the midst of daily life, thoughts of good and evil arise and cease without ceasing; this is precisely it. During the day these are discursive thoughts; at night they are dreams.
Unceasing day and night, they are the very root of the cycle of birth and death. If you were to realize the eternally abiding true mind, none of this would exist.
As soon as you fail to be aware, delusive thoughts arise; thus it shall continue for all kalpas until the end of the future.

There is an end to this. Now, one must seek to transcend birth and death. The foremost requirement is to recognize one’s own true mind, as clearly as seeing the palm of one’s hand when reaching out, or as identifying one’s own parents amidst a vast and crowded multitude; once this is done, there is no further question of whether it is so or not.
Having been able to recognize the mind, one naturally understands how to provide for oneself. What is meant by "providing for oneself" is, first of all:
In all activities and movements, accord with your own mind moment by moment; do not give rise to conceptual branches.
As days pass and years deepen, the "water buffalo" will naturally become proficient. Formerly, Chan Master Lan’an asked Baizhang, “I, your disciple, wish to seek the Buddha;
how is this to be done? Baizhang said, “It is very much like riding a buffalo while searching for a buffalo. Lan’an then asked, “After one has recognized it...”

apart from one’s own mind, there is no other Buddha. Layman, you should give rise to faith—faith in the Buddha within your own mind. If a person...

As for the emotional states of sentient beings at this very moment—from where do they arise? Examine them with precision and observe them with clarity, never letting go for even a single thought-moment.

In response to the letter sent by the scholar Han Ershu, I have fully understood your recent diligent practice, which greatly satisfies my humble mind. The Prajñā within a person is like a vajra;
it is absolutely impossible for it to be buried or extinguished. To feel shame, remorse, and repentance is itself the excellent medicine for the afflictions of worldly toil. According to this—

This mountain monk’s intention is this: it would be better to take charge of yourself from this moment on and set out. As the ancient masters said: "In the Buddha-dharma, what complicated matters are there? Practice it, and that is it.
