In response to Han Jixian, the scholar:

From the ordinary person to the sage, nothing exists outside the two characters "cause" and "effect. However, there are cases where the timing of retribution is indefinite, and there are also cases where the timing of retribution is fixed.
For example, if one commits evil in this life, retribution will certainly follow in the next life; yet that retribution must necessarily encounter its appointed time.
If the time has not yet arrived, the retribution has not yet been meted out; one can repent and reform their transgressions, and thus their sins may be extinguished.

However, if the time for retribution has already been fixed, then even a sage would have no means of escape. Therefore, spiritual cultivation is of the utmost importance: one must vigilantly guard the three karmas.

The three karmas pertain to the five precepts. By firmly upholding the five precepts, the three karmas become naturally pure; if the five precepts are not upheld, the path to the human and celestial realms is severed.
These are the Buddha’s sincere words—how could they deceive anyone? Your letter states: "I have not yet performed good deeds; I only know that evil must not be done.
While these words are certainly true, not doing evil is itself good, and not doing good is itself evil. Good and evil...
They proceed together, yet they do not coexist. To know that not doing good is itself evil—how could one merely stop at not doing evil?
Layman, you are a person of spiritual capacity; you should strive to practice according to this, and the fruits of human and celestial realms can certainly be expected.
As for what lies beyond, you must understand that in moments of evil there is no thought of good, and in moments of goodness there is no mind of evil.
Good and evil are like drifting clouds; neither has a place of arising nor of ceasing.

If one can see through to this clearly, one may immediately transform from an ordinary person into a sage right where one stands, never again placing oneself within the positions and phases of tainted causes. Be cautious!
To Layman Yuan Daosheng:

Your resolve for the Way must be earnest and urgent; you must not be complacent. A human life of a hundred years passes in the blink of an eye and becomes empty; it is only that one fails to perceive its suffering.
If one waits until the present moment has passed before seeking transcendence, there will never be a day of completion.
I often see those who are clever and quick-witted fall prey to this ailment; they waste an entire lifetime, sighing in vain at old age and death—how lamentable!
Layman, you are serene and tranquil, possessing a great capacity for approaching the Way; you shall surely not fall behind others. Yet, alas, what can be done about this old woman of the mountains?
What is the cause of your earnest concern? It has been over a year since we last parted at Kuangshan. I have written these few words as a means of mutual encouragement;
please take them to heart.
To Huang Mengyong, the scholar.
Your Reverence has long planted roots of goodness; thus, while dwelling amidst wealth, honor, and peace, you have not been buried by that wealth, honor, and peace.
You are truly a man of wisdom. As for the wise, even when they enjoy the pleasures of the various heavens, they know them to be impermanent;
how much more so the fleeting moments of the human realm? A sutra says: "The three realms offer no peace; they are like a house on fire. This refers to the heavens as well.
Humanity is, in its entirety, not the ultimate destination. Consider this for a moment: the six realms of existence are currently vast and boundless, with no place of final rest.
Within the drunken dream of birth and death, one remains unawakened throughout kalpas of exhaustion. From what source does this fault arise?
If you can discern the pain and itch here, only then will there be a point at which to apply yourself to practice; only then will there be room for discourse. Since this is not the case...
Awakening: When the mind refuses to let go, that itself is the practice. If you have a doubt, simply continue to doubt it.
Whether eating, resting, or rising from your seat, do not abandon it. The more you sever all communication with it, the more you press upon it.

Press until the path of the mind is entirely cut off, so that there is only this single doubt standing vividly before you, such that you cannot bear it. When you reach such a state, by no means give rise to heterodox thoughts.

To harbor thoughts such as "may there be swift efficacy" or "I await awakening" is, on the contrary, an obstacle; the ancients condemned these as the "thieving mind. In Zen practice, one must die to the thieving mind.
Only after the thieving mind has died can one have a sudden flash of realization (*pí dì*), and only then can one rejoice that one's life has finally reached fulfillment.

As the former sages said: "When investigating the profound and reaching the ultimate subtlety, take awakening as the standard. These words encompass it all. However, for a beginner practicing the Way...
This is truly difficult. There is no path forward, yet one loses their former dwelling; it is indeed a state where one cannot plant one's feet.

Unless one possesses a person of great capacity, there is none who does not fall back and regress. Moreover, the time since the Sage passed away is remote, and the power of Māra is strong while the Dharma is weak.

Those who have even a slight understanding of the direction of this gate, yet take the performance of merit and the practice of goodness as the ultimate goal, do not at all believe in seeing [the Truth] upon taking their stand.
This is the principle of attaining the Way through one's nature. Upon hearing that "mind is itself Buddha," those who can refrain from shaking their heads are truly rare.
Layman, your wisdom surpasses that of others; you should strive for it yourself. The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift;
do not merely treat this as a single phrase and recite it over and over in that manner.
I show that those who study the Way must value sincerity and urgency; for not even a single moment may be allowed to pass. For since beginningless kalpas, we have been deluded and unaware;
now that we have suddenly come to know shame, we are already thirty or forty years old. If we continue to be negligent, there will be even more...
A hundred years is but a mere instant. Since ancient times, those who have studied the Way have appeared as if they were simpletons or inert beings;

yet the deeper their realization of the Way became, the more pure their cultivation grew. Thus, they were able to overcome the power of karma through the power of the Way. But how could the power of karma possess any inherent essence?
Relying solely on the power of the Way to turn and transform oneself—this transformation truly depends upon the person.
Since a practitioner of the Way is already firm and patient in their orientation toward the Way, they should simply exert effort in its practice. One must know that all dharmas arise from the mind.
Past objects have already departed; future objects have not yet arrived; present objects do not abide. None of them can be apprehended. Why?
This is because one sees that they are utterly unattainable. To speak of what is right before one's eyes: at times, the world is filled with blue and yellow;

if you do not direct your attention toward them, you see as if you do not see. If you direct your attention toward them, then everything becomes vividly clear. Such is the presence or absence of phenomena.
They manifest from my own mind; no external objects can be found. An ancient master said: "All phenomena arise from the mind.
If the mind does not arise, phenomena have no basis to abide. This is the speech of the Supreme Person; it is not something that outsiders can hear.
Shishi Wengzong himself relates an ancient story:
once, when Caoshan was taking his leave of Dongshan, Dongshan asked, "Where are you going? Caoshan replied, "I am going to the place where there is no change.
Dongshan said, "In a place of no change, how can there be going? Caoshan said, "Even going does not change. Thus spoke the ancients.
The point of awakening is indeed certain; naturally, all leaks are cut off. May you personally realize this without neglect.

Those who study the Way must value knowing the right time. At all times, one must never let it slip away. It is like a person who always lives at home and need not worry that household affairs will not be managed.
Everyone possesses this one matter, spanning from antiquity to the present, whether there is a Buddha or not. The Dharma...

It is just so: delusion is not lost, and awakening is not attained. It is merely through the distinction between defilement and purity that the holy and the ordinary are made to appear vastly different.
The pure functioning of the sages is serene and uniquely liberated; the defiled functioning of ordinary beings leads to saṃsāra for long kalpas.
Therefore, one must rely entirely upon daily life, so that the illumination of wisdom may be penetratingly clear, washing away the seeds of habitual tendencies accumulated over immeasurable kalpas.
This means that the power of the Path surpasses the power of karma; there is a great transformation. Furthermore, the true mind is fundamentally pure and is not newly acquired.

The substance of deluded thought is empty; though defiled, it is not truly defiled. If one simply rests in this state, one will fall into the error of those who negate cause and effect by dismissing all phenomena.
Therefore, although it is defiled, it is not truly defiled, and thus it can turn defilement into purity. This purity is not newly acquired, yet it is not hindered [by the process].
Returning to purity and removing defilement—sages attain this skillful means and thereby achieve liberation; ordinary people lose this skillful means and thereby sink into the cycle of existence.
Transformation depends upon the person; there is no real dharma in either the sage or the ordinary person.
He showed the two young girls in the room of the layman Vimalakīrti. Among them was a goddess, twelve years of age, whose eloquence and wisdom were peerless and exquisite beyond compare.
The Venerable Śāriputra asked her, "Why do you not transform this female body? The goddess replied: "I—"
"For twelve years now, I have sought the marks of a woman, yet they are utterly unobtainable. What, then, is there to transform?
Furthermore, Master Guankui visited the nun Moshan and asked, "What is the master of Moshan? Moshan replied, "Neither male nor female. Guankui shouted, "Why do you not transform?
Moshan said, "I am neither a spirit nor a ghost; what would I transform into? Guankui then—
After prostrating, the Mountain Monk now asks you all: that which is neither male nor female—what is it?
He further says: "It is not a god, it is not a ghost; into what could it transform? Observe how steady and composed she is. The goddess said:
"For twelve years I have sought the marks of a woman, yet they are utterly unfindable. How then could there be anything to transform? Thus, [she is] the Buddhas of the three periods...
This is the Dharma-seal. Be careful not to miss it; the conduct of the great masters of the past has mostly emerged from this.
You have spent twelve years seeking the characteristics of a woman, yet not a single word can be found. Once you have seen through this thoroughly, [you will realize the truth].
Thus, one does not perceive the marks of the mundane or the supramundane. Internally, one does not perceive the existence of body or mind;

externally, one does not perceive the existence of the vessel-world (the physical universe). Above, one does not perceive the existence of sages; below, one does not perceive the existence of ordinary beings.
Even now, there is no birth-and-death to be seen, and ultimately, there is no nirvana to be seen. It was thus before King Vīkūṇin; it is thus even now. It is all-pervasive.
In future kalpas it shall be thus: not a single dharma can be attained, nor is there anything that cannot be attained.
Reaching this state, one returns with the mind empty and having passed the imperial examination. I write this to encourage you, and present two verses as well:

Neither male nor female, the true family style is revealed; how could gods or ghosts ever hope to resemble it? Last night the people of the eastern village sang a song; this morning the monk strikes the drum.
The five-watch bell: for twelve years it has been unattainable. Who is this one who walks, stands, sits, and lies down?
Desiring to hide it, it is ever more revealed, difficult to conceal. It is left as a guiding point for the monastic community.
Answering Han Youlong regarding matters of the literary lineage:
Only those of the highest capacity can directly take it up; for those of middling or inferior faculties, there is no way to penetrate.

No doors or windows are opened, and no paths are established; it is presented in its entirety face-to-face. One must realize it personally and attain it for oneself, with nothing more to be done—neither "how" nor "what. This is the ultimate.
To speak of it in brief: the single phrase "the mind itself is Buddha" exhausts the matter. Yet even this one phrase belongs to the realm of provisional guidance, as there are those who say so.
When one realizes it according to the capacity of the occasion, all breath ceases and all conceptual thought is extinguished; it is merely a silent resonance.
If it is not like this, then it is merely the false recognition of consciousness as the spirit, forcibly assuming the role of a sovereign. Because of that... [text truncated]
Throughout their days, they have never been able to give rise to the mind that seeks liberation from birth and death. Furthermore, their roots of goodness are feeble;

perhaps they study the logical paths of the scriptural teachings and take them to be their own understanding, thereby becoming negligent and failing to believe in awakening. They even go so far as to say that awakening is merely falling into the "second head."
Such instances as these are precisely what is meant by "using the conscious mind to speculate.
Those who uphold the True Dharma in later generations must distinguish between black and white. This is why Gaofeng’s raising of this case has such great significance.
At that time, I truly overturned the news based on this very cause and condition; thereafter, all points of confusion were thoroughly scrutinized and penetrated, and only then did I come to know.
The path of intellectual understanding (*jie*) and the gate of awakening (*wu*) appear superficially similar, yet in reality they are as far apart as clouds and mud.
Even Gaofeng merely distinguished between the paths of understanding and awakening, pointing directly to them so as to become a loyal minister to Mazu.

If one examines his *nian* (picking up) and *ti* (holding up), the meaning becomes naturally clear. As for ordinary people, they merely say that there is no Buddha outside the mind and no mind outside the Buddha.
"Mind. Is this not indeed an understanding? What is the Buddha? "Bamboo shoots emerge askew, pressed down by rocks; flowers grow upside down, suspended from a cliff.
One must also be such a person before one can attain it.
Regarding the practice of the Way with Senior Secretary Kim Jeong-hee, it simply requires finding the gate. If you find the gate, you will arrive whether you proceed swiftly or slowly;

if you lose the gate, you will not arrive regardless of whether you proceed swiftly or slowly. To speak with precision, it simply requires personally reaching the ground of non-doubt; there is no need for anything else.
I ask people: "It is thus when born; it is thus when dead; it is thus throughout all future kalpas.
If there is even the slightest trace of doubt here, it becomes a silver mountain and an iron wall, and you will immediately be subject to another's judgment.

If you further devise other schemes—studying the *yulu* (recorded sayings), investigating the teachings of the *śāstras*, or seeking [answers] from the mouths of masters—it will only cause the mind to become increasingly distracted.
It is like hemp remaining there. This is precisely what the Great Master Yuanwu meant when he said:

"How can you listen to the various teachers of all quarters, each saying one thing and another? If you instead force yourself into a state of blind ignorance and stubbornly assume the role of master, [you will fail].
In the end, there will come a time of exhaustion. Long ago, I, this mountain monk, told you, Layman, that conditioned mental dharmas must not be relied upon;
as days and years pass, they yield no benefit at all. You yourself have said, "These words are indeed true.

That being so, how could one who has long possessed wisdom wait for my redundant words? Observing the precepts and performing repentance rites are auxiliary causes for entering the Way; they lead to awakening.

One's own mind is the ultimate standard. Having heard that you, Layman, have thoroughly studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which "directly points to the human mind and reveals its nature so as to achieve Buddhahood," there is nothing that surpasses this scripture.
It is only when one personally consents to it that one will truly encounter it for oneself.
The literary scholars of Liang’s Weyang Palace were like fish that swallow boats; they were certain to fall into the hands of the fisherman.

Yet the fisherman did not dare strike immediately because the sea was vast and the waters deep, and the fish possessed great strength. He waited until the turbulence had somewhat subsided and their strength was exhausted and their spirits weary.
The fisherman obtained it by chance. Nearby there is a great-hearted ordinary person whose roots of goodness have been deeply planted and who is capable of continuing the lineage of the Buddhas;
yet, as a spiritual friend, I have not dared to urge him too hastily. The winds of sensory objects surge violently, the ocean of the five desires is deep, and the power of afflictions is strong;
thus, I shall wait for him for a while. This is what I mean by "I shall not stop until the end. The winds of sensory objects will eventually subside, and the five desires will eventually...

There are times of tranquility, yet even when one’s strength is great, there will inevitably come a time of exhaustion; it is merely a matter of whether that struggle comes sooner or later. The Buddha said that the outgoing breath is difficult to preserve as the incoming breath.
I often observe those who possess a self and wish to wait for the "right" time, yet the time does not wait for them.
Can you, O Wang Chang, remain unmoved by this? Huaśu (Huashou) is the place where we find our ultimate refuge. Pay heed a thousandfold to the True Vehicle (Saddharma). Recently, there has been...

Regarding the entry point: knowing what [the interlocutor] delights in hearing. This spring, I met Master Dong at Jiangzhou; while conversing about the ancestral Chan on the boat, I could not fully express it by word of mouth.
I have recorded this for the scholar Dengxian.

To cultivate merit without cultivating the Way was rebuked by the Patriarchs as the conduct of a deluded person; to practice generosity with an evil mind is pointed out in the sutras as the work of Māra.
Viewed from this perspective, there is nothing that compares to the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for the foremost merit.

If one does not recognize the Mind, the seeds of greed, hatred, and ignorance will certainly not be extinguished; even if one possesses heavenly merit, one will rise only to sink again, like being bound.
It is useless for a bird to fly high from its feet. Thus, for those who study the Way, cultivating merit is not as good as seeing one's nature.
If one can see one's nature, merit becomes inexhaustible. This teaching of this mountain monk values only walking the direct path of the Five Houses; it shall never be abandoned.
You should grant me your understanding.
To Layman Weng Shengwen:
The Buddha-nature of true suchness is eternally perfect and luminous. It was thus before one’s parents were born; it is thus now;
and it will be thus throughout the bounds of the future. Originally there is not a single thing. Since there is not a single thing, what can be called?
This is the original state. Within it, there is a point of insight that requires the least expenditure of mental effort. At all times, one does not overstep one's bounds.
As soon as a divergent thought arises, one must forcefully sever it oneself. This expedient is called concentration and wisdom, yet it is not a substantial reality.
If one discusses this mind, it is by nature originally settled and inherently wise. Huangbo said: "This mind is constantly round, luminous, and all-pervading.

People of the world do not recognize this; they merely take seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to be the mind. If one empties out seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, then the path of the mind is cut off. He further said:
"If you wish to recognize the mind, it is not separate from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. However, the original mind..."

It does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. Reaching this essential point, one must truly examine oneself; it does not reside in words and speech. Excessive talk distances one further from the Way.
When you have realized it through introspection, you will know the timing yourself; there is no need to ask others. All deluded thoughts and emotional attachments will naturally dissolve and vanish.
This is the verification of studying the Way: a thousand instances of emptiness are not equal to one instance of reality. If not...
It is thus. No matter how much you exert your mind or seek spiritual efficacy day after day, it all belongs to the impermanent and ultimately returns to arising and ceasing.
The Patriarch said: "If you wish to practice in order to seek Buddhahood, you do not know where to look for the truth.

If you can see the truth within your own mind, that very truth is the cause for attaining Buddhahood. Not seeing your own nature and seeking the Buddha elsewhere is to give rise to [deluded] thoughts."
In short, you are all great fools. I pray you reflect upon this deeply and do not neglect it. Since my departure last year, the mountain monk has encountered many perils.
Master Bi did not rise [from his illness], and my heart grew even more desolate. I was glad that Xi Li arrived at the mountain, yet he had already become a butcher with a broad forehead.
A great man should indeed act thus. As for the words and sounds, let them remain as they are; you should likewise not slight the heart of your ancestors.
My sons have already returned first; I send this brief message for now. Be well.
The *Lanju Gongwenxuejing* states:
"In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding.

Thus understanding the events of the three periods of time, one transcends all expedient means and accomplishes the ten powers. Now, this single thought-moment does not arise from the past limit (*pūrvānta*), nor does it abide in the middle.
Abiding at the limit, it does not cease at the subsequent limit; it encompasses past and present, pervades day and night, cuts off coming and going, and has no boundaries or manifestations.
It is without movement or agitation; one cannot find it by seeking, nor can one avoid it by fleeing. To know where one returns directly is for the whole body to manifest before one;

to be unaware of this very place is for a thousand phenomena to cause confusion. At the critical juncture between the ordinary and the sage, truly nothing transcends this. Yet, even this is still merely a verbal explanation.
To speak of principle is already to wound one’s lips. If we discuss our own school, everything is completely cut off—like a silver mountain or an iron wall—naturally severing all leaks.
Even the "view of Buddha" or the "view of dharmas" does not arise for us; how much less could the defilements of worldly toil and affliction ever arise?
Long ago, there was a Mara who followed the Bodhisattva Vajrasama for a thousand years, seeking to find him... [arising].
It cannot be found even within the stages of practice. Nanquan still regarded this as belonging to the stage of progressive cultivation;
thus we know that the matters of the ancestral tradition are not something that those of coarse minds or shallow understanding can fathom.
To reach such a state, simply look at when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No. If you can see through this word "no," I dare guarantee—

The great matter is now concluded. Regarding the previous karmic conditions concerning the wind and the banner, I fear they may involve the path of conceptual meaning; therefore, it is better to return to the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan as the wondrous.
This is in response to Layman Jiao Wengzi.

Delusion persists through kalpas of hearing the sutras, yet awakening occurs in a single kṣaṇa. The first Buddha, King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja), was not early; the last Buddha, Louzhi (Lokajyotir-dhvaja), was not late.
It depends solely upon whether the person’s own capacity for discernment is mature or raw; it is simply a matter of how well one accords with [the truth] or not.
If one truly perceives the source and root thoroughly, one’s conduct will be steady and profound; dwelling in the world as if without a body, one remains in the world as if...
There is no world. Not falling into the trap of seeing and hearing, and not following the shifting flow of deluded thoughts, one can exercise mastery amidst the sensory dusts.
Although one may emerge from or submerge in the sea of birth and death, one does not perceive that birth and death exist as something attainable.
My son, examine yourself: are you able to do so? If you are, then whether you wear black robes or white robes is of no consequence. If this is not yet the case, what is the use of mere exertion?
Furthermore, as for those whose resolve is set upon benevolence, this is beyond what a mountain monk can know.

When a scholar such as Guan Qigao or an ordinary person gives rise to the aspiration [for enlightenment], there are always causes and conditions involved. Only when these causes and conditions are fully complete can success be achieved. As the Treatise says: "For example..."
Fire exists within wood; yet if no one drills and rubs it, the fire will never be obtained. Nirvāṇa has three causes:

namely, the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*), the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), and the revealing cause (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*). Fire is a metaphor for the direct cause, which is the Buddha-nature present in all sentient beings.

Drilling and rubbing is a metaphor for the contributory cause, which refers to the inspiration provided by virtuous teachers and good friends. When the fire emerges and the wood is consumed, this is a metaphor for the revealing cause. The "wood" is [the metaphor for] affliction.
This refers to the affliction of birth and death. All sentient beings, if not stirred by a virtuous friend, possess the Buddha-nature even so;

yet, being shrouded and obscured by afflictions, it cannot manifest before them. How then could they attain liberation? Therefore, those who seek liberation must truly rely upon causes and conditions.
The mind of the Patriarch is the friend who stirs you from beneath your feet; you should have deep faith in this.

The Lay Practitioner Lin Deshan, Vice-Commissioner of the Ministry of Justice, possesses the root-capacity for the Chan school; however, his wisdom is abundant while his meditative concentration is scarce. Hearing daily that you are unwell, I urge you all the more to gather your mind through dhyāna-concentration.
For now, set aside the question of whether one has attained awakening or not; simply focus on the present moment and do not seek cultivation elsewhere apart from what is directly before you.

Practice. Yongming said: "For one who studies the Way, there is nothing particularly extraordinary; it simply requires that in the daily activities of the six sense faculties, one eliminates emotional thoughts and severs delusive conditions.
When confronted by the five desires and the eight winds, if the mind neither grasps nor rejects and remains as firm as a block of stone, only then does one have the capacity to study the Way.
A lay practitioner dreamed of the Great Being Vajrapāṇi, who said: "It only requires that you maintain mastery over yourself. Right...
This is the intended meaning. I hope you will rely upon the power of the mind as your foundation, rather than placing your hopes in the power of medicine.
Furthermore, I am greatly comforted to hear that your health is clear and at ease; you should redouble your diligent effort. But how is this diligent effort to be practiced? Is it not indeed so?

Knitting the brows and staring with bulging eyes, straightening the spine—is this diligence? Prostrating and reciting mantras during the six periods of the day, burning incense and scattering flowers—is this diligence?
Have you not heard it said: "If one gives rise to a mind of diligence, it is delusion, not diligence;
if one can remain without the mind arising, diligence is boundless. Layman, examine closely these three characters: "mind does not arise. Linji said:
What has already arisen should not be continued; what has not yet arisen should not be sought, lest it arise. This is superior to ten years of traveling on pilgrimage. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The mind does not falsely grasp at past phenomena, nor does it crave or cling to future events, nor does it dwell upon the present."
To thoroughly realize that the three periods of time are entirely equal—this is precisely this principle. While you are still strong and healthy, you must quickly seek a definitive resolution.
Constantly keep before you the circumstances of last year’s suffering; only then will you have the momentum to advance.
If you wait until old age has already set in, you will have squandered all the fine moments of the present. I fear that at that later time—
There was no time to act. Take care.
*Changqing Zongbao Duchi Chan Master’s Recorded Sayings*, Volume Five, Phonetic Glossary.

*Shù* (pronounced *shú*; the general name for various beans). *Yē* (pronounced *yàn*; the name for the constriction of the throat). *Zhì* (pronounced *zhì*; to place; synonymous with "to set down" or "to fix").

*Lì* (pronounced *lì*; a whetstone; the *Yanzī* mountain produces *lì*, stones that can be used to sharpen blades). *Kěn* (pronounced *gě*; the edge of the mouth). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chángqìng Zōngbǎo, Volume Six.
Re-edited by the Dharma-grandson of Danxia, the present-day monk Jinshi,
as a correspondence with the Provincial Governor Zimou Fangbo.
Once there was a monk who visited Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Fuchuan. Xuefeng said, "The sea of birth and death has not yet been crossed;
why then did you capsize your boat? The monk was speechless. He subsequently returned to Fuchuan and recounted the previous conversation.
Fuchuan said, "Why did you not say, 'He has no birth and death'? The monk returned to Xuefeng and answered exactly as he had been instructed. Xuefeng—
[The Master] said: "It must be like an overturned boat before it can be attained. The mountain monk said: "He has no birth-and-death; how could there be a second person?
Nowadays, from morning until evening, one's seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are each and every one truly genuine, each and every one luminously wondrous.

As soon as they fall into the faculty of conceptual thought (*manas*), they become a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions. Layman, if you wish to understand easily, it lies simply in the midst of daily activities—do not move the mind.
Roots. To observe with cool detachment is most effective in conserving effort; this is my final exhortation.

In response to Layman Cheng’s scroll concerning Huanglong, you say that people today are not equal to those of antiquity; this is certainly true. However, one must personally achieve a thorough awakening for oneself.
Standing firmly on the ground of reality, whether it be right or wrong, one naturally becomes free from doubt.

If one perceives even the slightest phenomenon as existing apart from the mind, then one has not attained thorough awakening. Therefore, if one perceives a "mind that can believe" and a "dharma that is believed," one has not yet entered the gate of faith.
When one truly reaches the state of no-mind, even the vision of the Buddha and the vision of dharmas do not manifest before one; how much less so the mundane world?

Is it worldly toil and affliction? If we speak of the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) under heaven share one and the same nostril.
However, if we speak of the grades of attainment and the realization through cultivation, there are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions.
As the Sūtra says: "All worthies and sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Have you not heard that Kāśyapa...?
"Did Ānanda not know the samādhi [of the Buddha]? Did Śāṇakavāsin not know the samādhi [of Ānanda]? Did Upagupta not know the samādhi [of Śāṇakavāsin]?
Yangshan said, "Nowadays, one simply needs to clarify the ocean of one's own nature and practice according to reality.
As for matters concerning the sages, do not attempt to force your mind toward them. At some point in the future, you will naturally possess it."

This is how it is. Why not speak clearly and directly? As you have said, when the ancients realized that "mind is Buddha," they were at once fully endowed with the five eyes and six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). But tell me, among all the patriarchs of the past, how many were truly so endowed?
If you consider those without such powers to be non-Buddhists, then there are no few among the externalists and celestial māras who possess them; how can you therefore regard this as heterodox?
The scales of correct judgment naturally fall away from divergent views. Guishan said: "One who has attained knows the timing for themselves;

'cultivating' and 'not cultivating' are dualistic expressions. If there are residual habits from the past that have not yet been suddenly exhausted, one must directly instruct them to purify the flowing consciousness of present karma.
Therefore, those who have awakened naturally understand how to make their living. This refers to the period after awakening.
If habitual tendencies remain as they were, then what is it that has been realized? Regarding your inquiry concerning the skillful means of healing, I say that others cannot apply their effort here;
the intricate details within this matter—I would find it a joy to explain them to you face-to-face.

Island. Relying on such self-centered calculations, though one may crave life and fear death—this being the common sentiment of humanity—how could one know that there are fixed karmic retributions that cannot be escaped?

This is not convenient. As the treatise is vast and extensive, it is difficult to consult regularly. Consequently, I have extracted the essential meanings from within the treatise and compiled them into a single work entitled *The Precious Mirror of the Avataṃsaka*.
As for the "Precious Mirror," it refers to the true wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This wisdom is the substance of all phenomena;
the Dharma-realm is established in dependence upon it, and it is also able to illuminate all phenomena with penetrating clarity. Therefore, it is called a "mirror."

Every single word and phrase within is the luminous mind of the Master of the Treatise; I, Daoxue, have not dared to rely on my own arbitrary views, but have merely recounted what was said without composing anything new.
Preface to the Re-engraved *Daśavidyā-śāstra*:
The Elder Tongxuan composed this *Daśavidyā-śāstra* before he produced the *Avataṃsaka-bhāṣya*; it serves as the key to the *Avataṃsaka-bhāṣya*.
Indeed, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) constitute the ocean of suffering in which all sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death.
This is the ocean of the Dharma-nature of Vairocana. The ocean of suffering of sentient beings and the ocean of Dharma-nature are fundamentally without substantial nature.
A single thought of delusion is the ocean of birth-and-death suffering; a single thought of awakening is the ocean of Dharma-nature. Their essence is non-dual.
It is solely through delusion and awakening that these names arise. Thus it is said: "Dharmas have no fixed characteristics; they are merely transformations of the mind.

The ocean of wisdom of the ancient Buddhas was obscured by ignorance; this rests entirely upon the person themselves. It is manifested through the power of the samādhi of skillful means (*upāya-samādhi*).

What is called the "samādhi of skillful means" is another designation for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Dharma attained by the Tathāgata is [the samādhi]..."

Adorned with the power of wisdom, one uses this to deliver sentient beings and personally achieves the unsurpassed path. To abandon meditative concentration and wisdom while seeking expedient means elsewhere—I know nothing of such a thing.
Now that the time since the Sage departed is distant, people are mostly indolent; they are merely followers of hearsay and oral tradition.
Through habituation, customs become the prevailing wind; following the current, one loses the source. To wander in delusion without returning is truly a matter for deep lamentation.
Therefore, I have re-carved this treatise so that those of like mind may have their eyes opened. Should they thereby return to the root and know the source, it would still be of benefit.

If some were to say, "This is merely the Vehicle of Teaching (Śāsana-yāna); the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) has its own distinct merits," then they would simply be willfully and arrogantly neglecting the Way themselves.

The Direct Explanation of the Heart Sūtra provides a general exposition of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. It is the essential pivot of the extensive *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and the true doctrine for attaining Buddhahood;
nothing surpasses this. As for the term "Heart" (*hṛdaya*), it refers to the wondrously luminous essence of the mind of sentient beings. The mind is itself the Buddha; the Buddha is itself...
Mind. Prajñā is the wisdom of the mind; the mind is the essence (tǐ), while wisdom is its function (yòng).

However, the essence inherently possesses the function of wisdom, which cannot be usurped by external conditions nor bound by sounds and forms; therefore, it is said to have "reached the other shore. Mind is itself the Dharmakāya.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is itself *prajñā*; the other shore (*pāra*) is itself liberation (*vimukti*). These three virtues are inherently possessed within a single mind.
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) being free from delusion is *prajñā*; *prajñā* being unattached is liberation; liberation being quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) is the Dharma-body.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all empty, and thereby delivered all [beings].
This refers precisely to the meaning of "suffering and distress. Regarding the statement that "form is empty": form has no self-nature; its entire substance is emptiness.
Emptiness has no self-nature; its entire substance is form. Since one aggregate (*skandha*) is empty, the other four aggregates are likewise so.

For the five aggregates encompass all phenomena (*dharma*) in the world. Therefore it is said: "The mark of the emptiness of these phenomena. This mark of the emptiness of phenomena is not annihilation.

"Emptiness" refers to the true emptiness of *prajñā*. Within the wisdom of true emptiness, there are no phenomena of arising and ceasing to be found among the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), or the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Nor are there any processes of the forward and reverse flow of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to be found.

There are no truths of suffering, accumulation, cessation, or the path to be found. Furthermore, there is no wisdom of increase or decrease to be attained. As the Sūtra says: "Because there is nothing to be attained."

This is precisely the mark of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*). It is the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:
"When a bodhisattva achieves this patience, even the Buddha-mind, the mind of nirvāṇa, and the bodhicitta do not manifest; how much less so the worldly mind of defilement?

If a person, for even a single thought-moment, accords with the wisdom of the emptiness of prajñā, they are able to extinguish the heavy [karmic obstructions] of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā.

Transcending all offenses, one stands solitary and detached, no longer bound by the conditions of karmic retribution. Remaining far removed from even subtle mental conceptions, mindfulness becomes eternally abiding, and one perceives the Buddha-nature;

this is called Nirvana. It is not only Bodhisattvas who do so, but the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time as well, who likewise rely upon this Prajñā—the wisdom of emptiness—to achieve Unsurpassed, Perfect, and Complete Enlightenment. Therefore, one should know that Prajñā possesses great majesty.

The deity possesses great radiance; most honored and supreme, there is none equal to him. He is the total retention (dhāraṇī) of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, and this is the gateway to the Great Dhāra� Master Páng said:
"The mind relies upon true wisdom, and principle follows the movement of the mind; when principle and wisdom are without obstruction..."
The mind, too, is without birth. In delusion there is a self; in awakening there is no sentience. When one penetrates great wisdom, all phenomena are not established. It is further said:
Relying on emptiness while acting in silence is precisely "practicing deeply. There is not the slightest dharma; whatever meets the eye is simply as it is.
There is no precept to be maintained, and no defilement to be purified. One thoroughly penetrates the empty mind, wherein dharmas have no life-span. If one can act thus, it is perfect penetration.
Ultimate! How rare indeed! Is this not what is meant by the true wisdom of Prajñā?
Regarding the preface to the *Lingbi Run’s Verses on Ancient Cases*:
Lingbi Run was my younger brother. From his childhood, he possessed a resolve to transcend the mundane world. I entered the Way at a young age; [he likewise did so].
Entrusting his aged mother to others, he was free from the anxieties of domestic care; he was truly a man of supreme filial piety and profound sincerity.

When his mother passed away in the year Wuchen (1688), he subsequently shaved his head before her spirit tablet and set out on a pilgrimage. In the year Gengwu (1690), while I was in retreat at Jinlun, my younger brother’s diligent practice became increasingly intense as he vowed to attain wondrous enlightenment.
One day, while conversing with two or three companions about the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner, he suddenly attained a breakthrough.

I had a realization. From then on, day and night, I pored over the recorded sayings and kōans of the ancient worthies; I delved deeply into their profound mysteries. Although they were extremely chaotic and confusing, I was able to penetrate through them all.
In the year Guiyou, I moved to Huangyan, where I served as an attendant to Guanzhong. During the spring rains, the dampness caused both I and my younger brother to fall gravely ill.
We subsequently went to Huiyang to seek medical treatment, but by then my brother was already beyond recovery. At the moment of his passing—
At the moment of death, he was serene and utterly detached. A fellow student asked him, "Can you still maintain mastery now? He replied, "I am simply suffering from physical pain.
When the student questioned him again as before, he gave the same answer as before. He then sat upright and passed away. [The student] searched through his bag.
There are only thirty-nine verses of ancient precedents (*gū*). These were composed by me in my own hand during moments of inspiration in my ordinary life, yet no one recognized them.

Observing the points where they penetrate the ultimate upward direction, it is clear they truly flow from the depths of my own breast. It is a pity that I was limited by my years and failed to repay the kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
My younger brother is grave, quiet, and speaks little; he does not reveal what he has attained, so people encounter him as if he were lacking wisdom. I [wrote this] in the year Wuyin.
Upon crossing the ridge, he showed it to the Head Seat, Li Zhong. Li Zhong regarded it as something quite ordinary; when questioned about it, however, Li Zhong had already seen it at Huangyan.
Furthermore, they were as compatible as water and milk, and it was commonly heard that he styled himself after Guyuan Puhua.
Alas! In the coming age of the Dharma’s decline, how could a person like my brother be found so easily? Moreover, reflecting upon the monastics, there are those among them who...

Those who were truly able to devote themselves to this path, yet whose secret accord and hidden realization remained unmanifest during their lifetimes—failing to achieve longevity or transcend the world, so that they were eventually submerged and left without renown—must have been numerous indeed. Thus, I have composed this preface to transmit them.
Biographical Account of the Venerable Monk Changqing, composed by his Dharma heir, Huanxi. The Master’s name was Daodu;
his style name was Zongbao, and his alternative name was Kongyin. He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Wuyi of Boshan. South.
He was the son of the Hai-lu family. When he was three years old, his mother took him up to a tower where they saw a spider weaving its web;

he stared at it for a long time with wide-open eyes, and a mixture of sorrow and joy welled up within him. Later, he once said to others, "In my recollections of the past forty or fifty years, not even a hair's breadth has been added."
I know from this that the Master possessed roots of virtue from his past lives. At the age of six, he lost his father and lived with his mother near a temple.

He would hasten there at dawn to pay homage to the Buddha; looking up at the image, time would pass until noon. Upon hearing the sound of the *brahman* chants, he could recite them from memory as soon as they passed his ears.

Having heard from an elderly monk the teaching that "realizing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood," his longing for it grew even more intense. Whenever he encountered someone, he would ask about it; though many people mocked him, he showed no sign of discouragement. He obtained the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch...

He was illiterate, yet he cherished the sutra within the folds of his robe. He prostrated himself earnestly before the Great Being (Mahāsattva). One night, while bowing, he became so exhausted that he fell to the ground.
Suddenly, he felt as though he had risen and was floating in mid-air; sweat drenched his back, and he felt lighter and more agile than usual. He lit a lamp, took out the sutra, and read it.

When he thought of a certain character, he asked others about it and found it was indeed correct. Consequently, he could recite several lines at once. From then on, he finally took leave of his mother and entered [the monastic life].

At the temple, he relied on the dharma of detachment from thought, sitting every day until dawn. At the age of fourteen, while practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) beneath a tree, his chest suddenly felt as if it were being split like a bamboo stalk.
Spontaneously, he composed a verse, saying: "The essence of perfect luminosity is steadfast; The world of things and self is carefree. This is the path of non-arising;
Yet within non-arising, one must further transcend. He spoke again: "In the state where neither good nor evil is contemplated, there is likewise nothing to be pursued. Rest!"
He said, "This is the Way; this Way is non-arising. When he read the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) to the passage, "The bamboo shoots emerge askew, pressed down by rocks;
the flowers grow upside down, suspended from a cliff," it again obstructed his mind. While walking in the mountains one day, he looked up and saw the mountain flowers in full bloom;

only then was he suddenly enlightened, as if ice were melting away. That year the Master was only sixteen years old. Finding no monk with whom he could take refuge to his satisfaction, he took a knife and went to a rock slab himself.
Shi Li bowed to the Buddhas of the ten directions and shaved his head. He bound himself with thatch and returned to Longshan Mountain, where he lived alone for over ten years.

He served his mother with the utmost filial piety; when she fell ill and required mountain spring water, he would carry it on his shoulders for twenty li every day, his palm prints only becoming visible upon reaching the city gates.
His mother passed away, and he lived in a hut at her grave for three months. At the age of twenty-nine, he entered Boshan. Previously, someone had brought a biography of the Master’s life to Boshan;
the Mountain Master (Yunqi Zhuhong) marveled at it and, whenever he saw a monk from Guangdong, would invariably ask, "Why has Zongbao not come?"
"Can this Way not reach Mount Bo? When he heard that the Master had arrived, he immediately summoned him into the abbot’s quarters and conversed with him throughout the night.
One day, regarding the saying, "Riding a cow backward into the Buddha hall," he commanded the assembly to offer their responses.

The Master presented a verse, saying: "In my haste for the journey, I did not realize it was dawn; The more I sought, the further away it became. Meeting him is precisely him himself; Just as I am, I am still intoxicated."

[The Master] turned [the millstone]. "An ant drags a great millstone; the stone man claps his hands and laughs. This is a distinct, living mechanism that does not fall into the scales of *gong* and *shang*.
As the entire assembly looked on in wonder, Yaoshan said, "How crude! The Master said, "A person of such great capacity—how could one open one's mouth before a true spiritual friend?
Yaoshan looked at him with a smile for a long while and said, "What need is there to say more? The Master prostrated himself, and only then did Yaoshan grant him [the Dharma].

He changed his name and received full ordination. He stayed for one month and then departed after nine months had passed. The Master of the Mountain would not permit him to leave. The Teacher’s resolve to remain on the mountain was firm;

though he entreated to depart two or three times, the Master of the Mountain finally agreed that he should return again in the eighth month. The Teacher knelt before the Master’s bed and said, “I have done wrong;
I pray you, Preceptor, do not let me off. The Master of the Mountain replied repeatedly, “It is so, it is so. You must not fail [your practice] at another time.”
The monk Fushan. This was the fourth month of the Gengwu year of the Chongzhen era. The Master passed away on the ninth month of that same year;
only then did [the author] realize the meaning of the words regarding his second visit in the eighth month.

At that time, the Master was in seclusion at Jilun, and later moved to Huangyan, where he was highly esteemed by such figures as Jin Neihan Zhengxi, Chen Duxue Yunyi, and General Xiong Xin-kai. He once visited...
Shi Wen Dao requested that the Master preach the Dharma, but the Master remained focused on the seclusion of mountain crags, having no aspiration for worldly emergence.

Upon the passing of Master Xue of Ying Shan, the literati Zhang Bie and Li Meizhou consulted with Minister He Zonggang of Xianggang and Grand Secretary Chen Qiutao, who earnestly entreated the Master to reside at Luofu Mountain and open the Dharma gate of Boshan.
As for the Way and Dharma of Boshan— [The text continues: ...it was not... (the passage ends here).

It was as if a thread had been severed; it was only thanks to the Master that he was able to revive it. Yet the Master withdrew from public life as if unable to bear the burden, his air of genuine simplicity causing him to abandon all worldly habits.

His compassionate vows permeated those around him without distinction; from men of integrity and literary talent down to merchants and commoners, there were none who did not become intoxicated by his spirit, all wishing to enter his discipleship. When the people of Min heard of his reputation, they [referred to him] as Yangu...
The Master of Xiaocha sent word to the Teacher; the Teacher also joyfully set sail across the ocean to meet him. Upon his arrival, however, Yanhu had been reduced to ashes by bandits.
The Teacher took up residence at Nantai, where he met Gong Kezhi, Fang Kongshuo, and Lin Yishan; upon seeing them, their minds were immediately won over.

Together with the various elders of the entire prefecture, they invited him to preside over Xican Monastery. Governor Tong renovated it for him, and at that time, his reputation for the Way spread everywhere;
his quarters were constantly filled with visitors. The Master grew somewhat weary of this toil, so he went to sweep the stupa at Boshan and returned to Guangdong on foot.
He arrived at Ji’ān and made plans to retire from public life. Shortly thereafter, the gentry of Huìyáng invited him to preach the Dharma by Fēng Hú.

Furthermore, the officials and subjects of Gǎngzhōu looked up to him with admiration; wherever his banner was raised, it soon became a precious monastery (bǎofāng). The Master sighed with emotion and said:

He intended to cease his worldly activities and rest, yet instead brought about exhaustion. In the second month of the seventeenth year of the Shunzhi era, he suddenly manifested symptoms of a skin ailment;
nevertheless, he continued to receive visitors without fail every day. In the fourth month of the following year, returning from Haitang to Ji’an, he finally declined all requests for instruction.
On the first watch of the night of the seventh day of the seventh month, [the Emperor] issued an edict to Huan Shi, saying: "My chronic ailment has persisted for a long time;

it is truly loathsome. I shall soon cast aside my arms [and depart]. Shi wept and pleaded earnestly, saying: "I beg the Master to remain in this world; the myriad living beings are worthy of compassion. The Master said:
"My Way has you; the heavy burden may now be laid down. What more is there to cling to? On the morning of the twenty-second day, he ate porridge and chewed wood as usual.
When an attendant requested that medicine be applied, the Master suddenly said, "Today, no medicine shall be applied.

Looking around at his attendants, he closed his eyes for a long while and passed away while sitting upright. He was sixty-two years old; he had completed thirty-three summer retreats. (From the *Chuan*)
His stupa is located on Mount Luofu, south of the West Creek at Huashou Terrace. Throughout his life, the Master maintained himself through the Way and gathered others in through compassion.
He was pure and sincere toward all things and did not seek fame or reputation. Whether their capacity was great or small, shallow or deep, he taught each according to their own reception.

All his instructions were clear and penetrating, designed to enlighten others; whenever he could provide even slight benefit, joy would surely appear upon his countenance. Those who requested verses or hymns [were granted them].

He dictated the record as it came to him; when others wished to change certain characters or phrases, he would smile and comply. Someone stepped forward and said, "The Dharma is of great importance; how can you, Master, treat it so lightly?

The Master assumed a solemn expression and replied, "The *Platform Sutra* says: 'That good spiritual friend has a great karmic affinity, which is to say, he brings about transformation and deliverance.
The faculties of people—whether sharp or dull—cannot be made uniform. One need only possess utmost sincerity; how could one possibly fail [to benefit]?"

[The Master] replied, "It is so. As for the Great Dharma of our School, it is difficult for those of middling or inferior capacity to perceive. An old monk like me possesses his own standard of judgment;

how could it be known by such as you? Thus, during more than twenty years of my teaching, from the time I first received the mallet and whisk and was granted the seal of transmission, I have never bestowed it indiscriminately upon anyone other than Huanshi and Huanke.
Since I began to manifest illness over a year ago, in every daily activity, whether great or small, minute or subtle..."
There was nothing left out; yet, when he addressed the assembly at the time of his passing to entrust various matters, he remained entirely silent.

For thirty years, Master Bozan maintained a rigorous and meticulous lineage tradition, and this master truly had no cause for shame. On the day he entered *parinirvāṇa*, both internal and external disciples mourned for an entire month;
like the single assembly at the Great Enlightenment (Dajue) or the Twin Trees (Shuanglin), their lamentation shook the Brahma Heaven, and they shared in the same sorrowful yearning. Its...

The compassionate light enters all things; its reality is beyond the reach of thought or deliberation. If one says that the Dharma is profound and stable—easy to see yet difficult to know—it has been circulated through various records and heard and seen throughout the land; this is not something that I, Hanyi, ought to speak of.

The Chan Master Wúyí of Bóshān had a Dharma heir named the Venerable Chángqìng Kōngyǐn, whose name was Dáodú. Initially...
His courtesy name was Zongbao. He was the son of the Lu family of Nanhai. When he was three years old, his mother took him up to a tower to observe a spider weaving its web;

he stared at it for a long time with unblinking eyes, unable to contain his mixture of sorrow and joy. Later in life, he said of himself: "In the forty or fifty years since then, my memory has not added even a hair’s breadth [to what I knew then].
Such were his innate roots from his youth. At six, he lost his father and lived with his mother near a temple, where he would hasten there every morning to pay his respects.
The Buddha gazed upon him until midday. Upon hearing the old monk’s words that "seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha," he conceived a profound faith as deep as a nail driven into wood.
Having obtained the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*, he held it with reverence and wore it upon his head. He prostrated before the Great Being (Guanyin) to seek instruction in reading;

exhausted, he fell to the ground, whereupon he suddenly felt his body soar into the air and sweat break out from every pore. As he read the sutra by the light of a bright lamp, he vaguely recognized it to be [the work of] a certain [master].
He inquired of others and found it to be indeed so; consequently, he could recite several lines at once. At the age of fourteen, he took leave of his mother to enter a monastery.

While practicing meditative concentration beneath a tree, his mind suddenly felt as if split like a bamboo stalk, and he spontaneously uttered verses that startled the elder monks. This occurred when he was sixteen years old.

He sharpened his blade upon a rock, performed prostrations, and shaved his head. Binding himself with reeds, he returned to Longshan, where he lived alone for over ten years. His mother suffered from thirst;
every morning he carried mountain spring water on his back for twenty li, reaching the city walls only when his palm prints were still visible. At the age of twenty-nine, his mother passed away.
Together with his younger brother Lingbi, he packed his belongings and went to visit Boshan. Upon seeing him, Boshan said, "The Dharma-lineage..."
"Baowang has long awaited your arrival. He then brought up the story of "riding a cow backward into the Buddha hall" to test the assembly;

when none of their responses were in accord, the Master presented this verse: "In my haste, I did not realize it was dawn; The more I sought, the more remote it became. Meeting him now, he is truly he."
"Merely being so is still an inversion. An ant pulling a great millstone—this is a living mechanism of a different sort, beyond the scales of *gong* and *shang*.
Shan Wei-xiao said, 'Too crude. That evening, during the *poṣadha*, he addressed the assembly:
'Do not say there is no one at Boshan; now there is someone who grants permission. He changed his name to Deng, received full ordination (*upasampadā*), and resided there for nine months."

He took his leave and instructed him, saying, "Return in the eighth month; do not fail the old monk. In the ninth month of that year, the Master [Shan] passed away, and it was only then realized that this had been his final entrustment.
The Teacher [Yunqi Zhuhong] remained in seclusion at Jinlun and later moved to Huangyan, intending solely to dwell in the mountains without any thought of entering the world.

He accepted invitations to visit patrons. When people prostrated at his feet upon his arrival, he would spread his hair on the path for them; thus, the bridge he provided for others grew somewhat weary, and he manifested slight signs of illness.

In the fourth month of the year Wuxin (1821), he returned from Hai-chang to Jie-’an. He determined the date of his departure for himself: on the twenty-second day of the seventh month, he sat upright and passed away.
His worldly age was sixty-two, and he had completed thirty-three summer retreats. The Master had two great disciples.

He said, "Tianran is Master Gong. Master Gong’s ancestral heart was that of Master Ke. Because Master Ke suffered persecution for the sake of the Dharma, he passed away while seated at Qianshan in Shenyang.
The Master wept bitterly for him, saying, 'The Way of our school is lost. More than a year later, the Master manifested illness.

Master Tianran entreated him to remain in the world, to which the Master laughed and said, 'As long as you are here, how could I die? Thereupon, Master Tianran enshrined the Master’s entire body in a stupa."
To the south of West Creek at Huashou Terrace on Mount Luofu, [the Master’s] attendant Jinxi submitted a letter of introduction and commissioned me to compose an inscription for his memorial stele.

He traveled over five thousand *li*, braving all hardships, to present gifts and petitions to me. I reflect that our Master possessed superior faculties and sharp wisdom, refined through many lifetimes;
the four characters "seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha" were, for him, like the very core of the *Tathāgatagarbha* and its essential links. "Mind is Buddha"—this was his constant practice.

The fixed barrier is firmly closed; it is neither mind nor Buddha—this is the designation for "severance. Thus, the true command is fully upheld, and the gateway to awakening is pointed out through indirect means.
Regarding the two modes of expression—negation and affirmation—one may compare them to Yongming; regarding the single mind of the Dharma-realm, one may hold up the mirror of Zao Bo.

From the beginning, there has not been a single word that falls into the narrow or a fragment of speech that goes too far. Yet nowadays, people clutch at deluded talismans and harbor counterfeit contracts within their homes;

they peddle the Dharma of the Tathāgata while reviling the Chan of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. As medicine and disease have become entangled, this madness cannot be reversed. To mark this, I present this seal of rectitude.
To stem that surging tide—was this not the divine talisman of Prajñā and the precious sword of the Vajra?
There were two aspects of the Master’s profound mind and secret practice that were unknown to the world. Formerly, Daohui said:

"Though I am beyond the secular world, my heart of loyalty to the sovereign and love for the nation is equal to that of loyal and righteous gentlemen. Hong Juefan discussed Master Deng of Lumen as follows: [text continues].

Whether sowing seeds, wearing robes, or carrying alms bowls, they all return to the Dharma King; this is how they conceal within while manifesting without, providing silent support for the movement of the Dharma.

The ancients possessed clear insight into the Way, treating the relationship between teacher and disciple with great gravity, and they feared fame, profit, and material sustenance as they would frost and hail.
Some say that at the edge of a mattock in the deep mountains, one or two people are being sought out to serve as successors.
Others say that large houses are built to harbor idle men, and that the world they inhabit is adorned for the sake of fools.

The Master often said, "Boshan told me that twenty years after my passing, the ancestral style will have been swept from the ground, and even in the shrines of local deities, people will ascend the dais to give formal sermons."

I never imagined that I would see this in person; these words truly move me to tears. Those who have partaken of the wind of his teaching and savored its flavor are as numerous as clouds, yet those who have personally received his seal of transmission are but two.
People say that the Master was stern, cold, and solitary, and that he did not allow even a single thread of the Bozan lineage to pass through;

how could they know that his compassion for the Dharma-ending age was like saving one’s own head from fire? He strictly guarded the boundaries of his own school while establishing the foundations of other houses.
Is there not one who cannot help but weep and wail with grief? This is precisely how he followed established precedents and guarded the citadel of the Dharma.
Previously, when I visited the collected works of Master Hanshan, I sent a letter to Haitang. The Master rejoiced and praised me;
he donned his robes, burned incense, and struck the *ganḍī* bell to inform the assembly. While ill, he saw my commentary on the *Heart Sūtra*, and the Master [replied]...
Master Shengbian further requested my approval. Since I have been nourished by the milk of the Dharma from Master Shi, I am likewise a disciple among the reeds with my head wrapped in a cloth;
therefore, he has entrusted me with this inscription. How could I dare decline? The inscription says: [The Inscription] says: [Insert the actual verses here]
When the Vairambha winds blow at the end of the kalpa, destroying the world’s beginning, The fires of Mount Kunlun fan a vast furnace.

There is a great bhikṣu who raises the banner of the Dharma; Sitting alone upon a solitary peak in a corner of the sea, The moon of his mind shines universally and the clouds of his body unfurl, Like the dragon of Makara raining down upon the parched and withered.
His emanated bodies coil and twist, scales and manes complete; He raises his head and winds his tail, distinct in north and south.
A great cloud like the void covers Mount Kuanglu; The lightning of wisdom strikes and flashes at Mount Yiwulu.
Immovable in the center, he dwells in eternal peace; Beneath his chin, he naturally guards the maṇi jewel.
A mountain-dweller emaciated by the wilderness, his yellow skin wrapping his bones; monks and laypeople, like fish passing through a net, hasten toward him.
Sun and moon earrings merely entangle their forms; alas for the zhouyu deer amidst the wheels of knives and leaves of swords.
Beneath the tree, the three disputants now turn their chariots back; in the Crane Forest, the transformation to white occurs in but a moment.
Solitary and serene upon a single mat, he binds his legs in the double-lotus posture; With a wave of the hand, he takes a long farewell to the realm of filth and stench.
The Dharma-banner collapses and the Dharma-general departs; Those who entangle themselves with "creeper-vines" to buy their daily bread are all butchers.
As for the birds in the void and the rats—what are they doing here? "The very mind is Buddha"—the seal of the mind stands solitary.
Venerable generals maintain strict vigilance, holding their military tokens; Buddhas and patriarchs bear witness in unison—whom would dare to slander?

Demons and heretics flee in hiding, while the painted pavilions shine like Vairocana’s abode, surrounded by Dharma thrones upon which blue lotuses bloom. I dwell alone upon this solitary peak, remaining as I am.
The two knees following him leave nothing behind; Behold these two colts as they trample like dragon-elephants.
With a single incense offering, I turn toward his grace, not failing it; I compose this inscription with three sighs of admiration.
Such is the家风 (family style) of Boshan, which does not exist in this world; Blue-green ink and black lead, the old brushwork is sparse.
He went forth to stem the receding waves and establish a model for the world; though the banner-staff may fall, it must be supported by men.
Five hundred years hence, this promise shall not fail.
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zongbao of Changqing*, Volume Six (End).
